Oklahoma Cannabis & Hemp Research — Audited Final Report (Parts 0–12)

Last audited: 30 October 2026 (America/New_York). Original research date: 30 October 2026, both runs. This file contains, in order: (1) the full audit table, (2) everything still unverified with where to confirm it, and (3) the complete corrected rewrite of Parts 0–12. No section from the original was dropped or summarised; only what the audit changed was changed.

Election timing: the 3 November 2026 election had not yet been held on 30 October 2026. No 3 November 2026 result is reported anywhere in this file; 2026 state-question statuses are given as of 30 October 2026 and marked Verify where certification is still pending.

Federal baseline (given, held fixed, not re-audited): split scheduling — under a final rule at 91 FR 22714 (effective 28 April 2026), FDA-approved cannabis products and state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana are in Schedule III; all other marijuana, including all adult-use, remains Schedule I; the broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is NOT final. IRS §280E: Treasury has said rescheduling generally removes 280E as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances (guidance forthcoming); adult-use activity remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: Public Law 119-37 §781 takes legal effect 12 November 2026, but Public Law 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesized; the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply after 11 December 2026. USDA has delayed enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement until 31 December 2026. The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026. No federal cannabis banking law has been enacted. Any statement in the original contradicting this baseline was corrected to match it. Schedule III and the 280E change are applied to OMMA commercial licensees only; any non-medical possession is treated as Schedule I. Whether the federal rule treats Oklahoma's no-qualifying-conditions programme differently, and whether any tribal programme counts as "state-licensed", remain Verify — neither is supported by rule text opened in this audit.

Audit method: primary sources only — Oklahoma Statutes via OSCN, bill pages on oklegislature.gov, the Oklahoma Administrative Code and Oklahoma Register, OMMA (reports, licensee data, disciplinary actions), OBN, ODAFF, the Oklahoma Tax Commission, Attorney General official opinions and announcements, the State Election Board, Oklahoma and federal court records, official tribal government sources and codes, and official county and municipal sites and codes. Nothing was confirmed from news, law-firm blogs, trade press or AI summaries; where only a secondary source exists the verdict is Unverified. Verdicts: Confirmed, Corrected, Removed (wrong and no correct version found), or Unverified.

Audit totals — 574 rows: Confirmed 230, Corrected 70, Removed 7, Unverified 267. By slice: A (Parts 0–2) 131 rows — 59 / 13 / 3 / 56; B (Parts 3–6) 131 rows — 41 / 21 / 2 / 67; C (Parts 7–10) 196 rows — 112 / 18 / 1 / 65; D (Parts 11–12 + Notes) 116 rows — 18 / 18 / 1 / 79. The high Unverified count reflects the audit rule, not the original's quality: many original claims rested on secondary summaries, form-gated dashboards or sources that could not be opened directly, and this audit refused to upgrade those to Confirmed.

Key corrections applied throughout the rewrite (headline list — see the audit table for every row)

  • Run 1's "no official Oklahoma response to the federal hemp dates" is superseded: ODAFF's official Hemp Clarification Letter of 16 January 2026 states Total THC = THC + 87.7% of THCA, intermediates ≤0.3% Total THC dry weight after decarboxylation, and final products ≤0.4 mg Total THC per container — but the letter gives only the 12 November 2026 date and does not discuss the PL 119-103 §2019 staging to 11 December 2026, so the staging question for products other than non-naturally-produced cannabinoids stays Verify, and the letter's legal weight vs. OAC rules stays Verify.
  • The secondary claim that HB 3770 (2022), 63 O.S. §420A, confines intoxicating-hemp sales to OMMA dispensaries is rejected: the Legislature's own index shows HB 3770 as a 2026 bill referred to Rules, not a 2022 enacted dispensary-confinement law. No statute confining hemp-derived THC sales to OMMA dispensaries was confirmed; retail hemp sales are expressly licence-free under 63 O.S. §1-1431(C), subject to the legally-grown condition and food-safety law — but how §1-1431(C) interacts with SB 1257 (below) was not reconciled in any opened guidance and stays Verify.
  • SB 1257 is enacted (signed 20 May 2026, effective 1 November 2026): tetrahydrocannabinols move to state Schedule I; because 47 O.S. §11-902(A)(3) references the state schedule, the federal Schedule III move does not by itself remove the state DUI prong. The rewrite's DUI heading was corrected: there is no nanogram threshold, but §11-902(A)(3) is an any-amount Schedule I prong.
  • HB 2807 (2025) transporter warehouses are enacted law (became law without signature 25 May 2025, effective 1 June 2025), not Verify; SB 518's driving-warning label is in force from 1 November 2025, not Verify; the Sunny Roads recall was expanded 15 May 2026; the Greenleaf trigger was corrected to test-failed inventory remaining on shelves after the August 2025 cease-operations order.
  • Hemp processor/handler middle tier is $2,500 (not $2,000) on ODAFF's own 2025 form; university hemp research is corrected from USDA-direct licensing to ODAFF's USDA-approved state plan; the claimed Oklahoma SB 478 (2025) hemp reference was removed — no Oklahoma bill of that description was located.
  • Conflicting figures were resolved to single dated official figures in the rewrite (notably the 1 October 2026 OMMA table: 304,186 patients, 1,703 growers, 1,259 dispensaries, 557 processors, 41 transporters, 13 labs, 7 waste, total 308,803 — cited as printed, not relabelled "active" — and 2025 / Jan–Sep 2026 excise and sales-tax figures from the official OMMA tax table only). OMMA Licensing and Tax Data is an on-page archived table/dashboard, not a downloadable file; no file URL was invented for it.
  • No personal phone number or email for any individual licence holder is reproduced in this file; names are kept only with a link to the official source. Marketplace listings in Part 8 are reported as listing claims, not verified facts, and no listing is presented as a promise of a new OMMA licence under the moratorium (in force to 1 August 2028).

[C] §10.1.5 McGirtMcGirt v. Oklahoma, 591 U.S. ___ (2020), 140 S. Ct. 2452 (9 July 2020), 5–4, Gorsuch J.: Congress never disestablished the Muscogee (Creek) reservation, so it remains "Indian country" for federal criminal-law purposes; only Congress can disestablish, with clear explicit languageCorrectedhttps://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/spr-crt-us/2177478.html (Castro-Huerta opinion summarising McGirt) ; CRS https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/LSB10778Holding confirmed; CITATION CORRECTED to 591 U.S. 894 (2020). The "___" placeholder must not remain. Immediate consequence as stated (state courts generally lack jurisdiction to prosecute Indians in Indian country absent congressional authorisation; Major Crimes Act 18 U.S.C. §1153 federal jurisdiction for Indian defendants for enumerated felonies) is confirmed in substance.
[C] §10.1.5 McGirt extensionOklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals after McGirt recognised other reservations (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole, others) as likewise never disestablished — citing State ex rel. Matloff, Bosse v. State, 2021 OK CR 3, Roth v. State, 2021 OKCR 27 (via Castro-Huerta opinion)Confirmedhttps://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/spr-crt-us/2177478.htmlNo change. The "nearly half of Oklahoma, incl. most of Tulsa" point is correctly labelled a geographic description, not a cannabis holding.
[C] §10.1.5 Castro-HuertaOklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, 597 U.S. ___ (2022) (29 June 2022), 5–4, Kavanaugh J.: "the Federal Government and the State have concurrent jurisdiction to prosecute crimes committed by non-Indians against Indians in Indian country"; default is state criminal jurisdiction in Indian country unless preempted; General Crimes Act (18 U.S.C. §1152) / Public Law 280 preemption arguments rejected; McGirt not overruled outrightCorrectedhttps://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/spr-crt-us/2177478.html ; CRS https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/LSB10778Holding confirmed; CITATION CORRECTED to 597 U.S. 629 (2022). Facts confirmed: Victor Manuel Castro-Huerta, non-Indian, convicted in Oklahoma state court of child neglect against his Native stepdaughter on the Cherokee reservation; Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals vacated 29 Apr 2021 on exclusive-federal-jurisdiction grounds; Supreme Court reversed that exclusivity holding. Not a cannabis case.
[C] §10.1.5 cannabis applicationMcGirt/Castro-Huerta are jurisdiction cases, not cannabis cases; neither holds marijuana legal/illegal on any parcel or creates/destroys a tribal marijuana programme; "McGirt legalised/outlawed marijuana in half of Oklahoma" is wrongConfirmedhttps://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/spr-crt-us/2177478.htmlNo change. This is the slice's most important tribal-law discipline and it is correct.

[D] 12.3Effect of federal Schedule III (28 Apr 2026) and SB 1257 state Schedule I (eff. 1 Nov 2026) on § 11-902(A)(3)'s reference to § 2-204 — flagged Verify/unresolvedCorrected[https://www.oklegislature.gov/cf_pdf/2025-26%20FLR/SFLR/HB4248%20SFLR.PDF](https://www.oklegislature.gov/cf_pdf/2025-26%20FLR/SFLR/HB4248%20SFLR.PDF)PARTLY RESOLVED: § 11-902(A)(3) references § 2-204 of Title 63 — the STATE schedule. SB 1257 (signed 20 May 2026, eff. 1 Nov 2026) adds tetrahydrocannabinols to state Schedule I and leaves only dronabinol in Schedule III. From 1 Nov 2026 the state prong therefore reaches THC as state Schedule I regardless of the federal Schedule III move for state-licensed medical marijuana. Whether any court applies an OMMA-licensee exception to (A)(3) remains Verify (no case law located); do not state the federal move removes the state DUI prong.

Internal contradictions resolved

  • **School-buffer measurement:** original presented § 425(G) door-to-door vs OAC/OMMA property-line as an unresolved conflict. Resolved: current § 425(G) (2023 text) IS property-line-to-perimeter-wall for dispensaries, so statute and rule agree; the door-to-door text was superseded. The 500-foot allowance and the § 425(G)(3)(a) school-definition reference are removed/corrected with it.
  • **Moratorium end date:** original OAC text (through 16 June 2025) saying 1 Aug 2026 is superseded by OMMA's live pages and HB 3143 (2026): 1 Aug 2028.
  • **Card-fee formula:** original '2.25% of (fee + $2)' contradicts OMMA's printed example ($58.25 on $2,500) and its own tier tables ($58.30). Resolved to OMMA's formula (2.25% of fee, plus $2) with OMMA printed table totals prevailing and the $0.05 difference noted, not silently harmonised.
  • **Peak total:** original 400,377 (15 May 2022) vs OMMA table 400,732 (6 Jan 2022). Resolved to the printed 400,732, with its 3-unit component-sum discrepancy noted.
  • **2022 dispensary maximum:** original 2,477 (5 Oct 2022) vs OMMA table 2,599 (7 Dec 2022). Resolved to 2,599.
  • **Commercial peak:** original 13,785 defined without the waste-permit column sums to 13,784. Resolved: 13,785 includes the 1 waste permit on that row.
  • **HB 3144:** original's conflicting secondary reports ('enacted' vs 'pending' vs 'passed House only') resolved to: passed both chambers, SA's received 29 Apr 2026, no enrolled act/approval located — NOT law.
  • **SB 1242:** original's '$100,000 engrossed, status unclear' resolved to: Senate-engrossed only; House substitute replaced it with a $2,000 land reclamation fee and § 427.26 repeal; no approval shown — $100,000 is not law.
  • **Tribal hemp plans:** original 'no Oklahoma tribe on AMS list' contradicted by the current AMS list (six Oklahoma tribes with Approved Plans). Corrected.
  • **Population base:** original secondary-relayed 4,123,288 resolved to primary-confirmed Census QuickFacts July 1, 2025 estimate.
  • **Tier authority and employee-credential fee:** original Verify flags resolved (HB 2179/SB 813 via OMMA Tiered Licensing page; employee credential $30 + $2.72 via OMMA Apply/Employee Credentialing pages).
  • **Utility reporting:** original 'status unconfirmed, possibly current' resolved to: HB 4055, HB 1711 and SB 801 all died without enactment — no such duty confirmed.
  • **Section numbering:** duplicate § 3.4 resolved by renumbering (see audit row).

Timing note: The 3 November 2026 election had not yet been held on 30 October 2026. No 3 November 2026 result is reported in this file.

Federal baseline (given, held fixed, not re-researched): Split scheduling — state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; the broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final. IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to §280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026; after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026. The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026. There is no federal cannabis banking law.

Oklahoma application: Oklahoma's medical programme is state-licensed, so Schedule III / §280E discussion applies to OMMA commercial licensees. Because Oklahoma has no qualifying-condition list, whether the federal rule's text treats such a programme differently remains Verify. Any non-medical possession remains Schedule I federally. Whether any tribal programme counts as “state-licensed” remains Verify (Part 10: no Oklahoma tribal medical programme was located).

Run 2 correction to Run 1 — read this first. Run 1 stated that no official Oklahoma response to the federal hemp dates had been found. That is superseded: ODAFF issued an official Hemp Clarification Letter, 16 January 2026 (Hemp Program Administrator Joshua Rigdon), linked from ODAFF's Licensing & Permits page. It states current law as hemp products ≤0.3% Total THC = THC + 87.7% of THCA, and that the PL 119-37 change “placed into effect on November 12, 2026” sets intermediates ≤0.3% Total THC dry weight after decarboxylation and final marketplace products ≤0.4 mg Total THC per container (container = retail packaging: jars, bottles, cartridges), excluding cannabinoids not naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L. or synthesised outside the plant, expressly naming delta-8 and similar isomers. Products above those limits “are not considered hemp and cannot be marketed as such.” Two limits remain Verify: the letter gives only 12 November 2026 and does not discuss PL 119-103 §2019 staging to 11 December 2026, and the letter's legal weight versus statute/rule is not settled in this research. Audit correction: the letter gives only 12 November 2026; under PL 119-103 §2019 only the exclusions for cannabinoids not naturally produced or synthesised outside the plant apply from 12 November 2026, and the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply after 11 December 2026. Read the letter subject to that staging. Run 1's THCA 0.877 factor is therefore confirmed for ODAFF's stated method. The secondary claim that HB 3770 (2022), 63 O.S. §420A, confines hemp THC to OMMA dispensaries is rejected: the Legislature's Subject Index lists HB 3770 as a 2026 bill referred to Rules (H), not a 2022 enacted confinement law. Retail sale of legally grown hemp/hemp products is licence-free under 63 O.S. §1-1431(C) (Part 7).
How counts are reported: OMMA does not label its monthly-table figures “active” in the source as opened. Figures are reported with the definition as printed, and “issued”, “active”, “pending renewal” and “operating” counts are not mixed. Derived figures (for example implied retail sales = excise ÷ 7%) are labelled as arithmetic, not OMMA-published sales. Anything uncertain, conflicting or unavailable is flagged Verify or Unavailable. Proposed, failed or enjoined law is not presented as current law.

Cross-part headline figures (checked for consistency): 1 Oct 2026 OMMA table — 304,186 patients, 1,036 caregivers, 1,703 growers, 1,259 dispensaries, 557 processors, 41 transporters, 13 labs, 7 waste, total 308,803. Moratorium: HB 3208 26 Aug 2022 → HB 2095 → HB 3143 to 1 Aug 2028, renewals unaffected. Metrc mandatory 26 May 2022. Patient limits: 3 oz on person / 8 oz at home / 6 mature + 6 seedlings.

Federal baseline — fixed context, not re-researched

As instructed, the following is taken as fixed context. Anything found in this run that sits in tension with it is flagged, not silently reconciled:

  • Split scheduling: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final.
  • IRS § 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to § 280E.
  • Hemp: PL 119-37 § 781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 § 2019 limits it until 11 December 2026. After 11 December 2026, the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply.
  • USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026.
  • The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026.
  • There is no federal cannabis banking law.

What this means for Oklahoma, in plain terms

Oklahoma's programme is state-licensed and medical-only (see Part 1.1). On the fixed baseline, OMMA commercial licensees selling medical marijuana are therefore in the Schedule III / § 280E-lifted category federally, while any non-medical possession or sale in Oklahoma remains Schedule I federally and fully subject to § 280E. OMMA itself is reported to have said, in a corrected notice dated 28 April 2026, that "the 280E tax burden is removed for state medical marijuana licensed businesses, regardless of whether they pursue a DEA license" — see Part 2.5. Licensees are still advised in that notice to consult tax counsel on their own circumstances.

VERIFY — no qualifying-condition list: Oklahoma has no list of qualifying conditions (63 O.S. § 420(M): "There are no qualifying conditions"). Whether anything in the text of the federal Schedule III rule treats a no-list programme differently from a condition-list programme was not confirmed from the federal rule text in this run. Do not assume either answer. This is a follow-up for Run 2 / audit: open 91 FR 22714 itself and check its definition of "state-licensed medical" activity.

VERIFY — tribal "state-licensed" status: If any tribe operates a medical programme, whether it counts as "state-licensed" for the federal Schedule III / § 280E rule is Verify. No tribal medical programme is confirmed in Parts 0–2; tribal issues are Part 10 (Run 2).

Tension to flag — SB 1257 (2026, eff. 1 Nov 2026): Oklahoma in 2026 moved tetrahydrocannabinols from Schedule III to Schedule I under state law and expressly included chemically synthesised THC compounds, including those derived from industrial hemp, in the state definition (see Part 1.9). Secondary reporting says the Attorney General's office has said this will not affect OMMA-licensed patients or businesses and that dronabinol keeps Schedule III treatment. The interaction between a state Schedule I reclassification and the federal Schedule III treatment of state-licensed medical marijuana is Verify — the two schedules operate on different sovereigns' lists, and this file does not resolve whether SB 1257 changes any federal analysis. Do not present SB 1257 as reversing the federal Schedule III move.

PART 0 — HEADLINES

0.1 Medical-only, and shrinking fast

Oklahoma remains medical-only. Voters approved medical marijuana in State Question 788 on 26 June 2018 (56.86% Yes: 507,582 Yes / 385,176 No, per Election Board figures as relayed by Ballotpedia/Wikipedia — official Election Board results page not directly opened in this run, so the vote totals are marked as reported, not independently re-verified here) and rejected adult-use legalisation in State Question 820 on 7 March 2023 (38.33% Yes: 217,078 / 61.67% No: 349,284). No adult-use state question is on the 3 November 2026 ballot on the evidence found in this run (see §1.9 on SQ 837).

0.2 Licence moratorium — in force, now to 1 August 2028

Status on 30 Oct 2026: IN FORCE for new dispensary, grower and processor licences.

Step Instrument Effect
Start HB 3208 (2022), signed May 2022 Moratorium began 26 August 2022 for new dispensary, grower and processor licences. OMMA's own processor page states this date and instrument.
First extension HB 2095 (2023) End date moved to 1 August 2026.
Second extension HB 3143 (2026) End date moved to 1 August 2028, "unless OMMA's Executive Director determines all pending licensing reviews, inspections or investigations are complete." OMMA processor page, last modified 22 July 2026, states this verbatim in substance.
Renewals — Not affected. Current licensees may still renew.

OMMA processor page (accessed 2026-10-30): "A moratorium began Aug. 26, 2022, for new dispensary, grower and processor licenses. HB 3208 (2022)… HB 2095 (2023) extended the moratorium end date to Aug. 1, 2026, and HB 3143 (2026) further extended the end date to August 1, 2028, unless OMMA's Executive Director determines all pending licensing reviews, inspections or investigations are complete. The moratorium does not affect current licensees, who can apply for renewal." Source: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/processor-license.html

Correction to the task brief's premise: the brief asked to verify "HB 2095 (2023)?" — confirmed. It also implies the moratorium might have expired in August 2026. It did not: HB 3143 extended it before that date. Any source still saying "ends 1 August 2026" is out of date.

HB 3143 also — Verify detail: secondary reporting (Gies Law Firm, 30 Apr 2026) says HB 3143 formally prohibits licence transfers while administrative action (revocation, suspension, non-renewal, or OBNDD registration action) is pending, and bars a transfer application for at least six months after an annulment/revocation/suspension is completed. The enrolled text of HB 3143 was not directly opened in this run, so this transfer rule is Verify before republication.

HB 3144 grower cap — NOT presented as law: HB 3144 (2026) as introduced would cap commercial grower licences at 2,550 and repeal § 427.14a. It passed the House 82–15 (25 Feb 2026) and the Senate 34–12 (29 Apr 2026), with Senate amendments received by the House on 29 Apr 2026. No governor's signature / chapter number was located in this run, and OMMA's moratorium notice does not mention a cap. LegiScan summarises it as "died in chamber" / 50% progression. Status: Verify — do not present the 2,550 cap as enacted law. It is the single most important pending-vs-enacted distinction in this file. 0.4 Enforcement against illegal grows and unlawful ownership

Secondary reporting only in this run — no OBN/AG enforcement dataset was directly opened, so all figures in this paragraph are reported, not officially confirmed here:

  • The Attorney General's Organized Crime Task Force (created 2023, with OBN and OMMA) targets illegal grows; OBN's Marijuana Enforcement Teams (created 2021) are reported to have seized more than 2.4 million illegal plants and more than 295,000 lbs of processed marijuana since 2021, with more than 400 arrests (News 9, 7 Oct 2026, reporting OBN testimony to a Senate interim study on abandoned grows, 6 Oct 2026, Interim Study 2026-59).
  • July 2026 raids reported: five operations in Woodward (30,000+ plants, 200+ lbs); earlier Prague raids (nearly 49,000 plants, 1,800+ lbs) — secondary (Radio Oklahoma News, Sep/Oct 2026).
  • OBN is reported to have said registered grows peaked at ~8,400 farms with active OBN registrations in 2022, falling to ~1,350 — a different denominator from OMMA licences (see §0.3).
  • Abandoned grows are now a legislative topic in their own right (Senate interim study, Oct 2026): hazards cited include chemical contamination of ponds/creeks, raw sewage pits, illegal wiring and unsecured trash.

Follow-up for Run 2: open OBN and AG Organized Crime Task Force releases directly; do not carry the seizure/arrest totals forward as official until then.

0.5 New reporting and compliance rules (2025–2026)

  • Pre-packaging: HB 2807 — growers/processors must sell flower, trim, shake, kief and other non-concentrate products to dispensaries in pre-packaged units of 0.5 g to 3 oz, effective 1 June 2025; deli-style loose sales ended. Reported by secondary sources; enrolled text Verify before citing the exact product list.
  • Edibles / labelling — 1 Nov 2026 (see §1.9 for the mg-cap conflict): HB 4454 takes effect 1 November 2026. Consistently reported: packages and drinks must clearly state number of servings and THC per serving; edibles may not be attractive to children, shaped like humans, animals, cartoons or commercially available candy, or contain colour additives. Whether the enrolled bill retains a 10 mg per serving / 100 mg per package cap is RESOLVED by audit: it does not — OMMA's official quotation of 63 O.S. §423(C)(7) contains no mg cap (see §1.3).
  • Employment — 1 Nov 2026: HB 3127 (signed 17 Apr 2026) rewrites the § 427.8 employment protections — see §1.8.
  • State scheduling — 1 Nov 2026: SB 1257 (signed 20 May 2026) moves THC to Schedule I under state law — see §1.9 and the federal-baseline tension note above.
  • Hemp beverages — 1 Nov 2026 (proposed): HB 4248 would prohibit sale/furnishing/possession of hemp-containing beverages by/under-21s (new 63 O.S. § 7401). Senate floor version dated 9 Apr 2026 was located; final enacted status Verify — do not present as law yet.
  • Leadership change (context, not law): OMMA Executive Director Adria Berry stepped down effective 30 Oct 2026; Jason Yingling (deputy chief of compliance and enforcement) named interim director (Governor's office release dated 21 Oct, posted 22 Oct 2026, as reported 22–30 Oct 2026). Secondary only.

0.6 Tax changes

  • No change to the 7% medical excise rate in 2025–2026 on the evidence found. The rate remains 63 O.S. § 426(A) (see Part 2).
  • Excise collections fell every year since 2022 (official OMMA tax table): $55,040,503 (2022) → $51,008,462 (2023) → $50,481,088 (2024) → $45,300,591 (2025) → $32,024,393 (Jan–Sep 2026). State + local sales tax on medical marijuana: $70,668,557 (2022) → $58,389,526 (2025) → $41,590,752 (Jan–Sep 2026).
  • Proposed, not law: SB 2053 (2026) would authorise cities/counties to levy up to 10% local medical marijuana excise tax, administered by the Tax Commission (OTC fiscal note, 14 Feb 2026). Verify final status; do not present as law.
  • Litigation — Verify: Johnson & Neeley v. Oklahoma Tax Commission (Oklahoma County, filed Oct 2025) challenges the 7% excise as unconstitutional under Oklahoma revenue-bill rules and seeks refunds. Secondary reporting only; outcome Unavailable in this run. The tax remains in force and collectible unless/until a court orders otherwise — do not present the challenge as having struck the tax down.
  • Federal 280E change (see Part 2.5): the April 2026 federal Schedule III order is the year's largest tax event for licensees, even though no Oklahoma statute changed.

0.7 2026 state questions

  • No cannabis state question is on the 3 November 2026 ballot on the evidence found in this run.
  • SQ 837 (adult-use legalisation effort for 2026) failed to gather the 172,993 signatures required by the 3 November 2025 deadline and will not appear on the 2026 ballot (secondary: CannBus Q3 2026 summary; Drug Policy Watch brief). The brief's wording differs slightly ("withdrawn in November 2025 after falling short") — either way, not on the ballot. Final confirmation route: Secretary of State / State Election Board initiative-petition list — Verify before republication.
  • The 3 November 2026 ballot does include other (non-cannabis) questions, e.g. SQ 847 on property-tax valuation caps, which are out of scope here except to warn against confusing them with a cannabis question.

PART 1 — LAWS

1.1 Legal status: medical only

Medical marijuana is legal in Oklahoma for state-licensed patients, caregivers and commercial licensees. Adult-use (recreational) marijuana is illegal for everyone.

What is legal, in one paragraph: a person holding a valid OMMA patient licence may consume marijuana legally and possess within the § 420(A) limits (see §1.3); a caregiver may possess (not use, unless also a patient) for a homebound patient; a licensed dispensary may sell only to licensed patients/caregivers; licensed growers/processors/transporters/labs may operate only within their licence and OMMA rules (OAC 442:10). What is not legal: purchase, possession, sale, cultivation or transport by any non-licensee outside the narrow § 420(B) misdemeanour (see §1.3); sale by anyone other than a licensed dispensary ("Only a licensed medical marijuana dispensary may conduct retail sales of marijuana or marijuana derivatives" — § 421(D)); public consumption rules and local restrictions are covered in §1.6/Part 3, and driving/impairment in Part 12 (Run 2).

Federal overlay: non-medical marijuana remains Schedule I federally (fixed baseline), so state medical legality does not make non-medical possession federally legal, and does not create a federal right to possess, transport interstate, or use on federal land.

Verbatim — § 421(A)–(B) (opened 2026-10-30):

"A. The Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority shall make available on its website in an easy-to-find location an application for a medical marijuana dispensary license. The application fee to be paid by the applicant shall be in the amounts provided for in Section 427.14 of this title. … Dispensary applicants must all be residents of Oklahoma. Any entity applying for a dispensary license must be owned by a resident of this state and must be registered to do business in this state. The Authority shall have ninety (90) business days to review the application; approve, reject, or deny the application; and send the approval, rejection, or denial letter stating reasons for the rejection or denial to the applicant in the same method the application was submitted to the Authority."

"B. The Authority shall approve all applications which meet the following criteria: 1. The applicant must be twenty-five (25) years of age or older; 2. The applicant, if applying as an individual, must show residency in this state; 3. All applying entities must show that all members, managers, and board members are residents of this state; 4. An applying entity may show ownership of nonstate residents, but that percentage ownership may not exceed twenty-five percent (25%); 5. All applying individuals or entities must be registered to conduct business in this state; and 6. All applicants must disclose all ownership interests in the dispensary."

"Applicants with a nonviolent felony conviction in the last two (2) years, any other felony conviction in the last five (5) years, inmates in the custody of the Department of Corrections or any person currently incarcerated shall not qualify for a medical marijuana dispensary license."

Note the tension inside § 421 itself: subsection A says an entity "must be owned by a resident" while B(4) allows up to 25% non-resident ownership. The operative rule applied by OMMA, per its licence pages, is 75% Oklahoma-resident ownership (see OMMA processor page: "75% of the commercial applicant's ownership interests are Oklahoma residents as required in … 63 O.S. § 427.1 et seq."). Residency litigation is Part 4/Part 9 territory (Run 2) and is not resolved in Parts 0–2; the requirement remains on OMMA pages as of July 2026.

Verbatim — § 420(B) (opened 2026-10-30):

"Possession of up to one and one-half (1.5) ounces or forty-two and forty-five one-hundredths (42.45) grams of marijuana by persons who can state a medical condition, but are not in possession of a state-issued medical marijuana patient license, shall constitute a misdemeanor offense punishable by a fine not to exceed Four Hundred Dollars ($400.00) and shall not be subject to imprisonment for the offense. Any law enforcement officer who comes in contact with a person in violation of this subsection and who is satisfied as to the identity of the person, as well as any other pertinent information the law enforcement officer deems necessary, shall issue to the person a written citation containing a notice to answer the charge against the person in the appropriate court. Upon receiving the written promise of the alleged violator to answer as specified in the citation, the law enforcement officer shall release the person upon personal recognizance unless there has been a violation of another provision of law."

Note: the brief's guess "§ 426" for this misdemeanour is wrong — it is § 420(B). § 426 is the tax section.

Patient limits — verbatim § 420(A) (opened 2026-10-30)

"A person in possession of a state-issued medical marijuana patient license shall be able to: 1. Consume marijuana legally; 2. Legally possess up to three (3) ounces or eighty-four and nine-tenths (84.9) grams of marijuana on their person; 3. Legally possess six mature marijuana plants and the harvested marijuana therefrom; 4. Legally possess six seedling plants; 5. Legally possess one (1) ounce or twenty-eight and three tenths (28.3) grams of concentrated marijuana; 6. Legally possess seventy-two (72) ounces or two thousand thirty-seven and six-tenths (2037.6) grams of edible marijuana; 7. Legally possess up to eight (8) ounces or two hundred twenty-six and four-tenths (226.4) grams of marijuana in their residence; and 8. Legally possess seventy-two (72) ounces of topical marijuana."

In table form:

Patient possession Limit
On person — flower 3 oz (84.9 g)
At residence — flower 8 oz (226.4 g)
Mature plants 6 (+ harvested marijuana therefrom)
Seedling plants 6
Concentrate 1 oz (28.3 g)
Edibles 72 oz (2,037.6 g)
Topicals 72 oz

Counties/cities may allow patients/caregivers to exceed state limits: § 420(N) — "Counties and cities may enact medical marijuana guidelines allowing medical marijuana patient license holders or caregiver license holders to exceed the state limits set forth in subsection A of this section." Whether any jurisdiction has done so is Part 3 territory; none is asserted here.

Home grow: 6 mature + 6 seedlings per patient licence (above). Caregiver: may not cultivate for more than 5 patient licensees, and may not charge more than actual cultivation costs (§ 420(K)). Patient home-grow location/visibility rules from the Unity Bill (own property or owner's written permission; not accessible to / visible by the general public; no hazardous extraction — butane/propane/CO₂ — in a residence) are secondary summaries of HB 2612 — Verify against current §§ 427.x text before quoting.

Cultivation penalties (non-patient): unlawful cultivation is a § 2-401 manufacture offence (felony). Specific plant-count tiers, if any, were not confirmed from statute text in this run — Verify. Do not import another state's plant-count tiers.

Paraphernalia: see §1.2(C). Patient paraphernalia used for lawful medical use is within the licence; non-patient paraphernalia possession is the § 2-405 misdemeanour summarised there.

Public consumption: no freestanding "public consumption" offence was confirmed from statute text in this run. What is confirmed: (a) property/business owners may prohibit smoking/v vaporisation on premises, within structures, or within 10 feet of an entryway (§ 427.8(C) per secondary relay); (b) a patient may not be denied non-smoked/non-vaporised products on that basis; (c) employers need not permit use on premises or during job duties (§ 427.8(I), as amended — see §1.8). A general public-use ban, open-container rule (reported as enacted 2026 in one secondary summary), and local smoking ordinances are Verify for Run 2. Do not state a statewide public-consumption ban as confirmed law on this evidence.

Product types and THC limits — medical

Allowed types (from § 420(A) categories + § 421(D) pre-rolls + OMMA licence pages): flower, pre-rolls (≤1 g, ground flower only, no concentrates/derivatives, from 1 Nov 2021), concentrates, edibles, beverages (as edibles), topicals, seedlings/mature plants for sale by dispensaries. Vapes are sold as concentrate products; no separate statutory vape ban was found.

THC per serving / per package — medical, before 1 Nov 2026: No statutory mg cap was found in § 420 — the limits are by weight (ounces), not by milligrams of THC. That is the pre-November 2026 position.

THC per serving / per package — from 1 Nov 2026 (HB 4454): CONFLICT — Verify.

  • Introduced HB 4454: edibles ≤10 mg THC per serving, ≤10 servings / 100 mg per package; drinks ≤20 mg (later committee substitute: drinks ≤10 mg per serving).
  • Policy committee substitute summary (House Research, 17 Feb 2026): "an edible medical marijuana product must not contain more than 10 milligrams of THC per individual serving" and drinks "must not contain more than 10 milligrams of THC per individual serving", packages/drinks must state servings and THC per serving, and edibles must not be child-attractive / human, cartoon or animal shapes / commercially available candy / colour additives. The same summary says the substitute "removes the limits on servings in each package and in drinks that the introduced version contained" — i.e. the 100 mg package cap was dropped in committee.
  • A September 2026 secondary analysis of the enrolled bill states the enrolled bill "sets no mg cap per serving" and requires only serving/THC-per-serving labelling plus the shape/child-appeal bans.
  • OMMA's own November 2026 guidance as relayed by secondary coverage: "Packages must clearly indicate the number of THC servings per package and per individual serving. As of November 1, the authority prohibits the transfer of any non-compliant products to a dispensary."

Compiler rule: state the labelling + shape bans as the 1 Nov 2026 change only. Audit resolution: OMMA's official HB 4454 clarification quotes §423(C)(7) with no mg cap; the 10 mg / 100 mg figures were introduced/committee-substitute figures only and must not be published as enrolled law

1.4 Medical programme

Physician recommendation — no condition list (verbatim § 420(M), opened 2026-10-30):

"All applications for a medical marijuana patient license shall be signed by an Oklahoma physician licensed by and in good standing with the State Board of Medical Licensure and Supervision, the State Board of Osteopathic Examiners, or the Board of Podiatric Medical Examiners. There are no qualifying conditions. A medical marijuana patient license shall be recommended according to the accepted standards a reasonable and prudent physician would follow when recommending or approving any medication. No physician may be unduly stigmatized, penalized, subjected to discipline, sanctioned, reprimanded or harassed for signing a medical marijuana patient license application, provided the physician acted in accordance with the provisions of this subsection and all other rules governing the medical license of the physician in this state."

Patient licence (verbatim core, § 420(D), (G), (H), (L)):

"The license shall be valid for two (2) years. The biannual application fee shall be One Hundred Dollars ($100.00), or Twenty Dollars ($20.00) for individuals on Medicaid, Medicare or SoonerCare. … Reprints … shall be Twenty Dollars ($20.00)." "Medical marijuana patient license applicants shall submit their applications to the Authority for approval. The applicant shall be a resident of this state and shall prove residency by a valid driver license, utility bills, or other accepted methods." "The Authority shall review the medical marijuana patient license application; approve, reject, or deny the application; and mail the approval, rejection, or denial letter … within fourteen (14) business days of receipt of the application." "All applicants for a medical marijuana patient license shall be eighteen (18) years of age or older. A special exception shall be granted to an applicant under the age of eighteen (18); however, these applications shall be signed by two physicians and the parent or legal guardian of the applicant."

Note: OMMA's general FAQ still saying "one year" (flagged by a secondary site in Oct 2026) conflicts with the statute's two-year term. Statute controls: two years. The $20 discounted fee covers Medicaid/Medicare/SoonerCare; OMMA's Apply page extends the $20 tier to "100% disabled veteran" patients — that extension is OMMA-page only and should be cited as such, not as § 420 text.

Short-term licence (§ 420(E)): for applicants whose physician recommendation is valid only 60 days. "Short-term medical marijuana patient licenses shall be issued for sixty (60) days. The fee … and the procedure for extending or renewing the license shall be determined by the Executive Director." OMMA Apply page lists short-term in the $100 tier (with $4.30 card fee = $104.30 total) — OMMA-page figure.

Temporary (out-of-state) licence (§ 420(F), verbatim in substance, opened 2026-10-30):

"A temporary medical marijuana patient license application shall also be made available … for residents of other states. Temporary medical marijuana patient licenses shall be granted to any medical marijuana license holders from other states, provided that such states have state-regulated medical marijuana programs, and applicants can prove they are members of such programs. Temporary medical marijuana patient licenses shall be issued for thirty (30) days. The cost for a temporary license shall be One Hundred Dollars ($100.00). Renewal shall be granted with resubmission of a new application. No additional criteria shall be required. Reprints … shall be Twenty Dollars ($20.00)."

So: 30 days, $100, renewable by fresh application, only for holders from states with state-regulated medical programmes who prove membership. There is no reciprocity-by-recognition (an out-of-state card alone does not authorise purchase); a temporary OMMA licence is required. Whether a tribal medical card counts for this purpose is Part 10 / Verify.

Caregiver licence (§ 420(K), verbatim in substance): available for qualified caregivers of a homebound patient; "shall provide the caregiver the same rights as the medical marijuana patient licensee including the ability to possess marijuana, marijuana products and mature and immature plants … but excluding the ability to use marijuana or marijuana products unless the caregiver has a medical marijuana patient license." Criteria only: proof of patient's licence + homebound status, proof of designee status, caregiver 18+, caregiver state residency. Cultivation cap: no more than 5 patients; charges capped at actual cultivation costs. OMMA Apply page: caregiver no charge.

Minor licence: under-18 exception requires two physicians + parent/legal guardian signature (§ 420(L)). Minor fee treatment (whether the $100/$20 tiers apply identically) Verify from OMMA minor-licence page — not stated in § 420 text opened.

Changes to these rules: § 420 was amended by Laws 2024, c. 182 (emerg. eff. 26 Apr 2024) and Laws 2025, c. 209 and c. 494 (eff. 1 Nov 2025). The substance of the 2024/2025 amendments to § 420 was not isolated in this run (the history line lists them; the amended paragraphs were not diffed). Verify before attributing any specific patient-rule change to 2024/2025. One 2024 change visible in the record: SB 320 (2025) proposing a purchase cap was not enacted (see §0.8).

1.5 Hemp and intoxicating hemp

Definition and measurement (current, pre-federal-change)

  • State definition (2 O.S.): Cannabis sativa L. / any part, delta-9 THC ≤0.3% on a dry-weight basis. This is the 2018 Farm Bill definition as adopted by Oklahoma.
  • Measurement (OAC hemp rules, via Cornell relay): lab reports total delta-9 THC on a dry-weight basis plus measurement of uncertainty; compliant if the uncertainty range includes 0.3% or less. Remediation allowed up to 1.0% total delta-9 THC, retested to ≤0.3%.
  • Important distinction: Oklahoma's hemp test as relayed is total delta-9 THC (delta-9 + THCA conversion is not spelled out in the relayed definition — the relay says "total delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol content concentration level", not the federal total-THC formula THCA×0.877 + delta-9). Whether Oklahoma's lab method already applies the 0.877 decarboxylation factor is Verify from OAC 35:30-24 / the USDA-approved plan. Do not state Oklahoma already uses federal total-THC.
  • Federal change coming (fixed baseline): after 11 December 2026, the federal definition becomes a total-THC definition with a 0.4 mg total THC per container cap for hemp-derived products. Oklahoma's response to that change is addressed below.

Delta-8, delta-9 (hemp-derived), THCA, other hemp-derived THC

Position on 30 Oct 2026 (secondary consensus, statute text not opened — treat as reported, not confirmed statute):

  • Hemp-derived delta-8 THC: treated as legal in Oklahoma if derived from legal hemp. No Oklahoma statute banning delta-8 was located. The basis cited by every secondary source is the hemp carve-out from the "marijuana" / "tetrahydrocannabinols" definitions (see §1.2(E)).
  • Hemp-derived delta-9 THC: legal if ≤0.3% delta-9 by dry weight (the hemp definition itself).
  • THCA: treated as legal / not restricted in Oklahoma on secondary accounts as of 2026; no THCA-specific Oklahoma ban was located. Verify — THCA is the product most exposed to the federal total-THC change after 11 Dec 2026, because THCA converts to THC.
  • Other synthetics / isomers (THC-O, HHC, THCP, etc.): no Oklahoma-specific ban or permission was located in this run. Unavailable / Verify — do not list them as legal or illegal.
  • Sold only by OMMA dispensaries? NO — on current evidence, hemp-derived THC products are sold outside OMMA dispensaries (CBD/smoke shops, retail) without an OMMA licence, because they are hemp products, not medical marijuana. No statute was found confining them to dispensaries. Verify — this is the single most consequential hemp-retail point, and it rests on absence of a confining statute plus secondary retail accounts, not on a positive statutory permission. SB 1257 (state Schedule I, eff. 1 Nov 2026) may change this analysis for synthesised hemp THC — see below.
  • Minimum age for hemp-derived products generally: NO statewide statutory 21+ age was confirmed for all hemp-derived THC products in this run. Retailers commonly impose 21+ voluntarily, and secondary sources variously assert "21+" as if it were law — that assertion is not adopted here. The only age rule with a bill text behind it is the proposed HB 4248 hemp-beverage 21+ rule (Verify final status). Do not publish a general hemp-THC 21+ age as Oklahoma law on this evidence.
  • Testing / labelling for hemp products: SB 238 (2019) CBD labelling — country of origin + synthetic/natural disclosure (secondary). No comprehensive hemp-THC testing/labelling statute (potency, contaminants, per-serving disclosure) was located. Verify / Unavailable for hemp-THC testing beyond the ODAFF pre-harvest crop test.
  • THC beverages (hemp): HB 4248 (2026) would bar sale/furnishing to, and possession by, under-21s (new § 7401, eff. 1 Nov 2026 if enacted). Final status Verify. No hemp-beverage mg cap was located.

State response to the federal hemp dates (12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026)

Audit correction — this paragraph in the original run is superseded and replaced: An official Oklahoma response WAS issued: ODAFF's Hemp Clarification Letter, 16 January 2026 (Hemp Program Administrator Joshua Rigdon), linked from ODAFF's Licensing & Permits page. It states current law as hemp products ≤0.3% Total THC = THC + 87.7% of THCA, and that the PL 119-37 change sets intermediates ≤0.3% Total THC dry weight after decarboxylation and final marketplace products ≤0.4 mg Total THC per container (container = retail packaging: jars, bottles, cartridges), excluding cannabinoids not naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L. or synthesised outside the plant, expressly naming delta-8 and similar isomers. Products above those limits “are not considered hemp and cannot be marketed as such.” Staging correction: the letter gives only 12 November 2026 and does not discuss PL 119-103 §2019 staging; under that staging only the non-naturally-produced/synthesised cannabinoid exclusions apply from 12 November 2026, and the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg/container cap apply after 11 December 2026. The letter's legal weight versus statute/rule remains Verify. The Gies memo argument that much ODAFF hemp “must therefore be treated as medical marijuana under OMMA licensure” remains a firm's argument, not an official position

What follows mechanically (not as Oklahoma policy): from 12 Nov 2026 the federal provision takes effect but is limited until 11 Dec 2026; after 11 Dec 2026, hemp that exceeds the federal total-THC definition, and hemp-derived products exceeding 0.4 mg total THC per container, would fall outside the federal hemp definition. How ODAFF (state plan), OMMA (medical programme) and OBN (enforcement) each treat that material in Oklahoma after those dates is Unavailable on 30 Oct 2026 and is the top follow-up for any post-December update. The USDA DEA-lab enforcement delay to 31 Dec 2026 and the medical rider through 11 Dec 2026 (fixed baseline) are federal dates, not Oklahoma dates.

SB 1257 — the state-law wildcard for hemp THC (eff. 1 Nov 2026)

Secondary reporting (Marijuana Herald / MMJ Daily, Oct 2026) states SB 1257 "moves tetrahydrocannabinols from Schedule III to Schedule I under state law and explicitly includes chemically synthesized THC compounds, including those derived from industrial hemp, within the statutory definition", that the AG's office says it "will not affect patients or businesses licensed under OMMA's medical marijuana program", and that dronabinol keeps Schedule III treatment, with the stated purpose of closing a trafficking loophole (processing marijuana into THC products to face misdemeanour rather than felony charges).

Compiler rule: report SB 1257 as enacted state scheduling law effective 1 Nov 2026, report the AG's "licensed programme unaffected" position as reported AG position, not statute, and mark Verify: (a) the enrolled text's exact hemp-THC language, (b) whether hemp-derived delta-8 sold at retail falls inside the new state Schedule I definition, and (c) whether any enforcement guidance distinguishes hemp-derived from marijuana-derived synthesised THC. Until (b)–(c) are answered from official text/guidance, this file does not state that hemp-derived delta-8 becomes illegal in Oklahoma on 1 Nov 2026 — and it does not state that it stays legal either. That is a genuine open question on 30 Oct 2026.

Packaging / labelling (medical)

  • Pre-packaging: from 1 June 2025 (HB 2807, secondary), flower/trim/shake/kief/non-concentrates to dispensaries in pre-packaged 0.5 g–3 oz units. § 421(E) already prohibited customers handling unpackaged product (samples in separate display cases/jars excepted, display only, not for sale).
  • Dispensary pre-rolls: § 421(D) — ≤1 g, ground flower only, no concentrates/derivatives, tested/packaged/labelled per law and OMMA rules.
  • Edible labelling from 1 Nov 2026 (HB 4454): servings + THC per serving on package/drink; child-appeal/shape/candy/colour-additive bans (see §1.3 conflict note for mg caps).
  • General packaging/labelling/advertising rule numbers (OAC 442:10): not verified in this run. Advertising restrictions (e.g. distance from schools, youth targeting, required warnings) are Verify from OAC 442:10 — do not import another state's advertising rules.
  • Hemp labelling: SB 238 CBD origin/synthetic-natural rule only (secondary, §1.5).

Delivery / curbside

No delivery licence class exists in the OMMA licence list (grower, processor, dispensary, transporter, lab, waste, research, education — see Part 4 outline in §0.3 table). Whether dispensaries may deliver to patients, offer curbside pickup, or use a transporter for patient delivery was not confirmed from statute or OAC text in this run. Temporary COVID-era curbside practices, if any, are not carried forward as current law. Verify from OAC 442:10 and OMMA delivery guidance before stating any delivery rule. Do not state "delivery is prohibited" or "delivery is allowed" on this evidence.

Zoning and the school buffer — corrected citation

The statutory school buffer is 1,000 feet, and it is NOT § 425.

  • Dispensary: 1,000 feet from any public or private school, measured "from the nearest property line of such public school or private school to the nearest perimeter wall of the licensed premises" (SQ 788 § 421 as amended; OMMA dispensary page repeats the perimeter-wall test and requires proof). Grandfathering: a dispensary compliant at initial licensure may continue despite a later-established school / later rule change (per SB 1543-era amendment relay).
  • Grower: 1,000 feet, measured property-line to property-line (OAC 442:10-5-3(e)(6)).
  • Other buffers (parks, churches, etc.): no statewide buffer beyond schools was confirmed in this run. Local codes (e.g. El Reno's 300-ft park/church rule) are local, not state — Part 3 territory.
  • Municipal zoning limits (state law): § 427.8(B) (secondary relay, CaseMine) — "Municipal and county governing bodies may not enact medical marijuana guidelines which restrict or interfere with the rights of a licensed patient or caregiver to possess, purchase, cultivate or transport medical marijuana within the legal limits … or require patients or caregivers to obtain permits or licenses in addition to the state-required licenses." For businesses (as opposed to patients), the state requires a certificate of compliance from the political subdivision certifying zoning, municipal ordinances, and safety/electrical/fire/plumbing/waste/construction/building codes (§ 426.1; OAC 442:10-5-3(e)(8)), and once submitted, "no additional certificate of compliance shall [be required]" on the SQ 788 formulation — full current text Verify. The practical reading adopted in secondary guidance: municipalities may enforce generally applicable zoning/building/fire codes and issue the certificate, but may not use zoning to ban the state programme outright or impose a separate local medical-marijuana licence on patients/caregivers. Business-specific local bans/fees are Part 3 and must be checked jurisdiction by jurisdiction.

1.7 Seed-to-sale tracking — Metrc

Metrc is mandatory. Date: 26 May 2022.

  • OMMA announced the Metrc contract in September 2020 (secondary).
  • OMMA patient bulletin (May 2022, via GovDelivery): "the Metrc seed-to-sale statewide inventory tracking system, which all OMMA-licensed businesses must use by May 26" and "May 26 — Deadline for growers, processors, dispensaries and labs to be seed-to-sale compliant."
  • Untagged inventory: dispensaries had until 24 August 2022 to sell or dispose of untagged product; no new untagged purchases after 26 May 2022; monthly OMMA reporting template continued through 31 May 2022, then Metrc replaced it for tagged activity.
  • OMMA January 2023 legislative update: licensees not credentialed by 26 May 2022 were assessed a $500 fine; revocation actions followed for non-payment / continued non-credentialing.
  • Source: https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OKSDH/bulletins/3145606 (OMMA May 2022 bulletin); https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OKSDH/bulletins/347e272 (Jan 2023 update). Metrc monthly platform fee $40/licence is secondary (vendor guides), not an OMMA fee schedule — mark as such if used.

1.8 Employment and drug-testing protections

This section describes the law BEFORE 1 Nov 2026, then the HB 3127 change. The post-1 Nov 2026 text of § 427.8 was not opened — the HB 3127 summary below is from two law-firm analyses (JD Supra; Ogletree, 2026) that agree in substance, plus news coverage. Treat subsection wording as Verify against enrolled HB 3127.

Pre-HB 3127 position (§ 427.8, Unity Bill)

Secondary relay of § 427.8 (CaseMine) states in substance:

  • (B) Municipal/county limits on patient/caregiver guidelines (see §1.6).
  • (C) Property/business owners may prohibit smoking/vaporisation on premises / within structures / within 10 ft of entryway, but may not deny non-smoked/non-vaporised lawful products.
  • Employment — core protection: "No employer may refuse to hire, discipline, discharge or otherwise penalize an applicant or employee solely on the basis of a positive test for marijuana components or metabolites, unless: (a) the applicant/employee is not in possession of a valid medical marijuana license; [or other statutory exceptions, including safety-sensitive positions and on-the-job possession/use/influence]."
  • (I) Nothing requires an employer to permit/accommodate use on premises or during hours of employment; nothing requires reimbursement by government assistance, private insurer, workers' comp carrier/self-insured employer; nothing prevents written drug-testing/impairment policies under the Oklahoma Standards for Workplace Drug and Alcohol Testing Act, 40 O.S. § 551 et seq.
  • (J) Exclusive remedy for wilful violation = the remedies under the Standards for Workplace Drug and Alcohol Testing Act.
  • "Positive test" threshold: at/above the U.S. DOT cutoff or Oklahoma under-the-influence law, whichever is lower (per Ogletree summary of pre-amendment law; HB 3127 does not change the threshold).

"Safety-sensitive" pre-amendment: any job the employer reasonably believed could affect safety/health of the employee or others, plus a non-exhaustive duty list (hazardous materials handling; vehicle/equipment/machinery/power-tool operation; firefighting; critical infrastructure; firearms; volatile/flammable materials; direct patient/child care; etc.).

HB 3127 (2026) — signed 17 Apr 2026, effective 1 Nov 2026

Per JD Supra + Ogletree (agreeing):

  1. Employer discretion to designate safety-sensitive jobs is removed. "Safety-sensitive" is now a defined duty list only (handling/packaging/processing/storage/disposal/transport of hazardous materials; operation of motor/other vehicle, equipment, machinery or power tools; [firefighting, critical infrastructure, firearms, volatile materials — full list Verify]; carrying a firearm; direct patient care or direct child care). The "employer reasonably believes" catch-all is gone.
  2. Safety-sensitive positions are subject to a mandatory zero-tolerance drug and alcohol standard, regardless of the employer's policy for other positions.
  3. Broader action on positive tests for all positions: an employer may now refuse to hire / discipline / discharge / penalise solely on a positive test if the action is "taken pursuant to a written drug and alcohol testing policy adopted and enforced in accordance with the Standards for Workplace Drug and Alcohol Testing Act, 40 O.S. § 551 et seq." Pre-amendment, that route was effectively confined to safety-sensitive roles; HB 3127 extends it to any compliant written policy.
  4. What does NOT change: employers still may not act solely because someone holds a medical marijuana licence (status protection survives). Employers still need not allow use/possession/influence at the workplace or "while performing job duties" (HB 3127 replaces "during hours of employment" with the broader "while performing job duties" — Ogletree).
  5. Interaction with federal Schedule III: none stated in HB 3127 summaries. Federal rescheduling does not create an Oklahoma employment right; HB 3127 tightens, not loosens, employer action in Oklahoma from 1 Nov 2026. Do not present Schedule III as restoring pre-HB 3127 protections.

Compiler caution: because HB 3127 takes effect after the research date (1 Nov 2026 vs 30 Oct 2026), the file must date-label it as "enacted, not yet effective on 30 Oct 2026" wherever it is mentioned, and must not describe the pre-amendment protections as current after 1 Nov 2026 without the effective-date qualifier.

PART 2 — TAXES

2.1 The 7% medical marijuana excise — 63 O.S. § 426 (verbatim, opened 2026-10-30)

"A. The tax on retail medical marijuana sales shall be established at seven percent (7%) of the gross amount received by the seller."

"B. This tax shall be collected at the point of sale. Except as provided for in subsection D, tax proceeds shall be deposited into the Medical Marijuana Tax Fund created in Section 3 of this act."

"C. Pursuant to Section 255.2 of Title 68 of the Oklahoma Statutes, the Oklahoma Tax Commission shall have authority to assess, collect and enforce the tax specified in subsection A of this section including any interest and penalty thereon."

"D. For fiscal year 2022, proceeds from the levy authorized by subsection A of this section shall be apportioned as follows: 1. The first Sixty-five Million Dollars ($65,000,000.00) shall be apportioned as follows: - a. fifty-nine and twenty-three hundredths percent (59.23%) to the State Public Common School Building Equalization Fund, - b. thirty-four and sixty-two hundredths percent (34.62%) to the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority, a division within the State Department of Health, and - c. six and fifteen hundredths percent (6.15%) to the State Department of Health and earmarked for drug and alcohol rehabilitation; and 2. Any surplus collections shall be apportioned to the General Revenue Fund of the State Treasury."

"E. If any medical marijuana business licensee intentionally does not remit the taxes as required by the provisions of this section or the provisions of Section 1354 of Title 68 of the Oklahoma Statutes, the Authority shall permanently revoke the medical marijuana business license of the business licensee and the business licensee shall be permanently ineligible to receive any other type of medical marijuana business license issued by the Authority, including licenses for a dispensary, commercial grower operation, processing facility, transporter, research, education facility, and waste disposal facility."

History line (Justia): Added by SQ 788 § 7, eff. 26 July 2018; amended Laws 2021, c. 563 § 2 (emerg. eff. 28 May 2021); Laws 2022, c. 228 § 27 (emerg. eff. 5 May 2022); Laws 2023, c. 168 § 1 (1 Nov 2023); Laws 2023, 1st Ex. Sess., c. 34 § 1 (eff. 1 July 2023).

Apportionment — read the verbatim text carefully: the text as printed in the 2025 Justia compilation still frames subsection D as "For fiscal year 2022" and still describes OMMA as "a division within the State Department of Health" — language predating OMMA's standalone status (Nov 2022). Secondary sources state the formula has since changed twice and that OMMA is now funded by fees/fines, with excise going to education and substance-abuse programmes at the Legislature's discretion — but no current apportionment text was opened in this run. Therefore: the 59.23 / 34.62 / 6.15 split is stated here ONLY as the FY2022 text as printed, NOT as the current apportionment. Current (FY2026) apportionment is Verify — open the current § 426 on OSCN and the OTC apportionment reports before publishing any current split. HB 2057 (2025, introduced only) would have rewritten the apportionment again; it is not law and its figures must not be substituted.

Collection mechanics: point-of-sale collection by the dispensary; OTC assesses/collects/enforces (including interest and penalties) under 68 O.S. § 255.2; intentional non-remittance = permanent revocation + permanent ineligibility for any OMMA business licence (§ 426(E)). Monthly reporting: dispensary monthly sales report to OMMA due 15th of the month (§ 421(C)); OTC monthly remittance practice (due 20th per secondary tax guides) Verify against OTC rules.

2.5 IRS § 280E and Oklahoma decoupling

Federal (fixed baseline + OMMA notice): § 280E barred deductions/credits for businesses trafficking in Schedule I/II substances. For state-licensed medical marijuana, the 28 Apr 2026 Schedule III order "generally removes section 280E as a bar" (Treasury/IRS joint statement 23 Apr 2026, as relayed by Mondaq). OMMA's corrected notice (28 Apr 2026, via OMMA news page opened in search): "Dispensaries choosing not to participate [in DEA registration] may continue to operate in accordance with the existing regulatory framework in Oklahoma and may still be eligible for potential tax breaks. The DOJ's order indicates that the 280E tax burden is removed for state medical marijuana licensed businesses, regardless of whether they pursue a DEA license." OMMA adds: "Licensees should consult with tax counsel regarding the applicability of Section 280E to their specific circumstances." Source: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/about/news/2026/update-dea-provides-application-instructions-to-medical-marijuana-dispensaries.html

Adult-use: remains Schedule I federally, so any adult-use activity in Oklahoma (which is in any event illegal under state law) remains fully subject to § 280E. No Oklahoma adult-use market exists to decouple for.

Oklahoma decoupling — the honest answer is layered:

  1. No standalone Oklahoma decoupling statute was confirmed as enacted. HB 3347 (2022) and HB 2101 (2023) both proposed a § 2358 deduction "equal to the amount of any deduction for business expense … disallowed … pursuant to … Section 280E" for licensed medical marijuana activity (HB 3347: tax years from 1 Jan 2023; HB 2101: from 1 Jan 2024). The copies located are committee/introduced versions. Neither is presented here as enacted law. A 2025 tax guide states flatly "No state decoupling from IRC § 280E: only Cost of Goods Sold may be deducted for state income tax" — that was the pre-rescheduling position.
  2. Conformity argument (secondary, not a statute): Oklahoma's corporate income tax (4% flat, secondary) piggybacks on federal taxable income. On that reasoning, once federal § 280E no longer disallows the expenses, the Oklahoma starting point automatically reflects the deduction, without separate state legislation. CannBus's Q3 2026 summary makes exactly this argument ("receive the benefit automatically, on the same federal effective date, without needing separate state legislation"), while its own market report elsewhere says "No state-level 280E decoupling was found. Confirm entity-specific tax treatment with a tax advisor." Both halves are reported here because they are both in the secondary record — the statutory position (no decoupling act found) and the conformity argument (benefit flows through automatically) are different claims and must not be merged.
  3. Compiler rule: state (a) federally, § 280E is generally lifted for OMMA medical licensees from 28 Apr 2026 per the fixed baseline + OMMA notice; (b) no enacted Oklahoma § 2358 decoupling act was located; (c) whether Oklahoma taxable income automatically follows the federal change is Verify with OTC guidance / tax counsel — do not publish "Oklahoma decouples" or "Oklahoma does not decouple" as a settled statutory conclusion on this evidence. Individual (non-corporate) licensees' Oklahoma adjusted gross income treatment is likewise Verify (the § 2358 proposals covered both corporate and individual adjustments in different subsections; the enacted § 2358 text was not opened).
  4. DEA registration wrinkle (Verify): secondary reporting in 2026 (OBN warnings relayed by trade press) suggests manufacturers/distributors must obtain DEA registration, with state enforcement from 1 Jan 2027 and a 60-day application window from 28 Apr 2026. OMMA's notice says 280E relief does not depend on DEA registration. Whether OBN/AG enforcement treats unregistered licensees differently for state purposes after 1 Jan 2027 is Verify — do not conflate DEA registration with § 280E eligibility.
