PART 3 — LOCAL RULES

3.1 The state framework: what counties and municipalities can and cannot do

Oklahoma is a medical-only programme (SQ 788, 26 June 2018, codified principally at Title 63, Oklahoma Statutes §§ 420 et seq. and §§ 427.1 et seq., the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana and Patient Protection Act, as amended by the 2019 Unity Bill, HB 2612, and later bills). Local power over medical marijuana businesses is therefore not a local opt-out/ban power. It is a zoning + code-compliance power, exercised through a state-mandated local certificate, within two express state limits:

(a) The anti-ban rule — dispensaries only, and narrowly drawn

63 O.S. § 425(F), as amended (SQ 788 § 6, as amended Laws 2019, c. 509, § 3; Laws 2020, c. 161, § 46; Laws 2021, c. 553, § 5; Laws 2022, c. 251, § 5), provides verbatim in relevant part:

"1. No city or local municipality may unduly change or restrict zoning laws to prevent the opening of a medical marijuana dispensary. 2. For purposes of this subsection, an undue change or restriction of municipal zoning laws means an act which entirely prevents medical marijuana dispensaries from operating within municipal boundaries as a matter of law. Municipalities may follow their standard planning and zoning procedures to determine if certain zones or districts would be appropriate for locating marijuana-licensed premises, medical marijuana businesses or any other premises where marijuana or its by-products are cultivated, grown, processed, stored or manufactured. 3. For purposes of this section, a medical marijuana dispensary does not include those other entities licensed by the Department as marijuana-licensed premises, medical marijuana businesses or other facilities or locations where marijuana or any product containing marijuana or its by-products are cultivated, grown, processed, stored or manufactured."

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-425v1/ — accessed 2026-10-30.

Reading, carefully: (i) The ban on "undue" change/restriction applies by its terms to dispensaries; subsection (F)(3) expressly carves growers, processors and other premises out of the definition of "dispensary" for this subsection. (ii) "Undue" is defined as an act that entirely prevents dispensaries from operating within municipal boundaries as a matter of law. A city that zones dispensaries into some districts but not others is, on the face of the statute, following "standard planning and zoning procedures" — it is not automatically in breach. (iii) Nothing in § 425(F) as opened here gives a city power to ban dispensaries outright, nor does it give a dispensary a right to locate in any particular district. Verify: no Oklahoma appellate decision construing § 425(F)'s "entirely prevents" test was directly opened for this file; do not cite a case gloss for it.

(b) The certificate of compliance — the real local gate

63 O.S. § 426.1(E) (added Laws 2019, c. 509, § 4; amended Laws 2021, c. 553, § 7, eff. 1 Nov 2021; Laws 2022, c. 251, § 6, eff. 1 Nov 2022) provides verbatim in relevant part:

"Any marijuana-licensed premises, medical marijuana business or any other premises where marijuana or its by-products are licensed to be cultivated, grown, processed, stored or manufactured shall submit with its application or request to change location, after notifying the political subdivision of its intent, a certificate of compliance from the political subdivision where the facility of the applicant or licensee is to be located certifying compliance with zoning classifications, applicable municipal ordinances and all applicable safety, electrical, fire, plumbing, waste, construction and building specification codes. Once a certificate of compliance has been submitted to the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority showing full compliance as outlined in this subsection, no additional certificate of compliance shall be required for license renewal unless a change of use or occupancy occurs, or there is any change concerning the facility or location that would, by law, require additional inspection, licensure or permitting by the state or municipality."

Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/2022/title-63/section-63-426-1v2/ — accessed 2026-10-30.

Later reform — certificate of occupancy / affidavit on renewal (SB 1635, 2024): OMMA's own summary of 2024 laws states that once a certificate of occupancy (COO) showing full compliance has already been submitted in an initial application or previous renewal, a renewal applicant must only submit an affidavit stating the premises continues to comply with applicable zoning, municipal ordinances and safety codes; municipalities and the State Fire Marshal may implement inspection programmes to verify compliance. Source: OMMA, "New State Laws Affect Commercial License Applications, Credentials and Final Product Testing" (GovDelivery bulletin): https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OKSDH/bulletins/3a32f8b — accessed 2026-10-30.

The current OAC text reflects the same structure: OAC 442:10-5-3(e)(8)–(9) requires, "if applicable," a certificate of compliance on an OMMA-prescribed/authorised form from the political subdivision, plus all Certificates of Occupancy, Final Inspection Reports and Site Plans issued/approved by the body enforcing building and fire codes adopted by the Oklahoma Uniform Building Code Commission (OAC 748:20); where local authorities do not issue/approve those documents, they must be obtained from the Oklahoma Office of the State Fire Marshal under 74 O.S. § 324.11. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/oklahoma/Okla-Admin-Code-SS-442-10-5-3 — accessed 2026-10-30. OAC 442:10-5-2(c)(2) repeats that once a certificate of compliance is properly submitted showing full compliance, no additional certificate is required for renewal unless a change of use/occupancy or other change requiring additional inspection, licensure or permitting occurs. Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-5/section-442-10-5-2/ — accessed 2026-10-30 (Justia text current through Vol. 42, No. 19, 16 June 2025).

Practical consequence: A city/county does not issue the OMMA licence, but without its certificate (or, on renewal, the affidavit/COO route above) the OMMA application is incomplete. The certificate covers zoning classification + municipal ordinances + safety, electrical, fire, plumbing, waste, construction and building codes — i.e. ordinary building/fire/utility enforcement, not a separate local cannabis licence in state law. Any local fee for the certificate or for local inspections is set locally (see § 3.4); state law as opened here does not fix a statewide local fee.

Unincorporated areas: "Political subdivision" in § 426.1(E) covers a county as well as a city/town. A business outside any city/town must therefore seek the certificate from the county. This is stated in OMMA's transporter-page links (which include an "Example County Certificate of Compliance Letter") and in the City of Tulsa's 2019 notice ("Businesses in unincorporated areas … should contact their respective county"). Sources: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/transporter-license.html and https://www.cityoftulsa.org/press-room/tulsa-medical-marijuana-businesses-now-required-to-complete-certificate-of-compliance/ — both accessed 2026-10-30. Verify: the current OMMA county-form itself was not directly opened; do not quote its fields.

Also required with the application (state level, local effect): OAC 442:10-5-3(b)–(e) requires the applicant to identify the city/county of the premises, attest that no licensed premises is on tribal lands, and attest that the business has obtained all applicable local licences and permits for all licensed premises. Source: Cornell OAC 442:10-5-3 link above — accessed 2026-10-30.

[AUDIT CORRECTION — § 3.1(c) school buffer.] The door-to-door measurement and 500-foot error allowance quoted below are from a superseded version of 63 O.S. § 425(G) and are not current law. Current § 425(G) (2023 text, as amended through Laws 2022, c.251): a medical marijuana dispensary is prohibited within 1,000 feet of a public or private school, measured from the nearest property line of the school to the nearest perimeter wall of the licensed premises; a dispensary meeting the rule at initial licensure may continue operating and is not subject to nonrenewal/revocation due to subsequent events, and a school established within 1,000 feet after licensure does not bar renewal or warrant revocation. The statute and OAC 442:10-5-3(e)(6)/OMMA pages therefore agree for dispensaries. The grower 1,000-foot distance is rule-based (OAC), not in § 425(G). The superseded quotation is retained below for traceability but must not be quoted as current law. Source: 63 O.S. § 425 (2023 text).

(c) The statewide school buffer — and a measurement conflict to flag

Two operative texts were directly opened and they do not measure the same way. Both are reproduced so the parent compiler does not silently pick one:

  1. Statute — 63 O.S. § 425(G): "Except as otherwise provided in this subsection, the location of any retail marijuana dispensary is specifically prohibited within one thousand (1,000) feet of any school entrance. On and after the effective date of this act, for purposes of calculating the 1,000-foot setback distance, the measurement shall be determined by calculating the distance in a straight line from the school door nearest the front door of the retail marijuana dispensary to the front door of the retail marijuana dispensary." Grandfathering: if a school is established within 1,000 feet after a licence has issued, the setback does not apply while the property is used for its original licensed purpose; and OMMA "shall not" deny issuance/renewal, deny a transfer on change of ownership, or revoke, for an error in measurement or failure to measure before an original licence issued — subject to § 426.1 municipal compliance. "Error in measurement" allows up to and including 500 feet on remeasurement after an original licence issued. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-425v1/ — accessed 2026-10-30.

  2. Rule — OAC 442:10-5-3(e)(6): "If a licensed dispensary or grower, proof that the location of the facility is at least one thousand (1,000) feet from a public or private school. For a dispensary, the distance specified shall be measured in a straight line from the nearest property line of such public school or private school to the nearest perimeter wall of the licensed premise of such medical marijuana dispensary. For a grower, the distance specified shall be measured in a straight line from the nearest property line of such public school or private school to the nearest property line of the licensed premises of such medical marijuana commercial grower." Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-5/section-442-10-5-3/ — accessed 2026-10-30. OMMA's own licence pages use the rule's formulation: dispensaries must show "the nearest perimeter wall is not within 1,000 feet of the property line for any public or private school"; growers must show "their property line is not within 1,000 feet of the property line of a public or private school." Sources: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/dispensary-license.html and https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/grower-license.html — accessed 2026-10-30.

Flag — Verify: which measurement OMMA applies to a contested new application today (door-to-door under § 425(G) vs. property-line-to-perimeter-wall under OAC 442:10-5-3 and the OMMA pages) was not resolved from a directly opened OMMA measurement guidance document. Present both; do not collapse them. "School" is as defined in 63 O.S. § 427.2 (§ 427.2(61) [AUDIT CORRECTION — former § 425(G)(3)(a) reference was wrong]); a secondary summary (not relied on for the law) notes HB 2612 defined school to include preschools and exclude homeschools/daycare/childcare — Verify that definition against current § 427.2 before republication.

Local buffers beyond the state school buffer: State law as opened here imposes no statewide buffer from churches, parks, libraries, childcare facilities or other dispensaries for OMMA licensing. Any such buffer is purely local (see the Hobart example in § 3.4, which is not a statewide rule). A city that adds a local buffer does so through its zoning code and certificate process, subject to the § 425(F) "entirely prevents" limit for dispensaries.

3.2 Zoning, inspections, utilities and moratoriums — general position

Topic State/local position as opened Source (accessed 2026-10-30)
Zoning authority Cities follow standard planning/zoning procedures to decide which zones/districts are appropriate for marijuana premises; they may not entirely prevent dispensaries from operating within municipal boundaries as a matter of law (§ 425(F)). Growers/processors/other premises are not within § 425(F)'s "dispensary" definition. https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-425v1/
Certificate of compliance Required with application or location change, from the political subdivision (city or county), certifying zoning + ordinances + safety/electrical/fire/plumbing/waste/construction/building codes (§ 426.1(E)). Renewal: no new certificate unless change of use/occupancy or change requiring further inspection/licensure/permitting; SB 1635 (2024) COO + affidavit route on renewal. https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/2022/title-63/section-63-426-1v2/ ; https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OKSDH/bulletins/3a32f8b
Building/fire inspections (local) Certificate process in Oklahoma City expressly involves building, electrical, mechanical, plumbing, fire and industrial-waste inspections and a 2–3 week process (see § 3.4). Elsewhere, the inspecting body is the political subdivision or, where it has no jurisdiction agreement, the State Fire Marshal (OAC 442:10-5-3(e)(9); 74 O.S. § 324.11). https://www.okc.gov/Infrastructure-Development/Business-Licensing/Certificate-of-Compliance-Medical-Marijuana ; https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/oklahoma/Okla-Admin-Code-SS-442-10-5-3
OMMA inspections Application constitutes permission for entry/inspection of licensed premises and transport vehicles during hours of operation and other reasonable times. OMMA may perform two on-site inspections per calendar year of each grower, processor, dispensary or commercial transporter, plus additional inspections to correct/investigate violations; it may use secret shoppers. Labs: one pre-licensure inspection + up to two annually. Transporter warehouses: one pre-approval inspection per warehouse location. Research/education: up to two per calendar year, may be unannounced. https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/oklahoma/OAC-442-10-5-4 ; https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-4/section-442-10-4-4/
Utilities — water/electricity reporting Verify — do not present as current law. A 2022 bill, HB 4055, in conference form would have required public utilities to report monthly electricity/water supplied to licensed grows to OMMA in a format integrated with seed-to-sale software, with OMMA to make rules for non-utility supply (well water, gas generators), and permanent revocation for refusal/failure or use of an unpermitted water source. Later bills on the same subject were filed in 2023 (HB 1711: growers inform retail suppliers/cooperatives and transmit monthly electricity/water reports to OMMA; SB 801 in the same terms). Whether HB 4055 was enacted in that form and where, if anywhere, a utility-reporting duty is now codified was not confirmed from a directly opened current statute in this research. OMMA's separate, confirmed monthly-report duty is different: all commercial licensees must file an OMMA monthly report by the 15th of each month for the previous month's activity, even with no product on site (see Part 4, § 4.7). HB 4055 conference summary via search result (secondary fiscal summary, not a directly opened enrolled act) — Verify; HB 1711 text: https://pluralpolicy.com/app/legislative-tracking/bill/details/state-ok-2023-hb1711 ; OMMA monthly-report reminder: http://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OKSDH/bulletins/309933a
Local fees No statewide local fee. Fees are set by each city/county for its own certificate/inspection process (Oklahoma City and Norman examples in § 3.4; all other required jurisdictions: Verify — see § 3.3 table). See § 3.4
State licence moratorium (not a local moratorium) 26 Aug 2022 – 1 Aug 2028 for new dispensary, grower and processor licences (HB 3208 (2022); HB 2095 (2023) to 1 Aug 2026; HB 3143 (2026) to 1 Aug 2028, unless OMMA's Executive Director determines all pending licensing reviews, inspections or investigations are complete). Renewals unaffected. See Part 4, § 4.6 for full treatment and the HB 3144 caveat. https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/grower-license.html ; https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/dispensary-license.html ; https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/processor-license.html
Local moratoriums No statewide local moratorium was located, and no city-specific local moratorium ordinance was directly opened for any required jurisdiction in this research. Searches for a local (city council) moratorium returned only the state OMMA moratorium. That is a negative search result, not proof that no city ever imposed a temporary pause: Verify per city before stating that a given city has never had one. In particular, early local action in 2018–2019 was about creating certificate processes (e.g. Tulsa, Nov 2019), not about a published local licence freeze located here. Searches 2026-10-30; Tulsa notice: https://www.cityoftulsa.org/press-room/tulsa-medical-marijuana-businesses-now-required-to-complete-certificate-of-compliance/

3.3 Is there an official list of local rules? — No, and the jurisdictions checked

Finding: No official consolidated list of local (county/municipal) medical marijuana rules was located. OMMA does not publish, on the pages directly opened here, a directory of city/county zoning codes, certificate fees or local buffers. OMMA's licence pages point applicants to the "Commercial Application Checklist," FAQs and OAC 442:10, and to the political subdivision itself for the certificate. The applicant must therefore check (a) the state certificate requirement (§ 426.1(E)), (b) the city/county zoning code for the parcel, and (c) that jurisdiction's certificate/inspection fee schedule, one jurisdiction at a time.

3.4 Local permit fees and buffer rules where they exist (directly opened examples only)

Oklahoma City — Medical Marijuana Certificate of Compliance (MMCC)

Source: City of Oklahoma City, "Certificate of Compliance (Medical Marijuana)": https://www.okc.gov/Infrastructure-Development/Business-Licensing/Certificate-of-Compliance-Medical-Marijuana — accessed 2026-10-30. Municipal Code cited on the page: § 60-13-80.

  • Required for: OMMA business licence applications for both new and renewal licences (city page wording; note the state renewal position in § 3.1(b) — COO/affidavit — may now govern renewals, so the city page's "both" wording should be read with SB 1635 — Verify current OKC renewal practice).
  • Test: compliance with city codes on zoning, fire, waste and specific building safety codes. Each OMMA licence type requires a separate MMCC application.
  • Process: submit application + floor plan identifying all rooms/fixtures + legal description of property; payment at time of application; plans/application reviewed for building codes, zoning and related ordinances; fire, industrial waste and construction inspectors inspect; process generally 2–3 weeks; additional permits/inspections may be required before acceptance. If no construction work has been done, "status check" inspections are required (building/electrical/mechanical/plumbing, fire, and — for grow and processing facilities — industrial waste/pretreatment via the Utilities Department).
  • Fees (city page, as opened):
MMCC type Fee
Dispensary $615
Grow facility (+ engineered mechanical plans) $750
Processing facility $750
Research facility $750
Transporter $100
Education facility $750
Testing laboratory $750
  • Zoning (Oklahoma City): The city's medical-marijuana use-unit associations document (https://www.okc.gov/files/c676d6bc-1d4a-471a-a508-6ced133f564e/2-Medical-Marijuana-Use-Unit-Associations.pdf — accessed 2026-10-30) maps OMMA uses onto Chapter 59 use units. In summary: cultivation/processing uses fall under Agricultural Processing (general/limited) and related units — special permit/conditional use in most commercial/industrial districts; dispensaries fall under Retail Sales and Services: Medical Marijuana Dispensary — permitted use in NB, C-2, C-3, C-4, C-CBD, I-1, I-2, I-3, BC, DBD, DTD-2, and districts 4G and 5 of NC, SYD, and DTD-1 except Cottage District & Area-2; conditional use in O-2, with additional district restrictions possibly applying; growing as an accessory use to a dispensary only where the product grown is sold directly to the consumer by the on-site dispensary. All uses are subject to OMMA regulation, and the city may require building/electrical/mechanical/plumbing permits or licences before an MMCC issues. Verify the current Chapter 59 tables before advising on a specific parcel — the associations document is undated in the copy opened and district lists are paraphrased here, not quoted as code.

Norman — local licence fees (Ordinance O-2122-16, 2021–22) and FAQ

Source for fees: City of Norman Ordinance O-2122-16 (amending ch. 13 § 13-108 and ch. 22 zoning, adding medical-marijuana waste-facility uses and implementing 2021 state-law updates): https://mccmeetingspublic.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/normanok-meet-c7199f46cfa04fbc8939e65e0fa874c7/ITEM-Attachment-001-58e5d56022ce4dd4b7e1f715c8a1f2e2.pdf — accessed 2026-10-30.   • Local licence fees in O-2122-16, § 13-108: medical marijuana dispensary $600 initial / $450 renewal; Tier I/II processor $600 initial / $450 renewal (a Tier I or II processor that also holds a dispensary licence for the location gets a separate processor licence but pays no duplicative initial/renewal fee); Tier III processor $900 initial and renewal (hazardous and all-other classifications both $900 in the text opened). Note: Norman's local "Tier I/II/III processor" labels are local labels; they do not change OMMA's state processor fee tiers in Part 4, and the ordinance itself notes that Tier I local licences would no longer be issued after 1 Nov 2021 to implement state law on pre-rolls. Verify current Norman fee schedule — this ordinance is from the 2021–22 cycle.

Small-city illustration — NOT a statewide rule, NOT a required jurisdiction

A municipal code section located in searching (§ 92.02, Hobart, OK, via American Legal: https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/hobartok/latest/hobart_ok/0-0-0-3318 — accessed 2026-10-30) illustrates how far local variation can go: state licence required at that location; a municipal permit of $600/year for retail dispensaries and $1,500 for commercial growing/processing facilities; dispensaries limited to commercial districts, prohibited within 1,000 feet of a school entrance or within 300 feet of any church, and not on residentially zoned property; grows permitted in commercial/industrial/agricultural districts subject to the same 1,000-ft school / 300-ft church prohibitions and no residential zoning. This is Hobart's code only. It is included solely to show that a 300-ft church buffer exists somewhere locally; it must not be generalised to Oklahoma City, Tulsa, Norman or any other city, and it must not be cited as state law.

3.5 Business concentration — only what official sources state

Rule applied here: No ranking, clustering estimate or "top county" claim is made by this research. The only concentration statements below are those attributable to OMMA or to an OMMA spokesperson as reported, with dates. A county-by-county OMMA breakdown was not reproduced from a directly opened OMMA dashboard/list in this research, so no county table is given — that gap belongs to Part 5 (licence data sources), not to inference here.

  • Early concentration (secondary analysis of OMMA approvals, Nov 2018 — historical only): A November 2018 analysis of OMMA-approved applications reported Oklahoma County (532) and Tulsa County (232) as the two counties with the most approved applications at that date, with Oklahoma City the largest city total. Source: New Cannabis Ventures, "An Early Look at Over 2000 Oklahoma Medical Cannabis License Applications" (Nov 2018): https://www.newcannabisventures.com/an-early-look-at-over-2000-oklahoma-medical-cannabis-license-applications/ — accessed 2026-10-30. Do not use 2018 shares as a 2026 concentration finding.
  • Statewide contraction (OMMA figures as reported, dated snapshots — do not mix):
  • At the moratorium's start, 26 Aug 2022: 7,285 growers, 2,374 dispensaries, 1,464 processors (OMMA spokesperson via Oklahoma Voice, 13 Nov 2023). Source: https://oklahomavoice.com/2023/11/13/new-oklahoma-law-extends-marijuana-business-license-moratorium-until-2026/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • January 2026 (OMMA licensing/tax data as reported): 2,261 growers, 1,453 dispensaries, 710 processors. Source: OMMA figures as reported in secondary summaries of the OMMA dashboard, e.g. https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/ok_cannmir.html — accessed 2026-10-30. Verify against the OMMA dashboard itself before republication as a headline.
  • September/October 2026 (OMMA dashboard as reported, two nearby snapshots that differ slightly by report date): ~1,703–1,735 growers, ~1,259–1,295 dispensaries, ~557–574 processors (Sep 1, 2026 vs. Oct 1, 2026 reports). Sources: https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/ok_cannmir.html and https://www.cannabisnews.org/united-states-cannabis-news/oklahoma-omma-director-adria-berry-steps-down-jason-yingling-interim/ — accessed 2026-10-30. The range reflects different report dates, not a contradiction to be averaged; the parent compiler should pick one dated OMMA report and cite its date.
  • What OMMA itself states about geography: OMMA's licence pages require every application to identify the city/county of the premises (63 O.S. § 427.14(E)(2); OAC 442:10-5-3), and § 426.1(D) requires OMMA to make a list of licensed premises available to state agencies and political subdivisions to aid identification and compliance within their jurisdiction. No county ranking is stated on the OMMA licence pages opened here.

PART 4 — LICENCE TYPES

4.0 Overview and governing law

Licence categories created by statute: 63 O.S. § 427.14(A) (text effective 1 June 2023, as opened) creates the medical marijuana business licence in five categories: (1) commercial grower; (2) processor; (3) dispensary; (4) transporter; (5) testing laboratory. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/2022/title-63/section-63-427-14v3/ — accessed 2026-10-30.

Separate facility licences created elsewhere in Title 63: research facility (63 O.S. § 427.19 et seq.) and education facility (§ 427.20 et seq.), and waste disposal licence + facility permit (§ 430, Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Waste Management Act, SB 882 (2019)). OMMA's commercial-licences index lists all eight: grower, processor, dispensary, transporter, testing laboratory, waste disposal, research and education. The OMMA pages for each type are the primary source for "what each allows" below.

Common rules for all commercial types (unless a type page says otherwise): - Term: one year (12 months from issuance). OAC 442:10-5-2(a); OAC 442:10-4-2(a) for research/education. Sources: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-5/section-442-10-5-2/ and https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-4/section-442-10-4-2/ — accessed 2026-10-30. - Processing time: OMMA states it processes commercial applications within 90 business days (63 O.S. § 427.14(F) — approval, rejection, denial or status-update letter within 90 business days of receipt; an application rejected for missing information may be resubmitted within 30 days for reconsideration with no additional fee). - Fees are nonrefundable; applications must be complete and accurate, with full remittance (§ 427.14(E)(6)). - A grower, processor or dispensary licence is valid for a single location at the address on the application (OAC 442:10-5-2(b)). A grower, processor and dispensary, or any combination, may share the same address/physical location subject to the Act's restrictions (§ 427.14(E)(8)). - No limit on number of licences/categories per person/entity in § 427.14(E)(8) ("There shall be no limit to the number of medical marijuana business licenses or categories that an individual or entity can apply for or receive, although each application and each category shall require a separate application and application fee") — subject to the moratorium (§ 4.6), the waste-disposal history (§ 4.4, formerly capped at 10), any lab-ownership conflict rule, and any cap enacted by HB 3144 if enacted (see § 4.6 — Verify, do not treat as law). A separate OMMA rule amendment noted in rulemaking materials provides for one commercial grower licence for any one property (OAC 442:10-5-2(b) as amended) — Verify the current text of that paragraph before advising on multi-licence single-parcel structures. - Credit-card processing fee (where OMMA states it): 2.25% of the application fee, plus $2 [AUDIT CORRECTION — OMMA's printed formula; OMMA tier-table totals prevail where they differ by $0.05]. E.g. $2,500 → $58.30; $5,000 → $114.55; $10,000 → $227.05; $20,000 → $452.04; $500 → $13.30. The dispensary page's worked example uses $58.25 for a $2,500 fee (2.25% of $2,502) — a $0.05 rounding difference between OMMA pages; the fee itself ($2,500) is unaffected. Flagged here so the compiler does not "correct" one page from the other.

4.1 Licence-by-licence table (fees are annual, nonrefundable, unless stated)

Licence type What it allows (OMMA page) Annual application fee (base, excl. card fee) Official info page (accessed 2026-10-30)
Commercial grower Legally grow marijuana for medical purposes. May sell only to licensed processors, dispensaries and other growers — not directly to patients. Tiered — see § 4.2. Indoor/greenhouse/light-deprivation: $2,500–$50,000 + $0.25/sq ft over 100,000 sq ft. Outdoor: $2,500–$50,000 + $250/acre over 50 acres. https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/grower-license.html
Processor — hazardous or non-hazardous, by extraction chemicals Legally process marijuana for medical purposes. May sell to licensed dispensaries and other licensed processors. May also process marijuana into concentrated form for a patient licence holder for a fee. Tiered by biomass/concentrate volume — see § 4.2: $2,500 / $5,000 / $10,000 / $15,000 / $20,000. https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/processor-license.html
Dispensary Legally sell medical marijuana and medical marijuana products, including mature plants and seedlings. May sell only to other licensed dispensaries, patient licence holders, caregiver licence holders, research licence holders, and the parent/legal guardian named on a minor patient's licence. Formula, not flat: initial $2,500; annual renewal = 10% of the sum of 12 calendar months of combined annual state sales tax + state excise (medical marijuana) tax for that dispensary (state sales tax only — local sales tax excluded). Minimum $2,500, maximum $10,000. https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/dispensary-license.html
Commercial transporter (standalone) Transport medical marijuana/products between other licensed businesses, through licensed transporter agents. May not grow, process or sell its own medical marijuana — only transport others' products. May operate one or more warehouses (separate application per warehouse from the same online account; each warehouse needs its own Certificate of Compliance). $2,500 (+ $58.30 card fee) standalone. No additional fee when issued simultaneously with a grower, processor, dispensary or laboratory licence (for that licensee's own product). https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/transporter-license.html
Transporter agent (individual) Individual employees/owners/agents authorised to drive/transport on behalf of a licensed transporter, grower, processor, dispensary, laboratory, research or education facility. The business applies on the employee's behalf through its business account; the agent carries an OMMA transporter agent ID card while transporting. A separate application/fee is required per employing business. $25 per agent licence (OAC 442:10-3-3(b)). Valid 1 year; does not extend beyond the employing business licence's expiration/surrender/revocation. An agent licence appearing active in OMMA Verify is active even if the listed expiration date has passed, where a timely renewal was submitted. https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/transporter-license.html ; https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-3/section-442-10-3-3/
Testing laboratory Analyse harvested and processed medical-use marijuana for harmful contaminants. May charge other commercial licensees fees for compliance testing. Ownership conflict: lab owners may not hold a direct/indirect beneficial interest in a licensed dispensary, grower or processor (stated in 2019 legislative summary; Verify current OAC 442:10-8 text before republication). $20,000 (+ $452.04 card fee, for applications on/after 1 June 2023). https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/testing-laboratory-license.html
Research facility Grow, cultivate, possess and transfer, by sale or donation, marijuana to other licensed research facilities and licensed testing laboratories, for the limited research purposes approved in the application: (1) test chemical potency/composition; (2) clinical investigations of marijuana-derived medicinal products; (3) efficacy/safety research on marijuana as medical treatment; (4) genomic, horticultural or agricultural research; (5) research on marijuana-affiliated products/systems (63 O.S. § 427.19). Must supply a project description. Biomedical/clinical research subject to federal regulation/institutional oversight is not subject to OMMA licensure. Private-business applicants must supply ownership information; public-funds/public-institution applicants face additional criteria. $500 (+ $13.30 card fee). https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/research-license.html
Education facility Provide training/education on cultivation, growing, harvesting, curing, preparing, packaging or testing of medical marijuana, or production/manufacture/extraction/processing/packaging/creation of infused products, for the limited education/research purposes approved in the application. May transfer, by sale or donation, marijuana grown in its operation to licensed research licensees, and to licensed testing laboratories. Must be a non-profit and provide non-profit registration. Must supply a project description. Biomedical/clinical matters subject to federal/institutional oversight are not subject to OMMA licensure. Public-funds/public-institution applicants face additional criteria. $500 (+ $13.30 card fee). https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/education-license.html
Waste disposal facility (licence + permit) Possess, transport and dispose of medical marijuana waste. No person/entity may dispose of medical marijuana waste without a valid waste disposal licence (63 O.S. § 430(A)). OMMA issues only on proper application + a finding that the proposed site/facility is physically and technically suitable; it may issue a temporary licence for treatment/storage for up to 90 days where public health/safety requires emergency action. Note: commercial licensees/research/education facilities may destroy certain plant parts themselves without using a disposal facility under the Waste Management Act (see Part 11 scope — Verify the current list of self-destroyable parts). Licence $5,000 (initial); facility permit $500 per facility per year; revoked permit reinstatement $500 (§ 430(F)). Card fee for the $5,000 licence: $114.55 (secondary summary — Verify on the OMMA waste page, which was not directly opened for this file). Statute: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-430/ ; OMMA waste page not directly opened — Verify its URL/fee display before republication.

No other OMMA commercial licence type was located on the OMMA commercial-licences pages opened here. In particular: there is no separate OMMA "retailer" distinct from dispensary, no "microbusiness" category, no "delivery" licence (delivery by dispensaries is separately prohibited in OAC — Part 1 scope, not decided here), and no standalone "cultivation for adult use" licence, because Oklahoma is medical-only. Employee credentials (SB 1704 (2022)) and patient/caregiver licences are not commercial licence types and are not in the table above; employee-credential fee/requirements were not confirmed from a directly opened OMMA page — Verify (see § 4.8).

4.2 Tiered fees in full (grower and processor)

Grower — indoor, greenhouse or light-deprivation (canopy, sq ft). "Canopy" = total surface area within a cultivation area dedicated to flowering plants, including each tier/shelf of a tiered/shelving system, excluding areas used only for immature plants/seedlings prior to flowering; vertically grown cylinders measured by circumference × length (§ 427.14(D)(2)(d)). A combined indoor + outdoor operation at one location requires a separate licence for each type of grow operation, each with its own tier fee.

Tier Canopy Base fee Card fee Total (OMMA page)

4.3 Requirements — age, residency/ownership, background checks, OBNDD, land and bond

Age: Applicants must be 25 years or older (§ 427.14(E)(7)(a); stated on every OMMA commercial page opened). For entities, the age test is applied as OMMA's pages state it ("Licenses are available for Oklahoma residents who are at least 25 years old") — the precise application to entity principals is in the checklist, Verify if an entity has a principal under 25.

Residency and ownership — the 75% rule (current, and NOT struck down): - Individual applicant: proof the applicant is an Oklahoma resident (§ 427.14(E)(7)(b)). - Entity applicant: proof that 75% of all members, managers, executive officers, partners, board members or any other form of business ownership are Oklahoma residents (§ 427.14(E)(7)(c)). OMMA's transporter FAQ states the same for entities, and adds that members/managers/board members of entity applicants must all be Oklahoma residents in the FAQ's wording — read with the statute's 75% test; the FAQ wording and the statute are not identical, Verify which OMMA applies to a given entity form. - What counts as residency: proof of Oklahoma residency for at least 2 years immediately preceding the application or 5 years of continuous Oklahoma residency during the preceding 25 years (§ 427.14(E)(11); OAC 442:10-5-3.1). Acceptable documents (combination, covering the entire period): unexpired Oklahoma driver licence/Real ID, Oklahoma ID card, utility bill (excluding cellular/internet), residential property deed, rental agreement for Oklahoma residential property, and (per OMMA pages) Oklahoma tax returns or other documentation OMMA deems sufficient. Pre-30 Aug 2019 licensees are exempt from the 2-year/5-year requirement (§ 427.14(E)(11), last sentence). - Disclosure: all ownership interests must be disclosed (§ 427.14(E)(7)(e)), including, per the 10th Circuit's summary of § 427.2, any person holding an interest or convertible note in an entity that owns/operates/manages a licensed facility — Verify the current § 427.2 definition number before quoting it. - Foreign financial interest: state law requires growers, processors, dispensaries, labs and transporters to submit a Foreign Financial Interest Attestation to the Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs Control (OBNDD) within 60 days (secondary summary of OMMA guidance — Verify the current attestation form/deadline on OMMA/OBNDD pages).

Court rulings on residency — correction of the task premise: The task brief suggested a 10th Circuit/federal ruling "striking" residency. That is not what the cases found say:

  1. Original Investments, LLC v. Oklahoma, W.D. Okla., 4 June 2021 — residency challenge DISMISSED, merits NOT reached. A Washington firm sued, claiming the residency requirement (then 63 O.S. § 427.14(E)(7), barring non-residents from obtaining a licence and from owning more than 25%) violated the Dormant Commerce Clause. The court dismissed on the clean-hands doctrine — it would not use equitable power to facilitate activity illegal under federal law — and described the Dormant Commerce Clause claim only as "not frivolous." It did not hold the requirement unconstitutional, and it did not enjoin enforcement. Sources: Vanderbilt Marijuana Law blog summary, 2021: https://my.vanderbilt.edu/marijuanalaw/2021/06/did-federal-judge-give-oklahoma-a-free-pass-to-violate-the-constitution/ — accessed 2026-10-30; MJBizDaily, 7 June 2021 ("Judge refuses to overturn Oklahoma medical cannabis residency provision") via search result — accessed 2026-10-30.
  2. United States v. Stacy, 10th Cir. 2025 — residency requirement treated as operative law, not struck. The 10th Circuit's background section recites §§ 422(B)(4) and 427.14(E)(7)(c) (75% rule, disclosure) as the legal framework for a federal prosecution arising from a two-entity structure designed to hide out-of-state ownership; it affirmed denial of an injunction against prosecution because the defendant had not substantially complied with Oklahoma law (including non-disclosure of the structure to OMMA). It is not a holding that residency is unconstitutional. Source: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-10th-circuit/117755205.html — accessed 2026-10-30.
  3. State-court renewal litigation (secondary report, not a holding located here): A Tulsa-firm class action (Genesis Canna-Farms LLP et al., Oklahoma County District Court, reported 2020–21) alleged OMMA was denying renewals to businesses licensed in 2018 because owners did not meet the later 2-year residency rule or the changed school-measurement rules. No judgment striking the rule was located in this research — Verify outcome; do not cite it as authority that renewals are exempt. The statutory pre-30 Aug 2019 exemption in § 427.14(E)(11) is the only exemption directly confirmed here.

Bottom line for Part 4: As of 30 Oct 2026, the 75% / 2-year-or-5-in-25 residency rule appears on every current OMMA commercial page and in § 427.14, and no directly opened appellate decision strikes it. Present it as in effect, constitutionally untested on the merits at appellate level.

Background checks: - All applicants for a business, research or education licence, or renewal, must undergo an Oklahoma criminal history background check by the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation (OSBI) within 30 days prior to application, covering individual applicants, individuals applying on behalf of an entity, all principal officers, and all owners (§ 427.14(E)(9)). OSBI fees are the applicant's and may not exceed fees charged to any other person/industry (§ 427.14(E)(10)). - Disqualifier: proof the applicant/licensee "has not been convicted of a nonviolent felony in the last two (2) years, or any other felony conviction within the last five (5) years, is not a current inmate in the custody of the Department of Corrections, or currently incarcerated in a jail or corrections facility" (§ 427.14(E)(7)(f)). OMMA's transporter FAQ phrases it as: nonviolent felony in the last 2 years and any other felony in the last 5 years for any owner disqualifies. - National fingerprint check — transitional position: OMMA's transporter page states that a new attestation form + state background check temporarily meet the national background check requirement in HB 2095 (2023); all persons of interest and transporter agents must upload a completed OSBI state check and an OMMA Attestation Regarding National Background Check. OMMA's 2024-law summary states HB 1734 (2024) clarified national fingerprint-based checks via OSBI but "will take time to come into effect" and applicants should continue with the attestation + state check until OMMA updates them. Source: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/transporter-license.html and https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OKSDH/bulletins/3a32f8b — accessed 2026-10-30. Verify whether the national fingerprint process is live on 30 Oct 2026; do not state it is live. - Other bars (transporter FAQ, stated as application requirements): nobody with an ownership interest may be a sheriff, deputy sheriff, police officer or prosecuting officer, or an officer/employee of OMMA or of the municipality where the entity is located; entity applicants (unless sole proprietorship/general partnership) must submit an Oklahoma Secretary of State certificate of good standing issued within 30 days of submission; applicants must supply ownership-disclosure documentation and an Affidavit of Lawful Presence (if not a U.S. citizen) with supporting documents. Source: transporter page FAQ — accessed 2026-10-30. Verify whether each bar applies identically to every licence type or only as stated on the transporter page.

OBNDD registration: All licence applicants must submit a registration with OBNDD as provided in 63 O.S. §§ 2-302 through 2-304 (§ 427.14(E)(12)), and a new owner on transfer is not authorised to take possession/control until OMMA approval and OBNDD registration (OAC 442:10-5-2(f)).

Land ownership / lease disclosure and the grower bond: - Grower bond or 5-year ownership (both required to be proved on new and renewal grower applications): OMMA's grower page: applicants must submit proof of either (a) a surety bond of at least $50,000 per licence, or (b) proof the licensee has owned the licensed premises for at least 5 years. OMMA verifies the bond/ownership during review. Source: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/grower-license.html — accessed 2026-10-30. Statutory basis: 63 O.S. § 427.26 (SB 913 (2023) framework; OMMA/DEQ may require a higher bond for reclamation — secondary summary, Verify the current § 427.26 text). - Proposed increase — NOT current law on the evidence opened: SB 1242 (2026) as engrossed would raise the minimum to $100,000 per licence, effective 1 Nov 2026. Its final enacted status was not confirmed from a directly opened enrolled act in this research (BillTrack50 lists it as "Passed, Dead" in conflicting fields; secondary summaries disagree). Do not present $100,000 as the current bond. The OMMA grower page as opened still states $50,000. Flag SB 1242 as Verify on oklegislature.gov before any 1 Nov 2026 update. - Lease disclosure: OMMA's commercial application requires the premises address/county and ownership disclosure, and secondary guides state proof of ownership or lease is required for dispensaries/growers. The specific OAC paragraph requiring a lease instrument was not directly opened in full for this file — Verify OAC 442:10-5-3(e) lease language before stating that a lease (as opposed to ownership disclosure + certificate of compliance) is a standalone filing. What is confirmed: the licence is tied to the physical address on file (transporter FAQ: "Your physical address needs to match the one that OMMA has on file … Your license is tied to this location"), and a location change requires a new certificate/occupancy package (OAC 442:10-5-2(e)). - Waste-disposal land/facility suitability: OMMA must find the proposed waste site/facility physically and technically suitable (§ 430(A)); a DEQ permit is stated as required in secondary summaries — Verify on the OMMA waste page / § 430 screening text (see § 4.1).

4.4 Waste-disposal specifics (supplement to § 4.1)

  • Cap history: § 430(A) provided OMMA "shall not, until November 1, 2021, issue more than ten medical marijuana waste disposal licenses. Beginning November 1, 2021, there shall be no limit." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-430/ — accessed 2026-10-30. (An earlier bill text said 1 Nov 2020; the current Justia text says 1 Nov 2021 — use the current text.)
  • Screening: § 430(B) requires a screening process (sufficient liability insurance and physical/technical suitability are the elements named in secondary summaries). Insurance minimums stated secondarily as $5 million each occurrence for Pollution Legal Liability and $5 million each occurrence for Commercial General Liability — Verify against § 430(B) full text / OMMA waste page; not quoted from a directly opened official page here.
  • Waste licence holders need no separate transporter licence for transporting waste (§ 430, SB 882 enrolled text).
  • Commercial licensees must use a licensed waste disposal service for waste they do not lawfully destroy themselves (Waste Management Act) — Verify current self-destruction list (Part 11).

4.5 Testing-laboratory specifics (supplement to § 4.1)

  • Accreditation: applicants must show documentation of accreditation to ISO/IEC 17025 by ANAB, A2LA, PJLA, IAS or COLA (OMMA testing page). Source: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/testing-laboratory-license.html — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Pre-licensure inspection + proficiency testing: OAC 442:10-5-4(c) — one on-site inspection before licensure, which may include proficiency testing and verification of analyte-specific thresholds under OAC 442:10-8-2; up to two inspections annually thereafter.
  • Verify: whether a lab licence is within the moratorium (OMMA moratorium notices appear on grower/processor/dispensary pages only; the lab page as summarised does not carry the moratorium banner — see § 4.6).

[AUDIT CORRECTIONS — § 4.6.] HB 3144: the proposed 2,550 grower cap is not law (passed House 82–15 on 25 Feb 2026 and Senate 34–12 on 29 Apr 2026; Senate amendments received 29 Apr 2026; no enrolled act or approval located — died without enactment; the “2,500” figure in some secondary reports is wrong for HB 3144 as engrossed). SB 1242 $100,000 bond: not law (Senate-engrossed only; House substitute replaced the bond with a $2,000 land reclamation fee and repeal of § 427.26; no approval shown; current bond remains $50,000 or 5-year ownership). HB 3143 transfer bar and signing date (“5 May 2026”) remain Verify against the enrolled HB 3143 act. Utility reporting (HB 4055/HB 1711/SB 801) is not law — all three died without enactment (see audit.md).

4.6 The moratorium — which types, dates, extensions, and what is NOT frozen

Date / instrument Effect (as stated on OMMA pages opened)
26 Aug 2022 — HB 3208 (2022) Moratorium began on processing/issuing new dispensary, grower and processor licences. OMMA states it reviews/processes applications received on or before 26 Aug 2022 (OAC 442:10-5-3(h)).
HB 2095 (2023) Extended end date to 1 Aug 2026. (OAC text current through 16 June 2025 still states "Beginning August 26, 2022, and ending August 1, 2026" — that OAC text predates HB 3143 and is superseded for the end date by the OMMA pages below; do not cite the OAC end date as current.)
HB 3143 (2026) Further extended end date to 1 Aug 2028, unless OMMA's Executive Director determines all pending licensing reviews, inspections or investigations are complete. OMMA's grower, processor and dispensary pages all carry this exact banner (processor page last modified 22 July 2026). Secondary summaries date the signing to 5 May 2026 — Verify the enrolled HB 3143 text/date on oklegislature.gov; the OMMA banner is the primary evidence relied on here.
Renewals Expressly not affected: "The moratorium does not affect current licensees, who can apply for renewal." (OMMA banner on all three pages.) OAC 442:10-5-3(h) likewise excepts renewals.
Transfers / location changes necessitated by other events OAC 442:10-5-3(h) states the moratorium "shall not apply to" renewals and to "the issuance of a medical marijuana business license necessitated by [events stated in the full paragraph — text truncated in the copy opened]". Verify the full (h)(2) exception list before advising that a transfer is outside the moratorium. Separately, HB 3143 is secondarily reported to prohibit transfers while administrative action is pending (including action that could lead to revocation/suspension/non-renewal, or OBNDD registration action), requiring full resolution first and barring a transfer application for at least 6 months after an annulment/revocation/suspension — Verify against enrolled HB 3143; do not present the transfer bar as confirmed statute here.
Types NOT named in the OMMA moratorium banner Transporter (standalone), testing laboratory, waste disposal, research and education are not named in the banner on the grower/processor/dispensary pages, and OAC 442:10-5-3(h) names only dispensaries, processors and growers. Several secondary summaries claim the freeze covers four categories including transporter, or describe transporter/lab/waste/research/education as "open despite the moratorium" — the two secondary positions conflict. This file follows the OMMA banner + OAC text (three types frozen) and flags the four-category claim as Verify. In practice, a new standalone transporter/lab/waste/research/education application should be confirmed with OMMA before it is described as "open" in a client-facing document.

Are applications "open"? For grower, processor and dispensary: No — new applications are not being processed/issued (except pre-26 Aug 2022 applications and renewals). For the other types: Verify with OMMA per the paragraph above; do not state categorically that they are open. There is no lottery and no numeric cap in § 427.14(E)(8) for the frozen types — the freeze is time-based, not cap-based (again subject to the HB 3144 caveat below).

HB 3144 — grower cap — Verify, do NOT present as law. Secondary sources conflict sharply: one (CannBus, Q3 2026) lists "HB 3144 enacted (permanent 2,550 grower cap)"; another (same publisher's legal summary, earlier in 2026) lists it as pending; a third reports it passed the House 82–15 with no Senate enactment confirmed; a fourth reports it "passed both chambers in 2026, but it is not confirmed as law." No enrolled HB 3144 act was directly opened for this file. Treatment: HB 3144 is pending/unconfirmed as of 30 Oct 2026. Do not cite a 2,550 (or 2,500) grower cap as current law. If enacted, it would be the first numeric cap on growers (active growers were ~2,136–2,261 in early 2026 on OMMA figures, i.e. below 2,550 on those snapshots — secondary arithmetic, Verify).

4.7 Renewal, pending-renewal, transfer, relocation, inspections and site verification

Renewal — timing and late fees (OAC 442:10-5-2(c) and OMMA transfer notice): - It is the licence holder's responsibility to renew prior to expiration, with all applicable documentation, under OAC 442:10-5-3. - OMMA may require further information/documentation and additional background checks on renewal, and may refuse renewal for failure to meet Title 63 §§ 420 et seq. / §§ 427.1 et seq. / OAC 442:10, or the Waste Management Act. - Timely vs. late (current rule, from 1 Nov 2024): Only a renewal application submitted between 120 and 60 calendar days before expiration [AUDIT CORRECTION] is "timely" for the 90-business-day review guarantee (63 O.S. § 427.14(N), as summarised in OMMA's 7 Mar 2025 transfer notice). A renewal submitted less than 60 days before expiration but before expiration incurs no late fee, but the licence expires on its expiration date and remains expired until OMMA approves the renewal. A renewal submitted after expiration incurs a nonrefundable late fee of $500 per week the licence is expired, the licensee cannot operate while expired, and a licence expired for more than 60 calendar days shall not be renewed. Source: OMMA, "Important Notice Regarding License Transfers Under Senate Bill 1939" (GovDelivery, 7 Mar 2025): https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OKSDH/bulletins/3d5d74d — accessed 2026-10-30; OAC 442:10-5-2(c)(5) (Justia text, which also states the pre-1 Nov 2024 rule: $500 flat late fee, 90-day outer limit — the 1 Nov 2024 rule supersedes it for current renewals). - Pending-renewal / "expired but timely filed" status: There is no general "pending renewal = may keep operating" rule in the material opened, except the transporter-agent analogue (an agent licence appearing active in OMMA Verify is active even past its listed date if a timely renewal was submitted). For business licences, the OMMA notice above states the opposite for late-filed renewals (cannot operate while expired). Verify whether a business renewal filed ≥60 days before expiration confers continued operating authority past expiration while OMMA's 90-business-day review runs — the OAC/notice texts opened do not state it expressly, and it must not be assumed. - Certificate on renewal: see § 3.1(b) (no new certificate unless change of use/occupancy or change requiring further inspection/licensure/permitting; SB 1635 COO + affidavit route). - Grower bond/ownership on renewal: must be re-proved on renewal (OMMA grower page). - Tier fees on renewal: grower renewal fee is based on canopy harvested in the previous 12 months; dispensary renewal fee is the 10% formula on the previous 12 months' state sales + excise tax (§ 427.14(D)).

Transfer / change of ownership: - OMMA approval is required before the new owner takes possession, exercises control, or holds itself out as controlling the business; an unapproved transfer is grounds for revocation/nonrenewal (OAC 442:10-5-2(f)). - The new owner must be OMMA-approved and OBNDD-registered before control passes; the transferred licence term begins on OBNDD registration approval (OMMA transfer notice, citing §§ 427.14c(B)–(C), (H)). - Fees on transfer (OMMA 7 Mar 2025 notice, citing SB 1939 (2024), 63 O.S. § 427.14c): seller must keep the licence active throughout (including timely renewal + renewal tier fees); new owner pays an application fee of $2,500 plus the tier fee, with the tier fee calculated on the seller's use during the previous 12 months (§ 427.14); where renewal and transfer are both pending, OMMA processes the renewal first, then the transfer once renewal fees are paid. - Location-change fee: $500 (OAC 442:10-5-2(e)(2)(A), per OMMA transfer notice). - Material changes: licensees must obtain OMMA written approval in advance for any material change affecting licensure qualifications and may not operate under the changed conditions until approved (OAC 442:10-5-2, material-change paragraph). - HB 3143 transfer bar: see § 4.6 — Verify enrolled text.

Inspections and site verification: - See § 3.2 table: application = consent to entry/inspection; up to two OMMA on-site inspections per calendar year per grower/processor/dispensary/transporter (plus labs' pre-licensure + up to two annually, transporter warehouses pre-approval, research/education up to two, may be unannounced); additional inspections for correction/investigation/complaints; secret shoppers authorised (OAC 442:10-5-4(l)); records review and interviews authorised. - Site verification at application: OMMA reviews applications and "conduct[s] all investigations, inspections and interviews before approving" (§ 427.14(G)(1)); approval/rejection/denial/status-update within 90 business days (§ 427.14(F)). The certificate of compliance + certificate of occupancy/site plan package (OAC 442:10-5-3(e)(8)–(9)) is the documentary site verification; OMMA's lab/warehouse pre-licensure inspections are the physical site verifications expressly required by rule.

Reporting (commercial licensees): - OMMA monthly report: due by the 15th of each month for the previous month's activity, beginning in the month licensed and every month thereafter even with no product on site; separate report per licence; failure to file a timely, complete, accurate report and to correct within 30 days of written notice exposes the licensee to the Appendix C fine per violation and other administrative action (OAC 310:681-5-6.1(a) as cited in the OMMA reminder — note the old Title 310 citation; current codification is OAC 442:10 — Verify current monthly-report rule number). Source: OMMA Monthly Reporting Reminder: http://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OKSDH/bulletins/309933a — accessed 2026-10-30. - Seed-to-sale (Metrc) reporting is Part 1 scope and is not detailed here, except to note that OMMA's monthly-report and utility-report proposals (where they exist) are described as integrating with seed-to-sale software — Verify current Metrc rule citations in Part 1. - Electricity/water usage reporting: see § 3.2 — Verify, not presented as a confirmed current duty.

4.8 Limits per owner, and what is NOT limited

  • No numeric limit per owner in § 427.14(E)(8) (see § 4.0). Each licence/category needs a separate application and fee.
  • Practical limits that do operate as caps: (i) the moratorium (new grower/processor/dispensary licences frozen to 1 Aug 2028); (ii) one grower licence per property (rule amendment noted in § 4.0 — Verify current text); (iii) single-location validity per licence; (iv) lab ownership conflict (no beneficial interest in a grower/processor/dispensary — Verify current rule); (v) waste-disposal cap history (10 until 1 Nov 2021, then no limit — § 430(A)); (vi) any HB 3144 cap if enacted (Verify).
  • Employee credentials (related, not a commercial licence): SB 1704 (2022) created an OMMA employee credential authorising work in a licensed business. Fee, training and renewal details were not confirmed from a directly opened OMMA page in this research (secondary summaries state $30 + processing + OSBI check, 1-year term, owners exempt — Verify on the OMMA employee-credential page before use). Do not list the employee credential as a ninth commercial licence type.

4.9 Estimated startup costs — NO official OMMA total; non-official figures flagged

OMMA publishes no total startup-cost estimate on the licence pages opened. The table below therefore lists only confirmed cost components; any total built from them is arithmetic, not an OMMA estimate, and the secondary totals below it are labelled non-official and conflicting.

Confirmed components (state/local, per licence, annual unless noted): - OMMA application fee for the licence type/tier (§§ 4.1–4.2) + 2.25% card fee. - Grower bond: $50,000 face amount per licence (or 5-year ownership proof in lieu) — this is a bond amount, not a premium cost. The surety premium actually paid is not stated by OMMA and is not estimated here. - OBNDD registration (fee not confirmed from a directly opened page — Verify). - OSBI background checks (applicant-paid; fee capped at the general OSBI fee — amount not confirmed here — Verify). - Local certificate/inspection fees (Oklahoma City MMCC $100–$750 by type; Norman local licence $450–$900 by type — §§ 3.4; other cities Verify). - Secretary of State good-standing certificate, premises lease/purchase, build-out, security, insurance, Metrc/tags, testing, legal/compliance — no official figures located; do not estimate them from this file. - Transfer route (the only entry route for frozen types while the moratorium runs): new owner pays $2,500 + tier fee on transfer (plus seller's renewal/tier fees kept current) — but the purchase price of the existing business/licence itself is a private market price, not published by OMMA, and is not estimated here.

[AUDIT CORRECTION — § 4.9.] The secondary startup totals that follow ($80,000–$140,000 vs $150,000–$2,000,000) are Removed from the corrected report as figures; only the statement that OMMA publishes no total startup-cost estimate is retained. The conflicting totals are shown below solely for traceability and must not be quoted as findings.

Non-official secondary totals — DO NOT USE as a headline (conflicting): One secondary dispensary guide states $80,000–$140,000 (attributed to Cova Software) while the same guide's earlier version stated $150,000–$2,000,000; another guide states a $2,500 licence fee "on paper" but gives no reliable total. These ranges are not adopted. Any parent-compiler total must be labelled "non-official estimate, source + date" or omitted.

Parts 5–6 — Licence Data Sources, Market Data

Scope: Parts 5 (Licence Data Sources) and 6 (Market Data) ONLY. Date accessed for all facts below: 30 October 2026. The 3 November 2026 election had not yet been held on that date. Programme scope: Oklahoma is medical-only. There is no adult-use sale, licence or sales series to report. Every "sales" figure below is medical-marijuana sales/tax unless stated otherwise. Counting rule used throughout: OMMA's monthly licensing table is reproduced as OMMA labels it. Its columns are not labelled "active" in the text extracted, and this report does not relabel them. Where a secondary source calls the same table "active licences", that wording is flagged as the secondary source's, not OMMA's table heading. "Issued", "active", "pending renewal" and "operating" are not mixed: a figure is only called "active" where its source calls it active. OMMA's "Total" column is the sum of the patient, caregiver and commercial columns in that row (checked for October 2026 and December 2021 — see §5.2).

How to read the source inventory (§5.1): "Downloadable file" means a file the source itself offers for download. Where the source is a search page or a JavaScript dashboard, that is stated plainly and no download is invented. Where an exact file name or direct link could not be confirmed from a directly opened page, the entry says so and is marked Verify — it is not filled in by guesswork.

Its Oklahoma total (2,442) is below OMMA's October 2026 commercial count (3,581) and the categories do not map to OMMA types (DEA "manufacturers" ≠ OMMA growers+processors; one company may file for multiple activities/locations), the window closed 26 June 2026 with later applications still accepted, and applications remain subject to DEA review. Do not use 2,442 as an Oklahoma licence count. It is included only because a Run 1 reader will otherwise mistake it for one.

5.2.4 OBNDD registration counts vs OMMA licence counts — a comparison that must not be made naively

A secondary count (Leafy Updates, Aug 2026, based on OBNDD's public search on 21 Aug 2026 vs OMMA's 3 Aug 2026 table) reported: OMMA 1,323 dispensaries vs 1,067 active OBNDD distributor registrations (difference 256, 19.3%); OMMA 1,801 growers + 587 processors = 2,388 production licences vs 1,298 active OBNDD manufacturer registrations (difference 1,090). The same article itself warns that this "does not mean [the difference] dispensaries [are] operating illegally", that "no record-by-record match was performed", and that OBNDD's own guidance explains the gaps (one manufacturer registration can cover multiple licences at one name/address/ownership; a dispensary doing manufacturing holds a manufacturer registration, not a distributor one; registrations follow the location of controlled-substance activity). This report therefore does NOT adopt "256 unregistered dispensaries" or any OBNDD-shortfall figure. The OBNDD search (5.1.9) is a per-registrant verification tool, not a second licence census, and its totals are not published by OBNDD itself in the material found.

5.2.5 Enforcement aggregates that bear on licence counts (official-adjacent, not a dataset)

  • OBNDD registrations (testimony, Oct 2026, secondary: News 9, 7 Oct 2026, reporting OBN testimony to a Senate interim study): marijuana grows with active OBN registrations peaked at "about 8,400 farms" in 2022 and had fallen to "about 1,350" at testimony. Since 2021, OBN agents "have seized more than 2.4 million illegal marijuana plants and more than 295,000 pounds of processed marijuana", with "more than 400 arrests". These are OBN-registration counts, not OMMA grower-licence counts (compare OMMA growers: 8,306 in Jan 2022; 1,703 in Oct 2026) — the two series move together but are not interchangeable, and the 1,350 figure's exact date is the testimony date, not a month-end table date.
  • Attorney General enforcement (secondary, Sep 2026 radio/news summary): "more than 9,000 licensed marijuana grows" when the Attorney General took office in 2023, "fewer than 1,200 remained under the licensing measure it cited" by July (2026, as reported) — the "licensing measure" is not defined in the secondary summary and this figure is NOT reconciled to OMMA's 1,703 growers; it is listed here only so the parent report does not mistake it for an OMMA count. Verify against the Attorney General's own release before any use.
  • OMMA administrative cases (May 2025 update, §5.1.6): "more than 1,400 administrative cases" filed (period to be verified); secret-shopper, complaint and investigation counts as in 5.1.6.
  • OBNDD "unaccounted for" claim — do not use as market data: OBN Director Donnie Anderson's claim (U.S. House Homeland Security Committee, Sep 2025, as reported by The Oklahoman, 17 Jan 2026, secondary) that 87,210,960 plants logged Mar 2024–Mar 2025 vs ~1.6 million pounds sold at dispensaries leaves "over 85 million pounds… unaccounted for" assumes one pound per plant. OMMA told the same newspaper: "We don't have data that supports this claim." This report records the dispute and adopts neither figure as a sales or production total. The underlying Metrc plant-log figure (87.2 million plants logged in a year) is a log-event count (plants entered/tagged, including clones/immature plants and re-logging), not a harvest count, and must not be used as production.

5.2.6 What is NOT in any OMMA/OBNDD public source found

  • No public list of pending-renewal licences, surrendered licences, or expired-but-in-grace-period licences as a separate series. Renewal/pending-renewal counts, if OMMA tracks them, are not on the Licensing and Tax Data page.
  • No public list of employee credentials by business, and no public transporter-agent count (transporter agents are verified individually via OMMA Verify under the pre-MedPortal guidance).
  • No public county licence table in text-extractable form (dashboard only, §5.1.2).
  • No public tribal licensee list (5.1.16).

PART 6 — MARKET DATA

6.1 Medical sales and tax collections — the OMMA tax table is the primary series; "sales" must be derived, not quoted from it directly

OMMA publishes tax collected, not sales, in its tax table. Because the SQ 788 tax is 7% of the gross dollar amount received by the dispensary for medical marijuana/marijuana products (OAC 442:10-5-7(a), rule text — Part 2 territory), an implied retail sales figure can be calculated as excise ÷ 0.07. That calculation is labelled "calculated" below and is not an OMMA-published sales figure. It will differ from dashboard "total reported sales" because the dashboard's total combines retail and wholesale (see 5.1.2).

See §5.2.3 for the full selected-date table. Headline: 386,913 (15 May 2022, peak in the OMMA table) → 304,186 (1 Oct 2026), −21.4%. Temporary/out-of-state patient licences are not broken out in the OMMA monthly table — their counts, if published anywhere, are Unavailable in this run (Part 1/4 territory for the licence rules themselves).

Market saturation (official basis only): the saturation case does not need prices. It rests on: (a) the licence collapse in §5.2.2 (commercial 13,785 → 3,581) under a moratorium in place since 26 Aug 2022 (HB 3208; extended by HB 2095 (2023) to 1 Aug 2026 and by HB 3143 (2026) to 1 Aug 2028 — OMMA licence pages, Part 4 territory); (b) the June 2023 OMMA-commissioned supply/demand study finding supply outpacing demand "by at least 32 times" (quoted in multiple secondary sources; the study itself was not directly opened in this run — Verify the study text before quoting the 32× figure as OMMA's own words); (c) live plants falling from 7,388,470 at 20 Nov 2024 (TEXOMA HIDTA snapshot, secondary, Mar 2025) to 4,297,074 at 28 Oct 2026 (NCS Dashboard, §5.1.2) — −41.8% (calculated), but note the two sources/methods differ (HIDTA snapshot vs dashboard), so this is an indicative, not like-for-like, decline; (d) falling patients (−21.4% from peak) alongside falling excise (−31.6% from the 2021 calendar peak to 2025, calculated: $45.30m vs $66.17m). The correct saturation summary is: fewer patients, fewer licensees, lower tax, and a still-large plant count relative to patient numbers — contraction, not growth — with the moratorium now protecting incumbents rather than expanding supply.

Dispensaries per capita (calculated, with stated base): using the Census Bureau July 1, 2025 population estimate for Oklahoma as relayed in secondary reporting (4,123,288; CannBus Q3 2026 citing Census QuickFacts/ACS 2024) — this population figure itself is secondary-relayed and should be replaced with a directly opened Census QuickFacts figure before republication (Verify): - 1 Oct 2026: 1,259 dispensaries ÷ 4,123,288 = 30.5 dispensaries per 100,000 residents; 1 dispensary per 3,275 residents. - At the dispensary peak (2,893, Mar 2023) on the same population base (anachronistic, for scale only): 70.2 per 100,000; 1 per 1,425 residents. - Patients per capita, Oct 2026: 304,186 ÷ 4,123,288 = 7.38% of the population holding a patient licence (on the monthly-table definition). - Commercial licences per capita, Oct 2026: 3,581 ÷ 4,123,288 = 86.9 per 100,000 residents. - Do not compare these per-capita figures to other states' figures computed on different population vintages or different licence definitions.

Consistency rule applied: Every fact below was checked against Run 1 (part02.md, part34.md, part56.md and the Run 1 HTML, ~/workspace/your_files/oklahoma-cannabis-hemp-run1/oklahoma-cannabis-hemp-run1-parts-0-6.html). §0 — CORRECTIONS TO RUN 1 FOUND IN THIS RUN (read first)

Correction 1 — Run 1's "no official Oklahoma response to the federal hemp dates" is WRONG

Run 1 (Part 1.5) stated: "No official Oklahoma response was found" to PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 and the 12 November / 11 December 2026 dates. That statement is superseded. ODAFF issued an official Hemp Clarification Letter dated 16 January 2026, signed by Hemp Program Administrator Joshua Rigdon, and it is linked from ODAFF's own Licensing & Permits page as "2026 Hemp Clarification Letter". It was opened directly in this run:

  • Source: https://ag.ok.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/2026-Hemp-Clarification-Letter.pdf (accessed 2026-10-30)
  • It states, verbatim in substance: "Under current law hemp products are restricted to test no more than 0.3% Total THC (Total THC is measured as THC plus 87.7 percent of THCA)."
  • It states the PL 119-37 amendment to 7 U.S.C. §1639o "will be placed into effect on November 12, 2026" and will impact marketable hemp products: (a) any intermediate hemp-derived product must contain no more than 0.3% Total THC on a dry-weight basis after decarboxylation; (b) any final marketplace hemp-derived cannabinoid product must contain no more than 0.4 milligrams of Total THC per container, with "container" defined as the retail packaging (e.g. jars, bottles, cartridges).
  • It states the amended definition excludes "cannabinoids not naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L. plants or those that are synthesized or manufactured outside the plant (e.g., delta-8 and similar isomer products)".
  • It states products above the 0.4 mg per container limit or the 0.3% Total THC level "are not considered hemp and cannot be marketed as such", including any post-harvest addition that would cause the product to exceed those limits.

Compiler rule: Replace Run 1's "no official response" with this letter. Note two limits of the letter itself: (i) it gives a single date, 12 November 2026, and does not discuss the PL 119-103 §2019 staging to 11 December 2026 given in the task's fixed federal baseline — so whether ODAFF treats the 0.4 mg cap as applying on 12 November or 11 December 2026 for products other than non-naturally-produced cannabinoids remains Verify; (ii) it is a clarification letter, not a statute or a promulgated rule — its legal weight vs. OAC 35:30-24/31 is Verify (see §7.6).

Correction 2 — Run 1's "THCA 0.877 factor Verify" is now CONFIRMED for ODAFF's stated method

Run 1 (Part 1.5) left open whether Oklahoma's lab method applies the 0.877 decarboxylation factor. The January 2026 clarification letter confirms it ("THC plus 87.7 percent of THCA"), and the ODAFF 2025 Hemp Grower License Application defines "postdecarboxylation" the same way (total potential THC = THC + THCA converted, by gas chromatography with heat or by liquid chromatography with a conversion calculation). The Run 1 statement that the relayed OAC definition said "total delta-9" without spelling out THCA conversion should therefore be read as superseded by these two ODAFF documents. Whether OAC 35:30-24-2 itself prints the 0.877 factor was not directly opened in this run — see Verify item V7-1.

Correction 3 — A secondary claim that hemp THC is confined to OMMA dispensaries by "HB 3770 (2022), 63 O.S. §420A" is REJECTED, not adopted

A secondary 2026 brief (drugpolicywatch.info, "Oklahoma: 2026 Drug Policy and Enclosure Brief") asserts HB 3770 (2022), codified at 63 O.S. §420A, "on paper restricts certain intoxicating-hemp sales to OMMA-licensed dispensaries, but enforcement is limited". Do not adopt this. The Oklahoma Legislature's own Subject Index lists HB 3770 as "Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority; creating the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority Act of 2026" with last action "REF TO RULES (H)" — i.e. a 2026 bill referred to committee, not a 2022 enacted dispensary-confinement law. Source: https://oklegislature.gov/SubjectIndex.aspx?MainSubjectRef=Marijuana&SubSubject=Oklahoma%20Medical%20Marijuana%20Authority%20(OMMA (accessed 2026-10-30). No 63 O.S. §420A text confirming a dispensary-only hemp rule was opened in this run. Run 1's finding therefore stands: no statute confining hemp-derived THC sales to OMMA dispensaries was confirmed. The HB 3770/§420A claim stays Verify only in the sense that the parent should not repeat it without opening the cited text — it must not be presented as law.
