PART 7 — HEMP LICENCES

7.1 Answer in one paragraph

Oklahoma runs its own USDA-approved state hemp plan through ODAFF — it does NOT use USDA direct producer licensing. There are two ODAFF hemp licence types in current use, and no others were confirmed: (1) Hemp Grower License and (2) Hemp Processor/Handler License (a single combined licence covering both processing and handling, one per facility). There is no separate standalone "handler" licence, no separate hemp retailer licence, and no separate hemp transporter licence located in ODAFF's current forms or statute — retail sale of legally grown hemp/hemp products is expressly permitted without a licence under 63 O.S. §1-1431(C) (see §7.5), and transport is dealt with under the grower/processor licence and ODAFF movement rules, not a standalone transport licence (standalone transporter status is Verify, §7.8). Hemp licences are annual, expiring 31 December of the year issued, and are not affected by the OMMA medical-marijuana moratorium (HB 3208/HB 2095/HB 3143), which by its terms and OMMA's own page covers only new OMMA dispensary, grower and processor licences.

7.2 State plan vs. USDA programme — confirmed directly

Question Answer Source (accessed 2026-10-30)
Does Oklahoma run its own USDA-approved state plan? Yes. USDA AMS list, updated 17 February 2026, row: "Oklahoma — OK Approved Plan (pdf)". https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review
Does Oklahoma use USDA direct licensing? No. USDA direct licensing applies only where a state/tribe has no pending or approved plan; Oklahoma has an approved plan, so growers apply to ODAFF, not USDA. Same AMS page; USDA grower guidance https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/information-for-hemp-growers

7.3 Statutory basis — verbatim operative text (opened directly)

2 O.S. §3-404 — License application; rules and requirements (Justia, 2025 Oklahoma Statutes; history: Added Laws 2018, c. 64, §4, emerg. eff. 23 Apr 2018; amended Laws 2019, c. 91, §5, emerg. eff. 18 Apr 2019; Laws 2021, c. 358, §1, eff. 1 July 2021; Laws 2024, c. 266, §3, eff. 1 Nov 2024). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-2/section-2-3-404/

"A. A person intending to engage in industrial hemp growth, cultivation, handling, or processing authorized under the Oklahoma Industrial Hemp Program shall apply to the Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food, and Forestry for a license prior to planting, handling, or processing the industrial hemp. 1. The application shall include: a. the name and address of the applicant, b. the legal description, global positioning system location, and map of the land area on which the applicant will engage in industrial hemp growth and cultivation operations, handling operations or processing operations, c. a statement of intended end use, and d. a criminal history record check for all key participants submitted with the initial or renewal application. 2. By submitting an application, the applicant acknowledges and agrees that: a. information provided to the Department may be provided to law enforcement agencies, b. the applicant shall allow and fully cooperate with any inspection and sampling that the Department deems necessary, c. the applicant will submit all required reports by the applicable due dates specified by the Department, and d. the applicant has the legal right to cultivate, handle or process industrial hemp on the registered land area and shall grant the Department access for inspection and sampling."

"B. The Department shall collect a nonrefundable fee from the applicant at the time of application. The Department shall set a fee schedule based on the size and use of the land area on which the licensee will conduct industrial hemp growing or cultivation operations and shall set the fee at a level sufficient to generate the amount of monies necessary to cover the Department's direct costs in implementing the Oklahoma Industrial Hemp Program. Denied applications for a license may be resubmitted within a twelve-month period. The Department may waive the fee for resubmitted applications."

"C. A license issued pursuant to this section is valid for one (1) year. In order to continue engaging in industrial hemp growth and cultivation operations in Oklahoma, the licensee shall annually apply for a license in accordance with subsection A of this section. The Department may set a separate fee schedule for renewal of existing licenses in good standing."

"D. All industrial hemp plant material shall be planted, grown and harvested under a valid license. Any plant material that is not harvested in the license period in which it was planted or volunteer plants that are not destroyed must be declared for inclusion in a subsequent license."

"E. If the licensee wishes to alter the land area … within thirty (30) days of any new license, before altering the area, the licensee shall submit to the Department and the United States Department of Agriculture Farm Service Agency an updated legal description, global positioning system location, and map specifying the proposed alterations."

"F. Each licensee shall report any changes to information provided in the license application within ten (10) days of such change to the Department and the United States Department of Agriculture Farm Service Agency."

"G. A licensee shall maintain all records pertaining to the license and growing records for a minimum of three (3) years."

2 O.S. §3-407 — Inspection and sampling (Justia, 2019 text; amended Laws 2019, c. 91, §7, emerg. eff. 18 Apr 2019). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/2019/title-2/section-2-3-407/ — plants subject to at least annual routine inspections and sampling; handling/processing licences subject to at least annual inspections plus compliance inspections; licensee pays inspection/laboratory costs within 30 days of invoice; costs waived if no inconsistencies/violations are found in a non-routine inspection.

2 O.S. §3-408 — Causes to deny, revoke or suspend (Justia, 2022 text; amended Laws 2022, c. 265, §3, emerg. eff. 16 May 2022). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/2022/title-2/section-2-3-408/ - A licensee that negligently violates the programme three times in any five-year period is ineligible for five years from the third violation. - "Any person convicted of a felony relating to a controlled substance under state or federal law shall be ineligible during the ten-year period following the date of conviction to participate in this program." This is the hemp felony bar — it is 10 years, controlled-substance felonies only, and is different from OMMA's 2-year/5-year bars (Run 1 Part 4). Do not conflate them. - Note: the federal 2014-pilot exception to the 10-year bar (for persons lawfully growing under a 2014 pilot before 20 Dec 2018) was not located in the Oklahoma §3-408 extract — Verify whether Oklahoma's rule reproduces it.

Related but distinct — 2 O.S. §§3-601 et seq., Oklahoma Industrial Hemp Remediation Program (Laws 2021, c. 159, §1, eff. 1 Nov 2021). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-2/section-2-3-601/ — this is a remediation pathway, not a third licence type to apply for in the ordinary way: if hemp tests noncompliant, the licensee may request ODAFF approval to remediate by having a licensed processor extract it into concentrate, which is then sampled by a certified laboratory (ODAFF's own lab or an Oklahoma lab certified by ODAFF); if below USDA THC levels for concentrate it may be sold commercially, if above it must be destroyed under 21 CFR §1317.15 with notice to ODAFF and USDA and destruction verified through tracking software. Its §3-601(B)(7) hemp definition requires hemp "grown from a certified seed" with delta-9 ≤0.3% dry weight and states hemp and hemp-derived cannabinoids "shall be considered an agricultural commodity and not a controlled substance". Whether the remediation programme has a separate licence form, or operates only through the grower/processor licences, is Verify — do not list it as a standalone licence type on this evidence.

7.5 Retail, labelling and the "no retailer licence" rule — verbatim statute

63 O.S. §1-1431 (2025), Labeling requirements for cannabidiol (Justia; Added by Laws 2019, c. 352, §1, eff. 1 Nov 2019). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-1-1431/

"C. Retail sales of industrial hemp and hemp products may be conducted without a license so long as the products and the hemp used in the products were grown and cultivated legally in this state or another state or jurisdiction and meet the same or substantially the same requirements for processing hemp products or growing hemp. The addition of derivatives of hemp, including hemp-derived cannabidiol, to cosmetics, personal care products and products intended for human or animal consumption shall be permitted without a license and shall not be considered an adulteration of such products. Nothing in this section shall exempt any individual or entity from compliance with food safety and licensure laws, rules and regulations as set forth under the Oklahoma Public Health Code."

Subsections (A)–(B) (label content for manufactured CBD products, and the FDA-approved-pharmaceutical exemption) were not fully extracted in this run — the parent should open §1-1431 in full before quoting label contents (Verify V7-10). The §1-1431(C) sentence is, however, the positive statutory basis for Run 1's "hemp THC sold outside OMMA dispensaries" finding, and it is stronger than the absence-of-a-ban reasoning Run 1 used: retail hemp sales are expressly licence-free, subject to the legally-grown condition and to food-safety/public-health law. Interaction with SB 1257 (eff. 1 Nov 2026, state Schedule I including synthesised hemp THC) and with the ODAFF January 2026 clarification letter (delta-8 excluded from hemp after 12 Nov 2026) is unresolved on 30 Oct 2026 — §1-1431(C) was enacted in 2019 and neither SB 1257's enrolled text nor any ODAFF/AG guidance reconciling it with §1-1431(C) was opened in this run. Do not state that §1-1431(C) survives SB 1257 untouched, and do not state that SB 1257 repeals it. Verify (V7-11).

Secondary note (not law, for Part 11/12 cross-check): a secondary summary (Thynk, 30 Oct 2026, https://www.thynk.guru/post/oklahoma-november-1-thc-law-is-not-the-federal-november-12-date) reports reading the SB 1257 enrolled bill as carving out industrial hemp with a combined delta-9 + THCA concentration ≤0.3% dry weight, post-decarboxylation, only for hemp grown under the Oklahoma Industrial Hemp Program, which "may be shipped intrastate and interstate". That reading is secondary and unverified against the enrolled text — do not quote it as statute.

7.6 Rules: OAC chapter discrepancy — still unresolved, narrowed

Run 1 flagged a discrepancy: Cornell LII relays OAC 35:30-24-2 ("Acceptable Hemp THC Level": lab reports total delta-9 THC + measurement of uncertainty; compliant when the uncertainty range includes 0.3% or less), while the Gies memorandum cites OAC 35:30-24 for the programme. This run found: - A current secondary summary (Sativa University, checked 27 Sep 2026) cites the processor fee rule as OAC 35:30-24-7 and states the total-THC standard "has been embedded in ODAFF Admin Code 35, Subchapter 24 since 2019" (via the ATLRX summary of the January 2026 letter). Source: https://sativauniversity.com/cannabis-laws/oklahoma/ - A secondary news item (Thynk, 30 Oct 2026) reports a proposed rule, OAC 35:30-24, with comments open through 16 Nov 2026 and a hearing 9 a.m. that day in Oklahoma City (app.ag.ok.gov/proposedrules). Proposed, not law — do not present as current rule. - The ODAFF grower form's own postdecarboxylation definition and the January 2026 letter together establish the substance (Total THC = THC + 0.877 × THCA; ≤0.3% dry weight; measurement of uncertainty per the Cornell relay) even though the chapter number is unresolved.

Compiler rule: Cite the substance with the ODAFF letter + form as authority, and cite the OAC chapter as "35:30-24 (Cornell relay) / 35:30-24 (Gies citation) — chapter number Verify". Do not silently pick one.

Other hemp-rule points confirmed in this run: - Negligent-violation remediation threshold: up to 1.0% total delta-9 THC, remediate and retest to ≤0.3% (Run 1, Cornell relay — not re-opened; Verify V7-1 with the same item). - Sampling/testing: pre-harvest sampling by ODAFF; testing by gas chromatography or high-performance liquid chromatography (postdecarboxylation method, per the grower form); DEA-registered lab requirement is a federal USDA-plan requirement (7 CFR Part 990) — whether ODAFF's own lab or only DEA-registered labs may test Oklahoma hemp was not confirmed from an ODAFF rule in this run (Verify V7-12; the Remediation Program's "certified laboratory" definition is ODAFF-operated or ODAFF-certified Oklahoma labs, §3-601(B)(2), which is a different, remediation-specific definition — do not generalise it). - USDA DEA-lab enforcement delay to 31 Dec 2026 is in the fixed federal baseline; it is not an ODAFF date.

7.8 What hemp licences do NOT do (boundaries vs. OMMA)

  • An ODAFF hemp licence does not authorise medical marijuana: it authorises only industrial hemp as defined (≤0.3% Total THC, and after the federal change, within the amended federal definition). Material above that line is marijuana under the OMMA programme / controlled-substances law, not hemp — see the January 2026 letter and SB 1257 (both Verify for exact boundaries).
  • An OMMA licence does not authorise hemp production: OMMA licences are valid only in Oklahoma "excluding any tribal trust or tribal restricted land or federal lands" (OAC 442:10-1-3, per Run 1 Part 5) and cover medical marijuana only.
  • The OMMA moratorium (to 1 Aug 2028) does not freeze ODAFF hemp applications: ODAFF's 2026 forms and online applications were live on the hub page at access, and a secondary 2026 guide confirms hemp farms are not affected by the moratorium. No ODAFF hemp moratorium was located.
  • Hemp licensees are not in Metrc on any evidence located: Metrc is the OMMA seed-to-sale system (mandatory 26 May 2022). Hemp tracking, if any beyond ODAFF reports, is via ODAFF's own reports and (for remediation) "tracking software" approved by ODAFF (§3-601(B)(15)) — Verify whether ODAFF uses a named tracking platform for ordinary hemp.

PART 8 — CANNABIS-ZONED PROPERTIES

8.1 How this section was built, and its limits (read first)

  • Sources searched: 420 Property (Oklahoma index page, opened directly), LoopNet (Oklahoma City cannabis-warehouse search), Crexi/Buildout sale brochures, Showcase (broker PDFs), BizTrader, Land.com / LandWatch / Land and Farm (hemp-suitable land), and general web search for Tulsa/Stillwater/Shawnee/Ardmore/Miami OK listings.
  • What "zoning type" means here: Only the zoning designation as stated on the listing itself is reported. Most cannabis-marketplace listings do not state a zoning code at all — they market by use ("grow facility", "dispensary") rather than by zoning district. Where the listing does not state zoning, this report says "Not stated on listing" rather than inferring a district from the city code. A property being marketed for cannabis use is not proof that its zoning permits that use, and a former grow/dispensary is not proof that a new OMMA licence can be obtained there — new OMMA grower/processor/dispensary licences are frozen by the moratorium to 1 Aug 2028 (Run 1 Part 4), so a buyer would ordinarily be acquiring real estate and, where stated, an existing/transferable licence or business, subject to OMMA transfer approval. Do not read any listing below as a promise of a new licence.
  • Status rule applied (per task): A listing is marked ACTIVE only where the listing page itself showed "ACTIVE" (or equivalent) on the extract; everything else is Verify (including listings whose price/date conflict between documents). 420 Property's Oklahoma index page showed "ACTIVE" badges on the featured listings below, but the index page does not carry per-listing update dates — so even "ACTIVE" here means "shown ACTIVE on the index page as extracted", not independently confirmed as still available on 30 Oct 2026. No listing below was confirmed by a live broker contact, and no listing should be treated as available without re-checking the source link.
  • Same-name discipline: Every property below was checked to be in Oklahoma (OK, Oklahoma county/city names). Excluded: any Fort Smith, AR property; any Stillwater MN, Shawnee KS, Ardmore PA, Miami FL, Weatherford TX or Yukon, Canada property. Tulsa, Oklahoma City, Edmond, Norman, Lawton, McAlester, Ardmore (OK), Shawnee (OK), Purcell, Claremore, Heavener, Hugo, Wanette, Lindsay, Enid, Dewey, Minco, Barnsdall, Warner, Roff and Chickasha are all Oklahoma places. Shawnee nuance: the "Turnkey 12K SF" listing's index entry says "Oklahoma City, OK" in its location line but its own description says "Location: Shawnee, OK" — both are reported, and the location is marked Verify (see table).
  • No personal contact details are reproduced from listings (no individual phone numbers or personal emails). Brokerage/company names are given only where they are the listing's public business attribution (Creek CRE, Frisbie Lombardi, Bauer & Associates) — individual brokers' personal contacts are omitted.

8.5 What was NOT found (negative findings — do not fill)

  • No cannabis-specific zoning district (e.g. a "cannabis overlay" or "marijuana business district") was confirmed for any Oklahoma city in this run. Cannabis businesses operate in ordinary commercial/industrial/agricultural districts subject to the state school buffer, certificate of compliance, and local zoning (Run 1 Part 3) — not in a cannabis-only zone. If a city has adopted a cannabis overlay since Run 1, it was not located and remains Verify for Part 3 follow-up, not asserted here.
  • No verified active listing was found for Stillwater (OK), Miami (OK), Weatherford (OK), Duncan (OK), Yukon (OK) or Guthrie (OK) in the searches run. That is a search-result limit, not proof that no property exists there — it means no listing for those cities is included in this report, and none should be inferred.
  • No listing was found that states both a price and a municipal zoning code for a grow facility (the two zoning-stated listings are the Ardmore retail storefront and the Tulsa CH commercial property, neither of which is a grow-facility sale with a stated price + zoning pair). The parent should not present a "zoning + price" table for grows as if it were complete — the table in §8.2 honestly shows "Not stated" for zoning in most rows.
  • Fort Smith, AR was excluded wherever it appeared in border searches. No Arkansas property is included in this report.

Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority (OMMA) The regulatory agency for Oklahoma's medical marijuana programme: commercial and patient licence applications, customer service, rulemaking under 63 O.S. §§ 420 et seq. and 427.1 et seq., enforcement of its rules, investigation of possible violations. OAC Title 442. https://oklahoma.gov/omma/ — About page: https://aem-prod.oklahoma.gov/omma/about/about-omma.html (opened 30 Oct 2026; last modified 1 Aug 2025 on the page) Main building / Patient Services Lobby: M.C. Connors Building, 2501 N. Lincoln Blvd., Oklahoma City, OK 73105. Mailing: P.O. Box 262266, Oklahoma City, OK 73126-2266. Call Center: (405) 522-6662, 8:30 a.m.–4:30 p.m. weekdays (closed state holidays). Commercial licensing/compliance email (agency address, not an individual): licensing@omma.ok.gov. Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs Control (OBNDD / OBN) State drug-enforcement agency; enforces the Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Act (Title 63); registers commercial marijuana businesses (OBNDD registration is separate from an OMMA licence — see Run 1 Part 5); runs the Marijuana Enforcement Teams (MET, created 2021) and the Marijuana Eradication Program/Teams; trains/supports state and local law enforcement; administers the Prescription Monitoring Program. Oklahoma Water Resources Board (OWRB) State water-management agency: appropriates stream water and groundwater through water-use permits. Cannabis/hemp-specific rule (official fact sheet, opened via search): "If you are self-supplying your own water from a groundwater well or surface water source to grow marijuana or hemp (i.e., not purchasing water from a municipality, rural water district, or other entity) a water use permit is required prior to using water. The associated permit number must be identified. Commercial irrigation (including marijuana/hemp) is not domestic use and is not permit-exempt. OMMA funding — verbatim from the OMMA About page (opened 30 Oct 2026)

"As of fiscal year 2024 (July 1, 2023, to June 30, 2024), OMMA does not directly receive any revenue. Instead, the Legislature appropriates OMMA's funding annually: A new state law — SB 18X (2023) — created two new funds under the Legislature's control. The Medical Marijuana Tax Fund receives medical marijuana excise tax revenue, which funds substance abuse programs and common education administered by other state agencies. The Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority Fund receives OMMA's fee and fine revenue, which funds OMMA's budget."

"As part of HB 1004X (2023), the Legislature set OMMA's fiscal year 2024 budget at $37 million."

This sits alongside Run 1 Part 2's §426 apportionment caveat: the Justia 2025 text of §426 still printing a FY2022 split (59.23% schools / 34.62% OMMA-as-division / 6.15% rehab) is historical text, not asserted as current. The SB 18X two-fund structure is the current structure as described by OMMA itself. Reconciling the current §426 text with SB 18X is a Verify follow-up for audit (open the current OSCN §426 text).

Headline finding — no Oklahoma tribal medical-marijuana programme was located. No Oklahoma tribe was found operating a tribal medical-marijuana licensing programme, tribal dispensary, or tribal commercial marijuana operation as of 30 Oct 2026. That is a negative finding with the limits stated: it rests on the official/secondary sources checked below, not on a page-by-page audit of all 38 tribal codes (which would be a Part 10 follow-up). In particular:

  • Do NOT confuse Cherokee Nation (Oklahoma) with the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians (EBCI, North Carolina). EBCI's adult-use cannabis (Dinilawigi Ord. No. 63 (2024), Qualla Enterprises / Great Smoky Cannabis Co., Cherokee Code Ch. 17/17A, EBCI Cannabis Control Board) is North Carolina tribal law, on the Qualla Boundary, and has nothing to do with Oklahoma. Every EBCI result returned in this run (including the June 2025 veto overrides, Res. No. 464 / Ord. No. 391, and the 16 oz / 8-plant medical limits in EBCI Code § 17-80) is excluded from the Oklahoma analysis. The 2025 EBCI limits (16 oz, 8 plants, max 4 mature) must never be quoted as Oklahoma or Cherokee Nation (Oklahoma) limits.
  • Hemp ≠ marijuana programme. Several Oklahoma tribes have USDA-approved hemp plans (see table below). A hemp plan authorises hemp production under 7 CFR Part 990; it is not a marijuana licensing programme and does not make a tribe's marijuana "state-licensed" for federal Schedule III purposes (see §10.1.5).

10.1.2 Verbatim tribal operative text — Cherokee Nation (Oklahoma) only

These are the only tribal verbatim texts located from an official tribal source in this run. They are Cherokee Nation (Oklahoma) law, not EBCI law and not Oklahoma state law.

21 CNCA § 2208.1 — Exception for Marijuana (LA 28-20, eff. 14 Dec 2020) (Cherokee Nation Council PDF, opened via search result):

"Any act or omission involving medical or minor offenses of use or possession of marijuana, which would not be punishable if committed or omitted within the jurisdiction of the State of Oklahoma, or which would subject the individual to a lessor [sic] punishment than prescribed herein, by the laws thereof in force at the time of such act or omission, shall not be guilty under the laws of the Cherokee Nation or not subject to more severe punishment under the laws of the Cherokee Nation.

Provided that whoever commits an act or omission involving marijuana which would be punishable if committed or omitted within the jurisdiction of the State of Oklahoma, by the laws thereof in force at the time of such act or omission, shall be guilty under the laws of the Cherokee Nation of a like offense and subject to a like punishment."

Historical Data: LA 28-20, eff. December 14, 2020.

21 CNCA § 2208 — Schedule III (same LA 28-20) — operative listing (extract):

"The controlled substances listed in this section are included in Schedule III. 1. Unless listed in another schedule, any material, compound, mixture, or preparation, which contains any quantity of the following substances …: a. Marijuana …"

What these texts do and do not do: § 2208.1 is a conformity / non-escalation rule for tribal criminal liability for medical/minor use-or-possession offences: if Oklahoma would not punish it (or would punish it less), Cherokee Nation law does not punish it (or does not punish it more severely); if Oklahoma would punish it, Cherokee law imposes a like offence/punishment. It is not a tribal licensing regime, not a tribal dispensary authorisation, and not a statement that an OMMA licence is valid on tribal trust land. The interaction with federal law (CSA) and with tribal trust-land status is not resolved by this text and is Verify for any specific fact pattern. The 2018 Nimmo statement (possession/sale illegal on tribal property under tribal + federal law) predates LA 28-20 and must not be quoted as the current Cherokee position without the 2020 amendment alongside it.

No other verbatim tribal ordinance text was located for any other Oklahoma tribe in this run. In particular, no verbatim Muscogee Title 14 text, no Chickasaw/Choctaw/Seminole cannabis ordinance text, and no tribal regulator's enabling ordinance was opened. Those are Unavailable, not "no law exists".

The tribal hemp-plan PDFs linked from the USDA AMS list are the operative plan documents; their internal regulator/contact details were not opened in this run — Verify from the individual plan PDFs before naming a tribal hemp regulator.
  • For state purposes, OMMA/OBNDD do not license activity on tribal trust land by virtue of a state licence alone — but the precise boundary (trust vs fee land, tribal member vs non-member, tribal consent/compact) is fact-specific and Verify for any specific site. No Oklahoma tribal-state cannabis compact was located in this run (Unavailable — do not assert that none exists; assert that none was found).

That is coordination, not a tribal prosecution, and must not be rephrased as tribal enforcement.

10.1.5 McGirt and Castro-Huerta — what they actually decided, and what they mean for cannabis

McGirt v. Oklahoma, 591 U.S. 894 (2020), 140 S. Ct. 2452 (9 July 2020) — 5–4, Gorsuch J.

  • Holding (per CRS summary, https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/LSB10778)::) Congress never disestablished the Muscogee (Creek) Nation reservation, so that land remains "Indian country" for federal criminal-law purposes. Only Congress can disestablish a reservation, and only with clear, explicit language; no such language was found.
  • Immediate criminal consequence: "State courts generally have no jurisdiction to [prosecute] Indians for conduct committed in 'Indian country'" absent congressional authorisation (CRS, quoting McGirt). For offences within the Major Crimes Act (18 U.S.C. § 1153 — murder, manslaughter, sexual abuse, kidnapping and other enumerated felonies), federal jurisdiction applies to Indian defendants; tribal courts may have concurrent jurisdiction depending on offence/circumstances (secondary summaries).
  • Extension: Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals decisions after McGirt recognised, on the same reasoning, that several other Oklahoma reservations (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole, and others) were likewise never disestablished — see Castro-Huerta opinion summary citing State ex rel. Matloff, Bosse v. State, 2021 OK CR 3, and Roth v. State, 2021 OKCR 27 (via FindLaw opinion text: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/spr-crt-us/2177478.html). The land-area consequence (nearly half of Oklahoma, incl. most of Tulsa, on secondary summaries) is a geographic description, not a cannabis holding.

Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, 597 U.S. 629 (2022) (29 June 2022) — 5–4, Kavanaugh J.

  • Holding (verbatim from the opinion's question presented, FindLaw): "We conclude that the Federal Government and the State have concurrent jurisdiction to prosecute crimes committed by non-Indians against Indians in Indian country."
  • CRS summary: "the default is that States have criminal jurisdiction in Indian country unless that jurisdiction is preempted" — by federal law under ordinary preemption principles, or where it would unlawfully infringe tribal self-government. The Court rejected the arguments that the General Crimes Act (18 U.S.C. § 1152) or Public Law 280 preempted Oklahoma law, and declined Oklahoma's invitation to overrule McGirt outright.
  • Facts (not cannabis): Victor Manuel Castro-Huerta, a non-Indian, convicted in Oklahoma state court of child neglect against his Native stepdaughter on the Cherokee reservation; the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals had vacated on exclusive-federal-jurisdiction grounds (29 Apr 2021), and the Supreme Court reversed that exclusivity holding.

Application to cannabis offences — careful, layered, and partly Verify:

  1. McGirt/Castro-Huerta are jurisdiction cases, not cannabis cases. Neither opinion holds that marijuana is legal or illegal on any particular parcel, and neither creates or destroys a tribal marijuana programme. Any summary that says "McGirt legalised/outlawed marijuana in half of Oklahoma" is wrong.
  2. Who prosecutes a cannabis offence depends on (a) where, (b) who the defendant is, (c) who the victim is (if any), and (d) which law is charged — tribal code, Oklahoma law, or federal CSA. In broad outline (general Indian-law framework, not a cannabis-specific holding): Indian defendant + Indian country + Major Crimes Act offence → federal (and potentially tribal) jurisdiction, state generally lacks jurisdiction; non-Indian defendant + Indian victim in Indian country → state + federal concurrent jurisdiction after Castro-Huerta; non-Indian + non-Indian victim → state jurisdiction generally applies. Drug-possession/manufacture offences are not Major Crimes Act enumerated offences in the same way as murder/sexual abuse, so the Major Crimes Act row does not directly govern a simple possession case — the applicable route is the General Crimes Act / tribal jurisdiction / federal CSA, and the cannabis-specific jurisdictional map is Verify for any charged fact pattern. No cannabis-specific McGirt/Castro-Huerta application case was located in this run.
  3. Tribal law is a separate layer. Even where Oklahoma would not prosecute (or would punish less), a tribe's own code (e.g. Cherokee § 2208.1 conformity, Muscogee Title 14 prohibition on secondary evidence) governs tribal members on tribal land, and federal CSA liability is independent of both. An OMMA patient licence is a state licence; it does not by itself authorise possession, cultivation or sale on tribal trust land, and it does not displace tribal or federal law there. Conversely, a tribal member's lawful medical use under Oklahoma law is protected from tribal escalation by Cherokee § 2208.1 only within that section's terms (medical/minor use-or-possession offences, as defined there).
  4. Federal Schedule III / "state-licensed" — Verify (carried from Run 1). Whether any tribal programme (none located in Oklahoma) would count as "state-licensed" under the 28 Apr 2026 federal Schedule III order (91 FR 22714) is Verify from the federal rule text itself. The Cherokee Schedule III listing (tribal code, 2020) is not the federal Schedule III order and must not be conflated with it: Cherokee tribal Schedule III predates the federal 2026 order by over five years and operates under tribal sovereignty, not under 91 FR 22714.

10.1.6 Agreements or disputes with the state

  • No Oklahoma tribal-state cannabis compact, agreement, or memorandum was located in this run. Unavailable — not asserted to be non-existent.
  • Disputes in the background (not cannabis-specific): McGirt itself was a state-vs-tribal/federal jurisdiction dispute; Castro-Huerta was Oklahoma's (partially successful) attempt to restore state jurisdiction. The post-McGirt transfer of thousands of cases from state to federal/tribal forums (the State estimated >18,000 cases per year needing transfer, per the Castro-Huerta opinion summary) is a general criminal-justice consequence, not a cannabis enforcement statistic — do not quote it as a cannabis figure.
  • Enforcement coordination (OCTF + tribal police, §10.1.4) is the only located tribal-state cannabis enforcement relationship, and it is described in state (OAG) sources, not in a tribal-state agreement text.

10.2 Interstate issues

10.2.1 Hemp shipments

  • Federal framework (not re-researched beyond Run 1 baseline): Hemp produced under a USDA-approved state or tribal plan (Oklahoma state plan + 6 tribal plans, §10.1.1) is hemp under federal law; the 2018 Farm Bill's interstate-commerce protection for hemp is the general federal rule. Oklahoma-specific shipment rules (e.g. any Oklahoma manifest, transport, or out-of-state shipment permit for hemp) were not located in this run — Verify against ODAFF's hemp rules (OAC 35:30-24) before advising on a shipment.
  • What hemp is not: A shipment of material above the hemp THC threshold is marijuana, not hemp, and is subject to the medical-marijuana regime (OMMA licence + Metrc) or to criminal law if unlicensed — regardless of what the shipment is labelled. The forthcoming federal total-THC definition / 0.4 mg per container cap (after 11 Dec 2026, per the fixed baseline) will change what counts as hemp federally; no Oklahoma hemp-shipment-specific (manifest/permit) guidance was located; the general federal-dates guidance is the ODAFF Jan 2026 letter, which is not shipment-specific.
  • No Oklahoma hemp-shipment seizure, interdiction, or interstate hemp dispute case was located in this run. Unavailable.

10.2.2 Out-of-state patients buying in Oklahoma — the temporary licence (Run 1, confirmed on the OMMA page opened in this run)

Verbatim from the OMMA Patient Licenses page (opened 30 Oct 2026, https://oklahoma.gov/omma/patients-caregivers/patient-licenses.html)::)

"Residents of other states who have state-government-issued medical marijuana patient licenses are eligible for Oklahoma's 30-day adult or minor out-of-state patient licenses. Prescriptions or licenses issued by out-of-state medical providers are not honored for Oklahoma's out-of-state licenses."

"For example, among Oklahoma's bordering states with medical marijuana programs, patients from Missouri and Arkansas are eligible because those state governments issue the licenses. Patients from Texas are not eligible, because the state government does not issue the licenses."

  • Terms (OMMA page + 63 O.S. § 420(F) as quoted in Run 1): 30 days, $100 + $4.30 processing fee, renewable by fresh application ("Renewal shall be granted with resubmission of a new application. No additional criteria shall be required" — § 420(F) via Justia, Run 1). No Oklahoma physician recommendation is required for the out-of-state licence (OMMA table: Physician Recommendation = No for Out-of-State). Temporary holders are subject to the same patient possession limits (3 oz on person / 8 oz at home, etc. — Run 1 §1.3, secondary summary for temporary holders).
  • Bordering-state matrix (from the OMMA page's own examples + programme existence):
Bordering state State-issued medical licence? Oklahoma 30-day temporary licence?
Missouri Yes (state-issued) Yes — expressly named by OMMA as eligible
Arkansas Yes (state-issued) Yes — expressly named by OMMA as eligible
Texas No state-issued card under the Texas Compassionate Use Program (TCUP, low-THC, registry/prescription model) No — expressly named by OMMA as ineligible ("the state government does not issue the licenses")
Kansas No medical marijuana programme (Run 1 Kansas research: marijuana illegal for both medical and adult use in Kansas) No — no state-issued licence to present; Kansas patients cannot qualify on a Kansas licence
New Mexico Yes (state medical cannabis programme, state-issued cards) Eligible in principle under the OMMA rule as written (state-government-issued licence) — but New Mexico is not named as an example on the OMMA page extract opened, so this row is Verify against OMMA's full FAQ before stating it as OMMA-confirmed. Do not quote New Mexico as OMMA-named.
Colorado (not bordering Oklahoma, but the Nebraska v. Colorado context) Adult-use + medical Not a bordering-state temporary-licence example; a Colorado cardholder would fall under the general "state-government-issued licence" rule — Verify against OMMA FAQ for Colorado specifically.
  • Transport warning (federal, applies to every row): Buying lawfully in Oklahoma does not make it lawful to carry marijuana across a state line. Marijuana remains federally controlled, and the destination state's law applies the moment the border is crossed (e.g. Texas does not recognise an Oklahoma licence; Kansas has no medical programme). Temporary-licence holders must buy in Oklahoma and, in practice, use/possess in Oklahoma. This is the consistent secondary + OMMA-framework position; the federal transport offence itself is not quoted as statute in this file (Verify 21 U.S.C. provisions if a citation is needed).
  • Oklahoma residents buying out of state: No Oklahoma rule authorises an Oklahoma patient to buy in another state on an Oklahoma licence alone; reciprocity in the destination state (if any) governs. Verify destination-by-destination; do not present Oklahoma's temporary licence as reciprocal in reverse.

10.2.4 Residents of neighbouring states buying in Oklahoma — by state (summary)

  • Texas: The largest neighbouring-state buying flow in practice, but not via a Texas licence (Texas patients are ineligible for the temporary licence, §10.2.2). A Texas resident can only buy in Oklahoma lawfully by holding an Oklahoma patient licence (which requires Oklahoma residency + an Oklahoma physician recommendation — i.e. not available to a non-resident visitor) or by holding a state-issued licence from another state. In practice, secondary sources describe Texas residents crossing to Oklahoma dispensaries, but no official count of Texas buyers was located, and any such flow that involves carrying marijuana back to Texas is unlawful in Texas and federally. No official buyer-count figure is stated.
  • Kansas: Kansas has no medical programme, so Kansas residents hold no state-issued medical licence to present for a temporary licence. Kansas residents are in the same position as Texas residents for lawful purchase (Oklahoma residency + recommendation, or another state's licence). No official Kansas-buyer count located.
  • Arkansas and Missouri: Eligible for the 30-day temporary licence (§10.2.2). No official count of Arkansas/Missouri temporary-licence holders by home state was located in the OMMA monthly table (which reports patients in aggregate, Run 1 Part 5) — Unavailable by home state.
  • New Mexico: See the Verify row in §10.2.2. New Mexico is itself a medical + adult-use state, so the incentive to buy in Oklahoma is lower than for Texas/Kansas residents; no official New Mexico-buyer count located.
  • No interstate purchase agreement (e.g. a Texas–Oklahoma or Kansas–Oklahoma purchase compact) was located. Unavailable.

10.2.5 Interstate laws and agreements

Law / case / agreement What it is Status / relevance to Oklahoma
Nebraska v. Colorado, U.S. Supreme Court (2016) — filed by Nebraska and Oklahoma Dec 2014: Nebraska and Oklahoma moved for leave to file an original-jurisdiction complaint against Colorado, arguing Colorado's Amendment 64 (recreational legalisation, 2012) was preempted by the federal Controlled Substances Act, facilitated violations of federal drug law, and increased trafficking/costs in the plaintiff states. Relief sought: declaratory judgment of preemption + injunction against implementing Colorado's licensing/regulation/taxation provisions. Denied 21 Mar 2016, without opinion or explanation. The order simply states: "The motion for leave to file a bill of complaint is denied." Thomas J., joined by Alito J., dissented, arguing the Court was constitutionally/statutorily obligated to hear controversies between states. The denial is not a merits ruling that Colorado's law is lawful, and it does not bar all future challenges (Nebraska AG statement at the time, secondary). Verified (multiple secondary + case summaries agree on date, parties, and no-opinion denial). Sources: https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=128a427f-188e-43c4-a05e-459f9a84ffb9 ; https://www.nprillinois.org/2016-03-21/supreme-court-denies-marijuana-suit-from-colorados-neighboring-states ; https://www.studicata.com/summaries/united-states-supreme-court/nebraska-v-colorado-2016-7tr0zx/
Any later Oklahoma interstate cannabis suit or compact None located. No Oklahoma suit against another legalising state after Nebraska v. Colorado, and no interstate cannabis agreement (purchase, transport, enforcement, or tax) involving Oklahoma was found. Unavailable — do not assert none exists beyond the search in this run.
Federal interstate hemp commerce (2018 Farm Bill) Hemp produced under an approved plan may move in interstate commerce under federal law (general rule). Oklahoma's plan + 6 tribal plans (§10.1.1) are the Oklahoma-side plans. See §10.2.1; Oklahoma shipment-permit specifics Verify (ODAFF rules).
Federal transport of marijuana Marijuana remains federally controlled; interstate transport is a federal offence independent of state medical licences. General framework; specific statute citation Verify if needed (not quoted here).

PART 11 — OPERATIONS RULES

11.1 Testing: required tests, sampling, failed tests and recalls, licensed labs, OMMA QA lab

11.1.1 What must be tested — OAC 442:10-8-1(a) (verbatim, Justia reproduction, current through Okla. Reg. Vol. 42 No. 19, 16 June 2025)

"To ensure the suitability and safety for human consumption of medical marijuana and medical marijuana products, growers and processors are required to test medical marijuana and medical marijuana products for microbials, mycotoxins, residual solvents, pesticides, THC and cannabinoid concentration, terpenoid type and concentration, heavy metals, foreign materials and filth, and water activity and moisture content in accordance with the following standards and thresholds. No laboratory may test medical marijuana without a valid, unexpired testing laboratory license issued by the Authority. A licensed laboratory shall only send samples for testing to another Oklahoma licensed laboratory."

Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-8/section-442-10-8-1-d-1/ — accessed 2026-10-30.

Rule Content
Who tests Growers and processors must test; only a licensed, unexpired Oklahoma testing laboratory may test, and it may only send samples to another Oklahoma licensed laboratory.
Analytes (summary of (a)) Microbials, mycotoxins, residual solvents, pesticides, THC/cannabinoid concentration, terpenoid type/concentration, heavy metals, foreign materials and filth, water activity and moisture content. Numeric thresholds per analyte are in the body of OAC 442:10-8-1 — Verify the current threshold table against the OAC text before quoting a single number, as this run opened the purpose/batch/recall paragraphs, not every threshold row.
No sale before pass — growers "Growers shall not sell or otherwise transfer any medical marijuana from any medical marijuana harvest batch until samples of the harvest batch have passed all tests in accordance with this Subchapter, except that growers may sell or otherwise transfer harvest batches that have failed testing to processors for decontamination or remediation in accordance with OAC 442:10-8-1(l)(2)." Growers may also transfer to processors for decontamination before testing, provided decontaminated material is not processed into a solvent-based concentrate and is returned to the originating grower; decontaminated batches must pass all tests before transfer or sale.
No sale before pass — processors Processors shall not purchase, obtain, process, sell or transfer from any harvest or production batch until samples have passed all tests, except purchase/processing of failed batches for remediation only under (l)(2).
No sale before pass — dispensaries "Dispensaries shall not purchase, accept transfer of, sell, or otherwise transfer any medical marijuana or medical marijuana products that have not passed all tests in accordance with this Subchapter."
Batch sizes (OAC 442:10-8-1) Grower harvest batches ≤15 lb, except plant material to be sold to a processor to be turned into concentrate, ≤50 lb. Processor production batches ≤4 litres of liquid concentrate or ≤9 lb of non-liquid product; final medical marijuana products ≤1,000 g total delta-9-THC.

11.1.2 Sampling — OAC 442:10-8-3 and the 1 June 2024 standardisation rules (OAC 442:10-8-6.3)

  • Samples must be collected, handled, stored and disposed of under OAC 442:10-8-6.3. Persons collecting samples are "Samplers": they follow the testing laboratory's approved standard operating procedures, are trained on those SOPs, collect at the grower/processor/dispensary location, and affix a tamper-proof seal at collection. The sampling record includes batch number and total batch size by weight or unit count and sampling conditions including temperature. The laboratory must maintain inventory-manifest documentation (OAC 442:10-3-6) and use an electronic inventory management system meeting OAC 442:10-5-6(d) for each sample collected, transported and analysed; a controlled copy of the sampling SOP must be on laboratory premises and accessible to the sampler in the field. A laboratory shall not accept a sample below the minimum amount in OAC 442:10-8-3(b); reserve samples must be maintained and properly stored for at least 30 days.
  • Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/oklahoma/OAC-442-10-8-6.3 — accessed 2026-10-30. Note: § 8-6.3 applies, from 1 June 2024, to testing laboratories renewing their licence; refusal/failure to comply "shall result in the permanent revocation of the medical marijuana testing laboratory license" (Cornell text). Whether that permanent-revocation sentence applies identically to first-time licensees is Verify against current OAC text.
  • Laboratory accreditation and scope — OAC 442:10-8-2: every testing laboratory must obtain accreditation from an Authority-approved accrediting entity subscribing to ILAC, before applying, in chemistry and biology or cannabis, specific to the procedure used; renewal is contingent on maintaining accreditation; a laboratory may only report COA results for analytes within its accreditation scope, must notify the Authority of scope changes, and if it outsources testing and reports those results on a COA it must identify the laboratory that actually conducted the testing. External quality-control testing applies "upon operational status of the Authority's Quality Assurance Laboratory" at a frequency determined by the Authority or its designee.
  • Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-8/section-442-10-8-2/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Conflict of interest — OAC 442:10-8-2(d): a person who is a direct beneficial owner of a licensed dispensary, commercial grower or processor shall not be an owner of a licensed laboratory; a laboratory shall not test samples for any business in which an owner, employee or agent of the laboratory has any ownership or financial interest; laboratories must have policies preventing undue commercial/financial influence on testing. Safety: laboratories must comply with OSHA 29 CFR § 1910.1450. Personnel: a laboratory shall not operate unless a medical laboratory director is on site during operational hours (or a qualified written designee in absence).
  • Source: same Justia § 8-2 page — accessed 2026-10-30.

11.1.3 Failed tests, remediation, retesting, embargo and recall — OAC 442:10-8-1(g), (k), (l)

  • Retest rule (paraphrase of (j)/(k) as opened): a harvest or production batch that is retested and does not have two (2) successful tests for each analyte must either be remediated or decontaminated under the Act and Rules, or be disposed of under the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Waste Management Act, 63 O.S. § 427a et seq., and the Rules. If a sample fails, the batch may be remediated/decontaminated under the Rules, or if it is not or cannot be remediated/decontaminated it must be disposed of as waste (text truncated in the copy opened — Verify the full (k)(1)(B) sentence before quoting it).
  • Recall — OAC 442:10-8-1(g)(2), as reproduced on OMMA's Licensee Recall Responsibilities page (official, opened via search): if any medical marijuana or product tests above allowable thresholds, is subject to an embargo, is otherwise determined unsafe, or otherwise fails Subchapter 8 standards, then: (A) any commercial licensee with knowledge shall immediately notify the Authority; (B) all such product shall be immediately recalled and cannot be sold or transferred; (C) every licensee who is in possession or has ever had possession shall assist in the immediate recall, including measures to ensure no transfer, a distribution list (licensee name, licence number, address, contact information), a product list (category, description, net contents, batch number, and cultivator/manufacturer name and licence number where applicable), notice to all affected licensees and consumers once identified, and communication with the Authority with all required information/documentation within two (2) weeks unless granted additional time; (vi) failure to timely comply may result in revocation, suspension and monetary penalties, and the Authority may issue a public recall notice at any time if necessary to protect public health, safety and welfare; (D) the licensee whose harvest/production batch is being recalled bears the costs for disposal of all medical marijuana waste subject to the recall.
  • Source: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/recalls/licensee-recall-responsibilities.html — accessed 2026-10-30. OMMA's embargo/recall landing page states the same in summary: on embargo or recall, licensees must pause transfers of affected inventory and notify impacted downstream businesses and patients, and the originating licensee bears disposal costs; failure to comply timely may result in suspension/revocation or monetary penalties.
  • Source: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/recalls/embargoed-and-recalled-products.html — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Recent recalls (official OMMA news, dated — these are examples, not a complete recall history):
  • 20 Oct 2026 (updated 26 Oct 2026): recall of flower production batches from Blue Collar Criminals Collective, LLC (GAAI-NJVE-0Z9P), after a self-report and a dispensary report; OIE review of lab results and Metrc data confirmed yeast and mold failures; a portion of initially-passing batch BIS091326-2 that was later mixed with a failed batch was included, unmixed product from that batch was not. Source: same embargo/recall page — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • 19 Mar 2026: mandatory recall of products tested by Greenleaf Labs LLC (LAAA-MP4O-T1EE) between April 2023 and July 2025; OMMA ordered Greenleaf to cease operations in August 2025 after a routine inspection revealed testing inaccuracies, CORRECTED (audit): OMMA ordered Greenleaf to cease operations in August 2025 after a routine inspection revealed testing inaccuracies, and mandatory action followed test-failed products remaining in dispensary inventory; the notification point alone does not state the trigger. Source: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/about/news/2026/mandatory-recall-issued-for-products-tested-by-greenleaf-labs-llc.html — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • 23 Mar 2026: recall of pre-roll batches processed by Sunny Roads Processing 2, LLC (PAAA-8JA2-CK1Z), after reports about pre-rolls purchased at Miami Natural Health, LLC (Miami, OK — not Miami, FL); testing at multiple labs failed for pesticide content above allowable thresholds. CORRECTED (audit): OMMA EXPANDED this recall on 15 May 2026 to additional items; the 23 Mar 2026 list alone is incomplete. 11.2 Licence rules: transfers, ownership changes, renewal, residency, limits, relocation, surrender/revocation, insurance/bonding

11.2.1 Term, renewal timelines (OAC 442:10-5-2, Run 1 §4.7 — repeated here so Part 11 stands alone)

  • Commercial licences are issued for 12 months, expiring one year from issuance (OAC 442:10-5-2(a)). Research/education licences likewise 12 months (OAC 442:10-4-2(a)). It is the holder's responsibility to renew with all documentation before expiration under OAC 442:10-5-3; OMMA may require further information/documentation and additional background checks on renewal and may refuse renewal for failure to meet 63 O.S. §§ 420 et seq. / §§ 427.1 et seq. / OAC 442:10 or the Waste Management Act.
  • Timely vs late (from 1 Nov 2024, Run 1): only a renewal submitted at least 60 calendar days before expiration is "timely" for the 90-business-day review guarantee (63 O.S. § 427.14(N)); a renewal submitted less than 60 days before expiration but before expiration incurs no late fee but the licence expires on its date and remains expired until OMMA approves; late renewal (after expiration) carries $500 per week, the licensee cannot operate while expired, and more than 60 days expired means it cannot be renewed (it must reapply, subject to the moratorium). Verify the late-fee and 60-day-expired sentences against current OAC 442:10-5-2(c) text — they were summarised in Run 1 from OMMA's 7 Mar 2025 transfer notice, not quoted verbatim from the rule.
  • Monthly reporting (standing duty, Run 1): all commercial licensees must file an OMMA monthly report by the 15th of each month for the previous month's activity, even with no product on site.

11.2.2 Transfers and ownership changes — OAC 442:10-5-2(f) regime (effective 29 Oct 2024)

  • Definitions (OAC 442:10-5-2, Justia reproduction, current through Vol. 42 No. 19, 16 June 2025): a "change of ownership request" is any request that would change, amend or in any way alter ownership, including any shareholders of a corporate entity and all officers, any owners of any other legal entity, and any person holding an interest or convertible note in an entity that owns, operates or manages a licensed facility. A "license transfer application" is a request that would (A) transfer a licence from a prior owner to a new owner, (B) change the location due to a change in ownership, or (C) change the business name or the individual/entity holding the licence. Name-change requests must be submitted in a license transfer application, and a location-change request submitted due to a change of ownership, name or transfer must be included in that transfer application.
  • Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-5/section-442-10-5-2/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Procedure and fees: transfer applications are subject to all requirements in OAC 442:10-5-3 (the full commercial application, including ownership/residency proof — see §11.2.3). Applications submitted before 1 Nov 2024: $500 nonrefundable fee. Applications submitted on or after 1 Nov 2024: a nonrefundable fee equal to the annual licence/application fee for that licence type under 63 O.S. § 427.14 (i.e. the tier fee for growers/processors, the sales-based renewal formula for dispensaries — see Run 1 Part 4). The seller generates a transfer code and the buyer then begins the transfer application (secondary law-firm summary of the OMMA process — Verify the code step against OMMA's current transfer instructions before advising a client, as it is a portal step, not rule text).
  • Source (rule): same Justia § 5-2 page; source (process summary, secondary, Dec 2024): https://gieslawfirm.com/blog/navigating-ommas-new-rules-for-ownership-and-license-transfers — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Control does not pass early: the new owner may not take possession of or control any part of the business until OMMA approves the transfer and the new owner is registered with OBNDD; on OBNDD registration, the prior and new owner have 15 days after issuance, after which the prior owner is no longer a licensee. Any attempt to transfer a business, marijuana, concentrate or products without Authority approval is grounds for revocation or non-renewal of the licence and denial, revocation or non-renewal of current or future licences/applications with ownership held by any person involved in the unlawful transfer.
  • Source (secondary summary of the rule, Hall Estill, 17 Dec 2024): https://www.hallestill.com/index.php/news-insights/new-omma-transfer-license-process/pdf — accessed 2026-10-30. Verify the 15-day sentence against current OAC 442:10-5-2(f) text before quoting it as rule.
  • Ownership-change documentation (OAC 442:10-5-2, as opened): list of all owners and principal officers with supporting documentation under OAC 442:10-5-3(e)(1); affidavit of lawful presence for each new owner; documents under OAC 442:10-5-3(e)(7) establishing that the applicant, members/managers/board members and 75% of ownership interests are Oklahoma residents (see §11.2.3); bond or attestation under OAC 442:10-5-3.3 certifying compliance with 63 O.S. § 427.26 where applicable.
  • Publicly traded company exception: growers, processors or commercial transporters that have held a valid licence for at least 18 months and are operating in good standing may submit an ownership-change request to add a publicly traded company as owner; the publicly traded company shall not own more than 40% of the equity; the 75% residency test then applies to ownership excluding the publicly traded company, with a Secretary of State certificate of good standing issued within 30 days and a list of all owners excluding the publicly traded company's shareholders.
  • Source: same Justia § 5-2 page — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Moratorium interaction — Verify, do not present as settled: Run 1 flagged a secondary report that HB 3143 prohibits transfers while administrative action is pending (including action that could lead to revocation/suspension/non-renewal, or OBNDD registration action), requiring full resolution first and barring a transfer application for at least 6 months after an annulment/revocation/suspension. The enrolled HB 3143 text was not opened in Run 1 or in this run. Do not advise that a transfer is barred, or that it is outside the moratorium, until enrolled HB 3143 is opened. OAC 442:10-5-3(h) as opened in Run 1 excepts renewals and "the issuance of a medical marijuana business license necessitated by [events stated in the full paragraph]" — the full (h)(2) exception list is likewise Verify.
  • [Audit correction] HB 3143 (2026) is ENACTED (approved by the Governor 5 May 2026), including its transfer bar: a transfer application is prohibited while the licensee is subject to administrative action that may necessitate revocation, suspension or non-renewal of the licence or OBNDD registration, pending actions/appeals must be completed first, and the introduced text states a bar of not less than 6 months after an annulment, revocation or suspension term. The earlier Verify flag is removed. Source: https://oklahoma.gov/governor/newsroom/newsroom/2026/governor-stitt-signs-17-bills-into-law.html

11.2.3 Residency and ownership rules (Run 1 §4.3, repeated without change)

  • Age 25+ for commercial applicants; entity applicants: 75% of all members, managers, executive officers, partners, board members or any other form of business ownership must be Oklahoma residents (63 O.S. § 427.14(E)(7)(c)); individual applicants must prove Oklahoma residency; residency means at least 2 years immediately preceding the application OR 5 years of continuous Oklahoma residency during the preceding 25 years (§ 427.14(E)(11)), with a pre-30 Aug 2019 licensee exemption from the 2-year/5-year test; all ownership interests must be disclosed, including any person holding an interest or convertible note.
  • Court position (Run 1, unchanged): Original Investments, LLC v. Oklahoma, W.D. Okla., 4 June 2021 — challenge dismissed on clean-hands grounds, merits NOT reached, requirement NOT struck down or enjoined. United States v. Stacy, 10th Cir. 2025 — requirement treated as operative law in a prosecution arising from a structure designed to hide out-of-state ownership; not a holding that residency is unconstitutional. Present the 75% rule as in effect and constitutionally untested on the merits at appellate level.
  • Research/education exception: the 75% test does not apply to research facility applicants that are public institutions or Oklahoma non-profit entities registered with the Secretary of State (OAC 442:10-4-3(e)(4), Justia reproduction).
  • Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-4/section-442-10-4-3-d-1/ — accessed 2026-10-30.

11.2.4 Limits per owner, relocation, surrender/revocation

  • No numeric limit per owner: 63 O.S. § 427.14(E)(8) — "There shall be no limit to the number of medical marijuana business licenses or categories that an individual or entity can apply for or receive, although each application and each category shall require a separate application and application fee" — subject to the moratorium, the lab-ownership conflict rule (§11.1.2), and any cap enacted by HB 3144 if enacted (Run 1: Verify, do not treat a 2,550 grower cap as law). A grower, processor or dispensary licence is valid for a single location at the address on the application (OAC 442:10-5-2(b)); a grower, processor and dispensary, or any combination, may share the same address/physical location subject to the Act's restrictions. Run 1 noted a rule amendment providing for one commercial grower licence for any one property — Verify current OAC 442:10-5-2(b) before advising on multi-licence single-parcel structures.
  • [Audit correction] HB 3144 (2026) 2,550 grower cap is NOT law: House 82–15 (25 Feb 2026), Senate 34–12 with amendments (29 Apr 2026), no Governor approval or enrolled act located. Source: https://legiscan.com/OK/bill/HB3144/2026
  • Relocation: a location-change request must be in writing and accepted by the Authority; on written acceptance, the licensee must carry a physical copy of the written location-change approval while transporting product from location to location (OAC 442:10-5-2, Justia). If the location change is due to a change of ownership, name or transfer, it must be included in a license transfer application (§11.2.2). The $500 location-change fee reported in Run 1 Part 4 is Verify against the current fee schedule, as the transfer-fee change of 1 Nov 2024 may have superseded it for ownership-linked moves.
  • Surrender / non-renewal / revocation — liquidation: a research or education licensee whose licence is not renewed, revoked, suspended or voluntarily surrendered "shall cease all operations immediately upon expiration of the license and shall liquidate or dispose of all medical marijuana and medical marijuana products in accordance with OAC 442:10-5-2(d)" (OAC 442:10-4-2(d), Justia). The same liquidation rule is cross-referenced for commercial licensees in OAC 442:10-5-2(d); the full text of (d) (timeframe, method, Metrc closure) was not opened verbatim in this run — Verify before quoting a liquidation deadline.
  • Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-4/section-442-10-4-2-d-1/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Revocation grounds located in this run (non-exhaustive): failure to timely comply with recall provisions (OAC 442:10-8-1(g)(2)(C)(vi)); refusal to permit OMMA/OBNDD/OSBI/AG inspection of a waste facility (63 O.S. § 430(D)); unlawful transfer without approval (§11.2.2); failure to erect required grower signage within 60 days after renewal (OAC 442:10-6-1(c)(2) — "immediate revocation"); failure of a testing laboratory to comply with the 1 June 2024 standardisation rules (permanent revocation, §11.1.2 — Verify scope). A consolidated OMMA revocation-only register was not found in Run 1 Part 5.

11.3 Cultivation rules: canopy/plant limits by tier, indoor/outdoor/greenhouse, water/electricity reporting, patient home grow

  • Commercial tiers (Run 1 Part 4, repeated in summary — full tier tables are in Run 1 and are not re-printed with different numbers here): indoor/greenhouse/light-deprivation growers are tiered by canopy square footage — "canopy" is the total surface area within a cultivation area dedicated to flowering plants, including each tier/shelf of a tiered/shelving system, excluding areas used only for immature plants/seedlings before flowering; vertically grown cylinders are measured by circumference × length (§ 427.14(D)(2)(d)). Fees $2,500–$50,000 plus $0.25/sq ft over 100,000 sq ft (7 tiers). Outdoor growers are tiered by acres, $2,500–$50,000 plus $250/acre over 50 acres (8 tiers). A combined indoor + outdoor operation at one location requires a separate licence for each type, each with its own tier fee. Initial fee is on estimated canopy/acres to be harvested for the year; annual fee thereafter is based on canopy harvested during the previous 12 months (§ 427.14(D)(2)). There is no per-plant count cap for commercial growers in the tier scheme — the limit is canopy/acreage, not plant number. Verify the tier bill authority (HB 2179 (2022) / SB 813 (2023) per secondary summaries in Run 1) against oklegislature.gov before citing bill numbers.
  • Indoor/outdoor/greenhouse distinction: greenhouse and light-deprivation are treated as indoor for tiering (Run 1). No separate greenhouse-only rule was located in OAC 442:10 in this run beyond the tier treatment and the general security/construction rules (§11.4). Outdoor grows are subject to the same testing, Metrc, signage (§11.4) and certificate-of-compliance rules as indoor grows; any local outdoor-grow ban or setback beyond the state school buffer is a local rule (Run 1 Part 3), not a state cultivation rule.
  • Water and electricity reporting — Verify, do not present as current law: Run 1 found that HB 4055 (2022, conference form) would have required public utilities to report monthly electricity/water supplied to licensed grows to OMMA in a format integrated with seed-to-sale software, with rules for non-utility supply (well water, gas generators) and permanent revocation for refusal/failure or use of an unpermitted water source; later bills HB 1711 and SB 801 (2023) were in the same terms. Whether any utility-reporting duty is now codified was not confirmed from a directly opened current statute in Run 1 or this run. The confirmed, separate duty is the OMMA monthly report by the 15th (§11.2.1) and Metrc inventory tracking. See §11.6 for the DEQ water permit position, which is distinct from a utility reporting duty.
  • Patient home grow — 63 O.S. § 427.12 (verbatim, Justia 2025 reproduction):

    "A. All medical marijuana grown by medical marijuana patient license holders or caregivers may only be grown on real property owned by the patient license holder or on real property for which the patient license holder has the property owner's written permission to grow marijuana on the property. B. All medical marijuana plants grown by a patient or caregiver shall be grown so that the marijuana is not accessible to a member of the general public. No marijuana plants shall be visible from any street adjacent to the property. For purposes of this section, 'visible' means viewable by a person with 20/20 vision from a street adjacent to the property without the use of binoculars, drones, or any other visual aid. C. It is expressly prohibited to operate extraction equipment or utilize extraction processes if the equipment or process utilizes butane, propane, carbon dioxide or any potentially hazardous material in a residential property."

  • Added by Laws 2019, c. 11, § 12 (Unity Bill). Patient plant counts: 6 mature + 6 seedlings (§ 420(A), Run 1). OMMA patient guidance (opened via search) adds: patient-grown marijuana must be on property owned by the patient or with the owner's written permission; cannot be visible by someone with 20/20 vision from any adjacent street; extraction using butane, propane, carbon dioxide or any potentially hazardous material is prohibited in/on residential property; licensed patients are prohibited from sharing legally purchased medical marijuana with any other individual, licensed or not (OAC 442:10-2-9(a)(b)).
  • Sources: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-427-12/ ; https://oklahoma.gov/omma/patients-caregivers/patient-rights-and-responsibilities.html — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Caregiver home grow: caregivers for homebound patients only, maximum 5 patients (Run 1 Part 1); the same § 427.12 property/visibility/extraction rules apply to caregiver-grown plants (statute says "patient license holders or caregivers").

11.4 Security: cameras, alarms, storage, transport

  • OAC 442:10-6-1 — the OMMA general security rule is a standard, not a camera specification. Verbatim (Cornell reproduction, adopted 40 Ok Reg 382 eff. 1 Nov 2022 (emergency); 40 Ok Reg Vol. 22, 1 Aug 2023, eff. 11 Aug 2023):

    "(a) Commercial licensees shall implement appropriate security measures to deter and prevent the unauthorized entrance into areas containing marijuana and the theft and diversion of marijuana. (b) Commercial licensees are responsible for the security of all marijuana items on the licensed premises or all marijuana items in their possession during transit."

  • Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/oklahoma/OAC-442-10-6-1 — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • No OMMA rule was located in this run prescribing a specific camera count, camera retention period, or 24-hour video surveillance standard in OAC 442:10-6-1. Do not state an OMMA camera-retention number (e.g. 30/60/90 days) as OMMA law — Verify against OAC 442:10-6-2 (Construction of premises) and any current OMMA inspection form before advising. OMMA's November 2025 Grower Inspection Form (Version 5.3) asks only whether the licensee "has security measures to deter and prevent unauthorized entrance … and the theft and diversion of marijuana" (OAC 442:10-6-1(a)), and whether the inspector can perform an inspection — it does not, in the extract opened, list a camera-retention check.
  • Source (inspection form): https://aem-prod.oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/omma/forms/Grower%20Inspection%20Form.pdf — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Grower signage (OAC 442:10-6-1(c)): commercial growers must post signage at the site visible from the road at the primary entrance (the principal/main entrance used by staff/persons accessing the property), at the perimeter, at least 18 × 24 inches, font at least 2 inches, black standardised font on white background, complying with county/local ordinances, stating business name, physical address, phone number and medical marijuana business licence number. Failure to erect proper signage within 60 days after renewal of each grower application "shall result in the immediate revocation" of the grower licence.
  • OBNDD physical security — OAC Title 475, Chapter 20 (OBNDD, not OMMA): for non-practitioners/storage areas, controls must comply with 21 CFR § 1301.72; each registered premises must have a security alarm system that on unauthorised entry transmits a signal directly to a central station protection agency or a local/state police agency with a legal duty to respond, or a 24-hour control station operated by the registrant, or another source approved by the Director; controlled-substance storage areas must have self-closing, self-locking doors of substantial material (or a door kept closed and locked at all times when not in use and under direct observation of a responsible employee/agent when in use); storage areas accessible only to an absolute minimum number of authorised employees, with written-authorised observation for maintenance/business guests/visitors passing through; all finished, processed or packaged medical marijuana must be stored in a secure, locked storage area (closet, cabinet, safe or vault) to prevent diversion, theft or loss; safes/cabinets must be of substantially constructed steel, and if under 750 lb must be bolted or cemented to the floor so they cannot be removed. Manufacturing areas (OAC 475:20-1-4) add: all in-process marijuana returned to storage at termination of the process (unless a continuous process should not be interrupted), in which case the processing area/tanks/vessels/bins/bulk containers must be securely locked with adequate security; each building must have the alarm system described above and self-closing, self-locking doors; growing/processing/packaging/manufacturing areas accessible only to a minimum number of authorised employees.
  • Sources: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-475/chapter-20/section-475-20-1-3/ ; https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/oklahoma/OAC-475-20-1-4 — accessed 2026-10-30. Note: OAC 475:20-1-4 was amended by Okla. Reg. Vol. 41 Issue 21, 15 July 2024, eff. 4 Aug 2024 (Cornell note) — Verify the current OBNDD text, as the 2023 emergency amendment expired 14 Sept 2024 per the Cornell note.
  • Transport security: licensees are responsible for security of marijuana in transit (OAC 442:10-6-1(b)); transporters and transporter agents must implement security measures to deter/prevent theft/diversion during transportation (OAC 442:10-3-2(e); OAC 442:10-6-1(b), per OMMA inspection form). Each transport vehicle must be equipped with active GPS trackers capable of storing and transmitting GPS data — "The use of cell phones for GPS tracking does not meet this requirement" (OMMA Grower Inspection Form, citing 63 O.S. § 427.16(J)(1) and OAC 442:10-3-2(b)(1)); licensees must maintain updated and accurate transportation and GPS records on site and readily accessible. Transporter agents carry an OMMA transporter agent ID card while transporting (Run 1 Part 4, $25 per agent, OAC 442:10-3-3(b)). HB 2807 (2025) authorises commercial transporter licensees to use warehouse locations to temporarily store medical marijuana (OMMA 2025 rule impact statement, secondary relay of the bill — Verify the warehouse rule text in current OAC 442:10-3-1 / 442:10-3-6 before advising on warehouse storage).

The earlier Verify flag on warehouse authority is removed. Source: http://oklegislature.gov/BillInfo.aspx?Bill=HB2807&Session=2500

  • Secret shoppers: OAC 442:10-5-4(l) permits OMMA to employ secret shoppers to inspect licensed businesses covertly (OMMA 25 July 2024 permanent-rule release; SB 813 (2023)). This is an inspection tool, not a licensee security duty.
