11.5 Waste disposal rules and waste disposal facility licences

  • Statute — 63 O.S. § 430 (verbatim in part, Justia 2025 reproduction):

    "A. There is hereby created and authorized a medical marijuana waste disposal license. A person or entity in possession of a medical marijuana waste disposal license shall be entitled to possess, transport and dispose of medical marijuana waste. No person or entity shall dispose of medical marijuana waste without a valid medical marijuana waste disposal license. The Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority shall issue licenses upon proper application by a licensee and determination by the Authority that the proposed site and facility are physically and technically suitable. Upon a finding that a proposed medical marijuana waste disposal facility is not physically or technically suitable, the Authority shall deny the license. The Authority may, upon determining that public health or safety requires emergency action, issue a temporary license for treatment or storage of medical marijuana waste for a period not to exceed ninety (90) days. The Authority shall not, until November 1, 2021, issue more than ten medical marijuana waste disposal licenses. Beginning November 1, 2021, there shall be no limit to the number of medical marijuana waste disposal licenses issued by the Authority."

  • Screening ( § 430(B)): entity applicants undergo a screening process (full list not reproduced here — Verify against current § 430(B) before advising). Submission constitutes permission for entry/inspection during hours of operation and other reasonable times; refusal is grounds for non-renewal, suspension or revocation; OMMA, OBNDD, OSBI and the Attorney General may perform an annual unannounced on-site inspection (§ 430(D)). OMMA issues an annual permit for each facility, only on a finding of physical/technical suitability, revocable on a finding of unsuitability; emergency temporary permits up to 90 days (§ 430(E)). Fees: licence $5,000 initial; facility permit $500; all fees to the OMMA Revolving Fund (§ 430(F)). A waste licence holder need not obtain a transporter licence to transport medical marijuana waste (§ 430(G)).
  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-430/ — accessed 2026-10-30. Count (Run 1): 7 waste licences in the 1 Oct 2026 OMMA table (7 waste disposal facilities, not a separate "waste transporter" count).
  • What counts as waste, and what does not — OMMA/DEQ Waste Disposal FAQ (Sept 2025, official DEQ publication on Digital Prairie): all medical marijuana waste must be disposed of at an OMMA-licensed waste disposal facility. Battery-powered vapes containing medical marijuana must also go to an OMMA-licensed facility; the battery is hazardous waste managed as approved in the OMMA disposal licence, a DEQ hazardous waste permit, or under universal waste regulations 40 CFR §§ 273.10–273.20. Excluded from the definition of medical marijuana waste (OAC 442:10): seeds, root balls, stems, stalks and fan leaves. Disposal of excluded parts falls under DEQ authority; OAC 442:10-5-10 allows on-site disposal of excluded parts generated at the licensed location by open burning, incineration, burying, mulching, composting or any other DEQ-approved technique, with a disposal log required. Waste or excluded parts sent off-site to an OMMA facility must be disposed of using the method approved in that facility's OMMA licence and any DEQ/other-agency disposal permits.
  • Source: https://digitalprairie.ok.gov/digital/api/collection/stgovpub/id/732130/download — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Waste facility application — OAC 442:10-9-3: application on OMMA-prescribed form with establishment information including type of waste facility, attestation that premises are not on tribal lands, and a signed statement pledging not to divert marijuana to any person/entity not lawfully entitled to possess it; supporting documentation includes proof of sufficient liability insurance (§11.2.5: $5m/$5m), relevant waste permit(s) from DEQ or ODAFF, and building/fire code compliance information (OAC 748:20; 74 O.S. § 324.11 — full list truncated in the copy opened, Verify).
  • Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-9/section-442-10-9-3-d-1/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Processors and solid waste (secondary, Oklahoma Bar Journal, May 2025): processors are not permitted to obtain their own DEQ solid waste disposal licence; they must use OMMA-licensed waste disposal companies for solid medical marijuana waste. Labelled secondary — Verify against OAC 442:10-5-10 / DEQ solid waste rules before advising.
  • Source (secondary): https://cld.bz/5xqvaua/10/ — accessed 2026-10-30.

11.6 Environmental rules: water use and permits, pesticide limits, energy

  • Water — DEQ general permit OKG42T0000: under the OPDES Act (27A O.S. § 2-6-201 et seq.) and the Oklahoma Uniform Environmental Permitting Act (27A O.S. § 2-14-101 et seq.), owners/operators of medical marijuana grow facilities (as defined in OAC 442) are authorised to dispose of wastewater in surface impoundments, tank systems and/or through land application under Parts I–III of the permit. Covered wastewater: excess nutrient water, waste nutrient water, nutrient water runoff, wastewater from cleaning the facility/equipment, and reverse osmosis (RO) reject wastewater. The permit does not specify the treatment method. It does not cover discharges to waters of the state or potentially contaminated stormwater (those need a different OPDES permit), discharges to a publicly owned treatment works (POTW), or processor wastewater — the DEQ grower factsheet (April 2026) states the general permit OKG42T primarily addresses cultivation wastewater and explicitly excludes processor wastewater, so processors must seek alternative permits if applicable.
  • Sources: https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/deq/documents/2020/12/OKG42T-Medical-Marijuana-Wastewater-Permit-and-Fact-Sheet.pdf ; https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/deq/documents/executive-offices/fact-sheets/Medical%20Marijuana%20Commercial%20Grower%20Requirements.pdf — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • DEQ grower requirements (April 2026 factsheet): grow operations not connected to public water/sewer may require DEQ permits for water, sewer and industrial wastewater; solid waste (trash, pots, containers, fertiliser sacks) must go to a permitted municipal solid waste landfill or transfer station; open burning of general solid waste is not allowed. Water wells serving buildings or employee facilities are considered a Public Water System and must obtain a DEQ permit before the well is drilled or placed into operation. On-site sewage systems are only for sewage, not industrial wastewater, and must be properly permitted and inspected by DEQ. Industrial wastewater (RO reject, excess/waste nutrient water, nutrient runoff including hydroponic water) — discharge is prohibited; storage in above-ground tanks with final disposal at a public sewage facility does not require a permit; impoundments, below-ground tanks or land application require permitting (OKG42T0000). Water from air-conditioning units and dehumidifiers is not regulated and may be discharged/disposed without a permit.
  • Source: same DEQ grower factsheet — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Pesticides: no Oklahoma-specific cannabis pesticide list or numeric pesticide limit was located as a standalone rule in this run. Pesticides are a required test analyte under OAC 442:10-8-1(a) (see §11.1.1), and products failing pesticide thresholds are recalled (see Sunny Roads, 23 Mar 2026, §11.1.3), but the numeric thresholds live in OAC 442:10-8-1's threshold table, which was not fully opened here — Verify before quoting any pesticide limit. Separately, ODAFF pesticide registration law applies generally to pesticide products sold/used in Oklahoma; whether ODAFF maintains a cannabis-specific approved-pesticide list is Unavailable in this run — do not state that any named pesticide is "approved for cannabis in Oklahoma" without an ODAFF source. The Oklahoma Bar Journal (May 2025, secondary) notes processors need ODAFF permits for purchase/resale of live plants and cannabis seeds and an OSDH food permit for edible products, and a Class VIII un-odorised LPG permit for propane/butane use — labelled secondary, Verify against ODAFF/OSDH/LPG rules.
  • Energy: no Oklahoma energy-efficiency, lighting, or carbon rule specific to cannabis cultivation was located in this run. Energy enters the regime only via (a) the unconfirmed utility-reporting bills (§11.3, Verify) and (b) general building/fire/electrical code compliance via the certificate of compliance (Run 1 Part 3). Do not state an energy cap or reporting duty as current law.
  • Water rights / Oklahoma Water Resources Board: no OWRB rule specific to cannabis grows was located in this run. Groundwater/surface-water appropriation, if any, would arise under general Oklahoma water law (82 O.S.) — Unavailable as a cannabis-specific rule; do not state that grows are exempt from, or subject to, a specific OWRB permit without an OWRB source.

11.7 Sampling, giveaways, discounts and promotions

  • Sampling (product samples, distinct from lab sampling in §11.1.2): no OMMA rule expressly authorising free product samples to patients was located in this run. The operative constraints are: dispensaries shall not sell or transfer product that has not passed all tests (§11.1.1); licensed patients are prohibited from sharing legally purchased product with any other individual, licensed or not (OAC 442:10-2-9(a)(b), OMMA patient guidance); commercial licensees shall not sell/transfer to, or purchase/accept from, any unlicensed individual/entity, except dispensary sales to licensed patients/caregivers and processor processing directly on behalf of a licensed patient/caregiver under OAC 442:10-5-5 (OAC 442:10-5-16(l)). A "free sample" to a licensed patient at a dispensary would therefore still have to be tested product transferred to a licensee — Verify whether OMMA treats a no-charge transfer to a patient as a "sale" for tax/Metrc purposes before advising. Do not state that sampling is banned or allowed as a blanket rule.
  • Giveaways / promotions / discounts: no OMMA rule banning discounts, loyalty programmes or first-time-patient deals was located in this run, and secondary market listings routinely show dispensary deals, bulk discounts and loyalty points (labelled secondary, not law). The binding advertising limits are in OAC 442:10-5-16 and OAC 442:10-7-3:
  • OAC 442:10-5-16(e): no commercial licensee shall engage in advertising prohibited under OAC 442:10-7-3.
  • OAC 442:10-5-16(f): no commercial licensee shall sell or offer to sell by means of any advertisement or promotion that includes any statement, representation, symbol, depiction or reference, directly or indirectly, which would reasonably be expected to induce minors to purchase or consume marijuana or medical marijuana products.
  • Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/oklahoma/Okla-Admin-Code-SS-442-10-5-16 (effective 14 Sept 2025, Cornell) — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • OAC 442:10-7-3 (advertising) full text was not opened in this run — Verify before quoting any advertising placement, sponsorship or social-media rule. Do not import another state's advertising rules.
  • Other prohibited acts relevant to promotions (OAC 442:10-5-16, Cornell, eff. 14 Sept 2025): (a) no consumption of alcohol or smoking/vaping of medical marijuana on licensed premises (except a residence-licensee only in non-business areas); (b) no employment of any person under 18; (c) no delivery of medical marijuana to licensed patients or caregivers (see Run 1 Part 1 delivery/curbside — delivery is prohibited, not merely restricted); (d) no physician located/office/recommendations/medical services at the same physical address as a dispensary; (j) no licensed grower shall possess, sell or transfer medical marijuana products (growers sell flower/pre-rolls/kief only, §11.7 note: growers may package and sell non-infused pre-rolls and kief under (r)); (q) no alcoholic beverage infused with medical marijuana; (s) dispensaries shall not package or alter packaging/labelling except to package/sell non-infused pre-rolled marijuana and other stated exceptions (full (s) list truncated — Verify).
  • Source: same Cornell § 5-16 page — accessed 2026-10-30.

11.8 Drug testing, background checks and employee credential rules

  • Employee credentials — 63 O.S. § 427.14b (SB 1704 (2022), Justia 2025 reproduction): "Beginning January 1, 2024, the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority shall require employees of a medical marijuana business licensee to apply for and receive a credential authorizing the employee to work in a licensed medical marijuana business." OMMA may contract third-party vendors for credentialing; the vendor conducts background checks and verifies eligibility. On successful completion of the national fingerprint-based background check conducted by OSBI within 30 days before the application, completion of the educational training required, and verification of eligibility, OMMA shall issue the credential. "Beginning January 1, 2027, in order to receive an employee credential, all employees of a licensed medical marijuana business shall annually complete an educational training course provided by or approved by the Authority" (training may include state statutes/rules, patient privacy, safe handling/storage), with proof of completion submitted in the credential application. Applications may only be rejected/denied for failure to meet Patient Protection Act or OMMA rule standards.
  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-427-14b/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • OMMA credentialing page (official): renewal application window opened 1 Jan 2025; credentials valid for one year after approval; applicant must provide an OSBI name-based background check dated within 30 days of submission establishing no disqualifying conviction, and an Attestation Regarding National Background Check. "Employee" is defined at OAC 442:10-5-1.1(13). Secondary summaries add a $30 credential fee and an 18-year minimum age for facility work (OAC 442:10-5-16(b) confirms no commercial licensee shall employ any person under 18) — the $30 fee and the OSBI $15 name-check fee are secondary, Verify against OMMA's current fee schedule/portal before quoting them as official fees. The 2025 OMMA rule impact statement notes 24,427 credentialled employees in Oklahoma and an FBI background-check cost set in 74 O.S. § 150.9 at $41, with HB 2807 (2025) updating statutory language needed for FBI approval of the national fingerprint-based check (OAC 442:10-5-1.1; 63 O.S. § 427.28).
  • [Audit correction] The $30 OMMA credential fee is CONFIRMED from OMMA's official employee-credentialing page; only the $15 OSBI name-check fee remains Verify (OSBI fee schedule not opened). Source: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/employee-credentialing.html
  • Sources: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/employee-credentialing.html ; https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/omma/content/rulemaking-process/rules/2025-12-15/Chapter%2010%20Rule%20Impact%20Statement.pdf — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Owner/officer background checks: commercial applicants and specified individuals must undergo a state criminal history background check within 30 days of application (OAC 442:10-1-5, Run 1 Part 4); felony bars — nonviolent felony 2 years, other felony 5 years (Run 1). National fingerprint-based checks are being implemented via HB 2807 / § 427.28 (see above) — Verify whether the national fingerprint check is fully operational for all credential types on 30 Oct 2026, as the impact statement describes it as language "necessary for OMMA to secure approval from the FBI," which suggests a transition, not a completed rollout.
  • Drug testing of employees — this is the § 427.8 / HB 3127 employment regime, covered in Run 1 Part 1 §1.8 and summarised in the consistency lock above. In brief, on 30 Oct 2026 the pre-HB 3127 § 427.8 text still governs (no action solely on status or solely on a positive test, with safety-sensitive and at-work-use exceptions under 40 O.S. § 551 et seq.); from 1 Nov 2026 HB 3127 replaces the employer-designated safety-sensitive category with a duty-list only, mandates zero-tolerance for safety-sensitive roles, and allows action on a positive test under any compliant written policy, while status protection survives. Do not apply the HB 3127 text to conduct before 1 Nov 2026.

11.9 Research and university cannabis and hemp licences

  • OMMA research facility licence — 63 O.S. § 427.19 et seq.; OAC 442:10 Subchapter 4: authorises the licensee to grow, cultivate, possess and transfer to other licensed research facilities and licensed testing laboratories, by sale or donation, marijuana for the limited research purposes approved in the application. Every applicant must supply a project description. Biomedical and clinical research subject to federal regulations and institutional oversight is NOT subject to OMMA licensure or regulations. Research applicants using public funds or working with public institutions must provide information/documentation of their involvement and meet additional criteria; if the research includes a public institution or public money, OMMA shall review any reports to determine if the research continues to meet qualifications. Licence valid one year; nonrefundable fee $500 plus $13.30 card processing fee; OMMA processes commercial applications within 90 business days. Research licences are valid for a single location; a multi-location project needs a separate licence per location. The 75% residency test does not apply to public-institution or Oklahoma non-profit applicants (§11.2.3). Applicants must attest the premises are not on tribal lands, attest the project does not involve biomedical/clinical research subject to federal oversight, attest to 45 CFR Part 46 (Protection of Human Subjects) adherence, and pledge not to divert marijuana to any person/entity not lawfully entitled to possess it.
  • Sources: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/businesses/commercial-licenses/research-license.html ; https://regulations.justia.com/states/oklahoma/title-442/chapter-10/subchapter-4/section-442-10-4-3-d-1/ — accessed 2026-10-30.

None of these was confirmed from an OMMA, OSU, OU or Langston official page in this run. Do not present any named university as holding an OMMA research licence, or as running an OMMA-funded project, until an official source is opened. The correct official follow-ups are: OMMA research licence page / OMMA Verify (single-licence), OSU and OU research offices, Langston University news, and NIDA grant records.

PART 12 — CONSUMER AND SOCIAL RULES

12.1 Paraphernalia and smoke shop rules

  • Statute — 63 O.S. § 2-405 (Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Act, Prohibited Acts E — Penalties), Justia 2016 reproduction (last amendment noted: Laws 2004, c. 301 and c. 396, eff. 1 Nov 2004 — Verify current text on OSCN, as the 2016 reproduction may not reflect later amendments):
  • (B) "No person shall use drug paraphernalia to plant, propagate, cultivate, grow, harvest, manufacture, compound, convert, produce, process, prepare, test, analyze, pack, repack, store, contain, conceal, inject, ingest, inhale or otherwise introduce into the human body a controlled dangerous substance in violation of the Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Act, except those persons holding an unrevoked license in the professions of podiatry, dentistry, medicine, nursing, optometry, osteopathy, veterinary medicine or pharmacy."
  • (C) "No person shall deliver, sell, possess or manufacture drug paraphernalia knowing, or under circumstances where one reasonably should know, that it will be used [for the same purposes] in violation of the [Act]."
  • (D) Any person 18 or over who violates (C) by delivering/selling paraphernalia to a person under 18 is guilty of a felony.
  • (E) Violation of (A), (B) or (C) is a misdemeanour: first offence up to 1 year in county jail and/or fine up to $1,000; second offence (secondary summaries) up to 1 year and/or fine up to $5,000 — Verify the second-offence fine against current § 2-405(E)(2) before quoting it.
  • Definition (secondary summary of § 2-101): paraphernalia includes metal, wooden, acrylic, glass, stone, plastic or ceramic pipes with or without screens, water pipes, carburetion tubes/devices, smoking/carburetion masks, roach clips, miniature cocaine spoons/vials, chamber/carburetor/electric/air-driven pipes, chillums, bongs, ice pipes/chillers; it does not include separation gins for tea/spice, clamps for electrical equipment, water pipes designed for ornamentation, or pipes designed for smoking tobacco. The definition turns on "used or intended for use" — see Lady Ann's Oddities, Inc. v. MacY, 519 F. Supp. 1140 (W.D. Okla. 23 July 1981), a due-process challenge to the 1981 paraphernalia act (labelled as a court opinion, not statute).
  • Sources: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/2016/title-63/section-63-2-405/ ; https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/FSupp/519/1140/1427325/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Interaction with medical use: § 2-405(B) by its terms prohibits use "in violation of" the UCDSA. Licensed patient use within § 420 limits is not a UCDSA violation, so patient possession of a pipe/bong for licensed medical use is not, on the statute's face, a § 2-405 offence — but no OMMA or court source was located in this run expressly holding that patient paraphernalia is exempt, and the professional-licence exception in (B) does not mention patients. Verify before advising a patient that paraphernalia possession is lawful. Non-patient possession of paraphernalia intended for unlawful marijuana use remains a misdemeanour under (B)/(E).
  • Smoke shops: no Oklahoma smoke-shop licence, registration or zoning regime specific to paraphernalia/hemp retail was located in this run. Smoke shops selling only tobacco pipes / ornamental water pipes fall outside the § 2-405 definition on its face (see exclusions above); a shop that sells, delivers or possesses paraphernalia knowing/reasonably should know it will be used in violation of the UCDSA commits (C). Whether any city (e.g. Oklahoma City, Tulsa) imposes a local smoke-shop permit is Unavailable in this run — Run 1 Part 3 found no consolidated local list. Do not state that smoke shops are "licensed by OMMA" — they are not OMMA licensees unless they also hold a dispensary licence.

12.3 THC driving limits and impairment testing

  • No THC nanogram threshold in Oklahoma — but § 11-902(A)(3) contains an any-amount Schedule I prong (CORRECTED heading, audit: the original heading contradicted the verbatim (A)(3) text quoted in this section). The statute is 47 O.S. § 11-902. Verbatim (A) (Justia 2025 reproduction, § 47-11-902v3):

    "A. It is unlawful and punishable as provided in this section for any person to drive, operate, or be in actual physical control of a motor vehicle within this state, whether upon public roads, highways, streets, turnpikes, other public places or upon any private road, street, alley, or lane which provides access to one or more single or multi-family dwellings, who: 1. Has a blood or breath alcohol concentration, as defined in Section 756 of this title, of eight-hundredths (0.08) or more at the time of a test of such person's blood or breath; 2. Is under the influence of alcohol; 3. Has any amount of a Schedule I chemical or controlled substance, as defined in Section 2-204 of Title 63 of the Oklahoma Statutes, or one of its metabolites or analogs in the person's blood, saliva, urine or any other bodily fluid at the time of a test …; 4. Is under the influence of any intoxicating substance other than alcohol which may render such person incapable of safely driving or operating a motor vehicle; or 5. Is under the combined influence of alcohol and any other intoxicating substance which may render such person incapable of safely driving or operating a motor vehicle."

  • (B) "The fact that any person charged with a violation of this section is or has been lawfully entitled to use alcohol or a controlled dangerous substance or any other intoxicating substance shall not constitute a defense against any charge of violating this section." A medical licence is therefore not a defence to a DUI charge.
  • First offence (misdemeanour): assessment/evaluation and follow recommendations, jail 10 days to 1 year, fine up to $1,000 (§ 11-902(C)(1) as reproduced).
  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-47/section-47-11-902v3/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Tension to flag, not resolve: paragraph (A)(3) on its face criminalises driving with "any amount" of a Schedule I substance or metabolite in blood/saliva/urine, which would be a per se rule for marijuana while it is Schedule I under state law — yet secondary legal guides state that mere presence of THC/metabolites alone does not prove impairment and that prosecutors must prove impairment under (A)(4), relying on officer observation, field sobriety tests and Drug Recognition Expert evaluations followed by blood/urine testing. How Oklahoma courts reconcile (A)(3) with (A)(4), and what effect the federal Schedule III move for state-licensed medical marijuana (28 Apr 2026) and SB 1257's state Schedule I move (eff. 1 Nov 2026, Run 1) have on (A)(3)'s reference to § 2-204, is Verify against current case law and the current § 2-204 schedule — do not state either "no per se limit" or "any amount is per se" without that qualification. The safe summary is: no THC nanogram threshold exists; the statute contains both an "any amount of Schedule I" prong and an impairment prong, and their interaction is unresolved in this run.
  • [Audit correction] PARTLY RESOLVED (audit): § 11-902(A)(3) references § 2-204 of Title 63, the STATE schedule. SB 1257 (signed 20 May 2026, eff. 1 Nov 2026) adds tetrahydrocannabinols to state Schedule I (dronabinol only remains in Schedule III), so from 1 Nov 2026 the state prong reaches THC as state Schedule I regardless of the federal Schedule III move for state-licensed medical marijuana. Any OMMA-licensee exception to (A)(3) remains Verify (no case law located).
  • Sources (secondary, labelled, for the impairment-evidence point only): https://jpcannonlawfirm.com/2026/02/can-you-get-a-dui-with-a-medical-marijuana-card-in-oklahoma/ ; https://legalclarity.org/is-weed-legal-in-oklahoma-laws-and-regulations-explained/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Labelling overlay: SB 518 (2025) requires an additional warning label stating it is illegal to drive while under the influence of marijuana or marijuana products (OMMA 2025 rule impact statement, OAC 442:10-5-8(d)(7) / 442:10-7-1(d)(2)) — Verify the rule's effective date and whether it is in force on 30 Oct 2026, as the impact statement is a rulemaking document, not the final rule.
  • [Audit correction] CORRECTED TO IN FORCE: SB 518 became law without the Governor's signature 21 May 2025; OMMA's 31 Oct 2025 release states the driving warning is required from 1 Nov 2025 for products sold/transferred to a dispensary on/after that date. Source: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/about/news/2025/legislative-updates-new-labeling-requirements-patient-license-barcode-pre-packaging.html
  • Implied consent / refusal: secondary guides state refusal of a breath/blood test triggers automatic licence revocation (180 days first refusal, 1 year second within 10 years, 2 years third, plus Impaired Driver Accountability Program before reinstatement) — labelled secondary, Verify against 47 O.S. §§ 753–754 before quoting refusal periods, as this run did not open those sections.
  • Note on 2025–2026 DUI rewrites: secondary guides report SB 54 (Nov 2025) and HB 2104 (Jan 2026) rewrote parts of the DUI framework (aggravated DUI at 0.15% BAC, felony classes). Those changes concern alcohol BAC thresholds and are not stated here as changing the THC prongs — Verify the current § 11-902 text on OSCN before advising on any DUI penalty, as the Justia "v3" reproduction may predate the 2025–2026 amendments.

12.4 Expungement and record clearing for marijuana offences (SQ 780, SQ 805, and the general statute)

  • SQ 780 (2016) — passed, and its effect: SQ 780 reclassified certain non-violent drug and property crimes from felonies to misdemeanours, including simple drug possession (maximum 1 year in prison / $1,000 fine as a misdemeanour). It was not retroactive as passed — people already convicted got no relief from SQ 780 alone. HB 1269 (2019, signed May 2019) made SQ 780 retroactive in part: it instructs the state to identify and resentence people in prison for felony drug possession (up to ~800 people serving simple possession charges were reported eligible for release, secondary press report), and it added an expungement category (see below). People convicted of other offences in addition to drug possession, and people convicted of theft, must file a commutation petition to be considered (secondary summary — Verify against HB 1269 enrolled text).
  • Sources (secondary, labelled, for SQ 780/HB 1269 narrative): https://boltsmag.org/three-states-reform-drug-laws-oklahoma-colorado-illinois/ ; https://www.fff.org/explore-freedom/article/oklahoma-frees-some-of-its-political-prisoners/ — accessed 2026-10-30. Verify SQ 780's certified vote and HB 1269's chapter number against the State Election Board / oklegislature.gov before citing them as official results.
  • SQ 805 (2020) — FAILED, do not present as law: SQ 805, the Criminal History in Sentencing and Sentence Modification Initiative, was on the ballot 3 Nov 2020 and was defeated: Yes 38.92% (588,280 votes), No 61.08% (923,328 votes), total 1,511,608, results officially certified (Ballotpedia relay of certified results — Verify against the State Election Board canvass before citing as official). It would have prohibited using past non-violent felony convictions to enhance a sentence and provided sentence modifications for eligible people; it would not have applied to anyone ever convicted of a violent felony. Its failure means Oklahoma has no SQ 805 sentence-modification or enhancement-ban regime.
  • Source: https://ballotpedia.org/Oklahoma_State_Question_805,Criminal_History_in_Sentencing_and_Sentence_Modification_Initiative(2020 — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • General expungement statute — 22 O.S. § 18 (petition-based, not automatic for convictions): categories most relevant to marijuana offences (secondary summaries of § 18, with waiting periods that conflict between summaries and must be verified against current § 18 text — do not quote a single waiting period as settled):
  • Acquittal / not guilty, factual innocence (DNA / governor's pardon on factual innocence), arrest with no charges filed and statute of limitations expired, charges dismissed with no conviction and no pending charges and limitations expired or prosecutor confirms no refiling — petition available on those events.
  • Misdemeanour charge dismissed after successful deferred sentence: National Reentry Resource Center summary states 1 year after dismissal, no prior felony, no pending charges, under § 18(A)(8); a law-firm summary states 2 years for the same category and 5 years in another passage. Conflict — Verify against current § 18(A)(8).
  • Nonviolent felony charge dismissed after successful deferred sentence: NRRC states 5 years after dismissal, no prior felony, no pending charges, under § 18(A)(9); a law-firm summary states 10 years for nonviolent felony deferred dismissals and 10 years after a nonviolent felony conviction with a full pardon. Conflict — Verify against current § 18(A)(9) and § 18(A)(10)–(12).
  • Misdemeanour conviction: fine-only sentence under $500/$501 with no jail/suspended sentence, fine paid, no felony convictions, no pending charges — petition with no mandatory waiting period (law-firm summary — Verify); sentence involving jail, suspended sentence or fine over $500 — 5 years after end of sentence (law-firm summary — Verify).
  • HB 1269 category: a person convicted of a nonviolent felony subsequently reclassified as a misdemeanour under Oklahoma law may seek expungement if not currently serving a sentence in Oklahoma or another state, at least 30 days have passed since completion/commutation, restitution is paid in full, and any court-ordered treatment programme has been successfully completed (including a programme initially failed then later completed) — with a Pardon and Parole Board role (secondary summary of HB 1269 — Verify against enrolled HB 1269 / current § 18).
  • Offences in 57 O.S. § 571 (violent felonies) are ineligible for expungement (NRRC summary).
  • Sources (secondary, labelled): https://nationalreentryresourcecenter.org/cleanslate/compare-records-clearance-policies?page=119 ; https://www.oklahomalegalgroup.com/news/clearing-your-osbi-record ; https://www.cwilliamslegal.com/the-expungement-process-in-oklahoma/ — accessed 2026-10-30. A secondary "automatic expungement" claim (ExpungeMap: "Automatic for acquittals") is NOT adopted — § 18 is a petition process (court filing, OSBI criminal history report, $150 OSBI processing fee on grant per law-firm summary — Verify fees against current OSBI schedule).
  • No marijuana-specific automatic expungement / mass-clearing programme was located in this run. In particular, SQ 788 itself did not create an expungement programme, and no post-2018 Oklahoma law was found automatically clearing pre-2018 marijuana convictions. Any "140,000 expungements" type total that appears in other states' dossiers is not an Oklahoma figure and is not stated here. Unavailable: a dated official total of marijuana-related expungements granted in Oklahoma.
  • DUI expungement: DUI is a separate offence under 47 O.S. § 11-902 (§12.3); whether a DUI conviction is expungeable under § 18, and on what waiting period, is Verify — the 2001 SB 1646 engrossed bill that would have created a § 18a DUI/drug expungement route (3 years drug/alcohol-free, treatment, random testing for 1 year) is an old bill text, not current law, and is not presented as such.
  • Source (old bill, labelled not law): http://www.oklegislature.gov/cf_pdf/2001-02%20ENGR/sb/sb1646%20engr.pdf — accessed 2026-10-30.

12.5 Consumption lounges and events

  • No consumption-lounge licence exists in Oklahoma. The binding rules point the other way:
  • OAC 442:10-5-16(a): "No commercial licensee shall allow the consumption of alcohol or the smoking or vaping of medical marijuana or medical marijuana products on the licensed premises, except that if the licensed premises is a residence, a commercial licensee shall only be prohibited from consuming alcohol or the smoking or vaping of medical marijuana in areas of the licensed premises where operations of the business are conducted." A dispensary or other commercial premises therefore cannot operate as a smoking lounge.
  • OAC 442:10-2-11 / 63 O.S. § 427.8(L) (OMMA patient guidance): smoking and vaping medical marijuana outdoors in public (or indoors at a workplace) is subject to the same state laws as smoking tobacco — i.e. Oklahoma's tobacco smoking restrictions apply by analogy, not a cannabis-specific public-consumption permission.
  • Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/oklahoma/Okla-Admin-Code-SS-442-10-5-16 ; https://oklahoma.gov/omma/patients-caregivers/patient-rights-and-responsibilities.html — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Public consumption penalties: Run 1 Part 1 §1.3 covered public consumption; the public-consumption / open-container rule number was listed as Verify in Run 1 (OAC 442:10-2-11 is the OMMA guidance citation for smoking/vaping, but a standalone "public consumption" offence with a stated penalty was not located in this run either — Verify before stating a fine/jail term for public use).
  • Events: no Oklahoma consumption event licence was located. Industry events in Run 1 Part 6 (Cowboy Cup at Rocklahoma, Pryor, 4–6 Sept 2026; Cowboy Cup 2025, Tulsa Expo Square, 13–14 Dec 2025) are trade/competition events, not licensed consumption lounges, and no confirmed upcoming Oklahoma expo was located in Run 1. Whether any event permits on-site consumption under a private-property exception is Unavailable — do not state that consumption is allowed at any named event without an OMMA or event-organiser source.

12.6 Cannabis tourism and out-of-state patient rules

  • Out-of-state patients may buy in Oklahoma, but only on a temporary licence (Run 1 Part 1, repeated here): temporary out-of-state patient licence — 30 days, $100, renewable by fresh application, only for holders of a licence/card from another state's regulated programme. Short-term licences (60 days) are a separate category in Run 1 — do not conflate the two. Temporary licence holders are subject to the same § 420(A) possession limits as Oklahoma patients while in Oklahoma.
  • Tourism: no Oklahoma cannabis-tourism programme, visitor licence, or tourism-specific rule was located. Non-patients (including tourists from Texas, Kansas, Arkansas, Missouri and New Mexico, and from any other state) may not lawfully purchase medical marijuana in Oklahoma without a temporary licence, and non-medical possession remains unlawful (Run 1 Part 1: § 420(B) fine-only misdemeanour for up to 1.5 oz claimed for medical need without a licence; larger/ordinary non-patient possession under the UCDSA — see Run 1 §1.3 for amounts). Unavailable (official): any official figure for out-of-state patient share of sales or for tourism-driven sales (Run 1 Part 6).
  • Interstate purchase by Oklahoma patients elsewhere: no Oklahoma rule authorises an Oklahoma patient to purchase in another state; that depends on the other state's law (and, for neighbouring states, on their medical/adult-use status — outside this Part's scope except that Run 1 Part 10, in Run 2, will address interstate issues in full). Do not state that Oklahoma licences are honoured in Texas, Kansas, Arkansas, Missouri or New Mexico — none of those states' reciprocity rules was confirmed in this run.

12.7 Landlord and tenant rules, including patient protections

  • Anti-discrimination — 63 O.S. § 425(A) (verbatim, Justia 2024 reproduction):

    "No school or landlord may refuse to enroll or lease to and may not otherwise penalize a person solely for his or her status as a licensed medical marijuana patient, unless failing to do so would cause the school or landlord the potential to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or regulations."

  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-425v1/ — accessed 2026-10-30. Note the citation trap: § 425 is the discrimination / school-buffer section in the Justia "v1" reproduction; Run 1 corrected the school buffer citation to § 421 / OAC 442:10-5-3 for dispensary/grower location purposes — the two provisions are different paragraphs of related sections and must not be conflated. Verify the current § 425 / § 421 numbering on OSCN before citing either in a filing.
  • Property-owner smoking ban — 63 O.S. § 427.8(C) (verbatim, Justia 2025 reproduction):

    "Nothing in this act or Section 420 et seq. of Title 63 of the Oklahoma Statutes shall prohibit a residential or commercial property or business owner from prohibiting the consumption of medical marijuana or medical marijuana product by smoke or vaporization on the premises, within the structures of the premises or within ten (10) feet of the entryway to the premises. However, a medical marijuana patient shall not be denied the right to consume or use other medical marijuana products which are otherwise legal and do not involve the smoking or vaporization of cannabis when lawfully recommended pursuant to Section 420 of Title 63 of the Oklahoma Statutes."

  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-427-8/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Practical reading (statute text, not advice): a landlord may not refuse to lease / penalise solely for patient status (subject to the federal-benefit exception), but may prohibit smoking/vaping on the premises, in structures, and within 10 feet of an entryway, while non-smoked/non-vaped products cannot be denied on that basis. A lease that bans all cannabis use, including edibles/tinctures, would be in tension with the second sentence — Verify against case law, as no Oklahoma court decision on a lease ban was located in this run.
  • Home grow and tenancy: patient home grow requires property-owner written permission if the patient does not own the property (§ 427.12(A), §11.3) — a tenant without written permission may not home-grow, even though the landlord may not refuse to lease solely for patient status. The two rules operate together; neither overrides the other on the statute's face.
  • Municipal/county limits: 63 O.S. § 427.8(B) — municipal/county bodies may not enact medical marijuana guidelines that restrict/interfere with a licensed patient's/caregiver's rights to possess, purchase, cultivate or transport within legal limits, or require additional patient/caregiver permits/licences beyond state licences. This constrains government action, not private landlords (who are governed by § 425(A) / § 427.8(C) above).
  • Eviction / lease termination for unlawful use: no cannabis-specific eviction statute was located; general Oklahoma landlord-tenant law (41 O.S.) and the lease terms govern, subject to § 425(A). Verify before advising on eviction for licensed-patient use vs unlawful use.
  • Federally assisted housing: the § 425(A) federal-benefit exception ("unless failing to do so would cause … the potential to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law") is the hook landlords in federally assisted housing invoke; no Oklahoma guidance quantifying that exception was located — Verify against HUD guidance and the specific housing programme before advising.

12.8 Gun ownership conflicts for patients

  • State protection — 63 O.S. § 427.8(E) (verbatim, Justia 2025 reproduction):

    "A medical marijuana patient or caregiver licensee shall not be denied the right to own, purchase or possess a firearm, ammunition, or firearm accessories based solely on his or her status as a medical marijuana patient or caregiver licensee. No state or local agency, municipal or county governing authority shall restrict, revoke, suspend or otherwise infringe upon the right of a person to own, purchase or possess a firearm, ammunition, or firearm accessories or any related firearms license or certification based solely on their status as a medical marijuana patient or caregiver licensee."

  • Related: § 425(E) — no licensed patient may unduly be withheld from holding a state-issued licence by virtue of being a licensed patient, including a concealed carry permit. Oklahoma is a permitless-carry state (since 2019, secondary summary) — no permit is generally required to openly or concealed-carry a handgun — but that does not remove the federal conflict below.
  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-427-8/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Federal conflict — 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3): it is unlawful for any person who is an "unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance" to possess firearms or ammunition. ATF Form 4473, Question 21.e, asks whether the buyer is an unlawful user of or addicted to marijuana or any depressant, stimulant, narcotic drug or other controlled substance. Secondary guides state the ATF treats any marijuana user as an unlawful user regardless of state authorisation, and that answering "no" while holding a medical card risks a false-statement charge. Whether the federal Schedule III move for state-licensed medical marijuana (28 Apr 2026, fixed baseline) changes the § 922(g)(3) analysis for Oklahoma medical patients is Verify — the fixed baseline states the Schedule III move and the § 280E change, but it does not state a firearms consequence, and no ATF guidance on Schedule III medical patients was located in this run. Do not state that Schedule III resolves the firearms conflict.
  • Sources (secondary, labelled, for the federal point): https://legalclarity.org/do-you-need-a-concealed-carry-permit-in-oklahoma/ ; https://legalclarity.org/wp-json/wp/v2/posts/351277 — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Practical limits in the state text itself: the state protection is "based solely on status" — it does not protect carrying/using a firearm while under the influence of medical marijuana (secondary summary — Verify against 21 O.S. § 1290.10 / Self-Defense Act preclusions), and safety-sensitive employment duties include "carrying a firearm" (§ 427.8(K) list, pre-HB 3127 text — see Run 1 §1.8 for the HB 3127 change from 1 Nov 2026).

12.9 Pet and veterinary products

  • No Oklahoma statute or OMMA rule specific to pet/veterinary cannabis or CBD products was located in this run. The relevant general points are:
  • CBD is not included in Oklahoma's state definition of "marijuana" (OSDE FAQ, 10 Sept 2018, non-binding guidance: "CBD … is not included in Oklahoma's state definition of 'marijuana.' It is therefore not subject to the same restrictions as medical marijuana. By definition, CBD can contain only up to a trace amount of THC") — that FAQ is about schools, not veterinary products, and is labelled non-binding in the document itself.
  • Source: https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OKSDE/bulletins/20b973d — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • OMMA patient guidance treats medical marijuana products like pharmacy products for child/pet safety: dispensaries must sell in packaging hard for a child under 5 to open (including re-sealed), products should be kept out of reach of children and pets, and stored in a safe/lock box (OMMA patient page, §11.3 cross-reference). No pet dosage, pet product licensing, or veterinary prescription rule was located.
  • Source: https://oklahoma.gov/omma/patients-caregivers/patient-rights-and-responsibilities.html — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Unavailable: whether a veterinarian may recommend/prescribe CBD or THC for animals in Oklahoma, whether pet CBD products are regulated by ODAFF, the State Board of Veterinary Medical Examiners, or OMMA, and any age/labelling rule for pet products. Do not state that pet CBD is "legal" or "illegal" in Oklahoma as a settled rule — the hemp definition (§ 2-3-402, Run 1) covers hemp derivatives generally, but no pet-specific application was confirmed. The professional-licence exception in § 2-405(B) lists veterinary medicine among professions whose unrevoked licensees are excepted from the paraphernalia prohibition — that is a paraphernalia exception, not a veterinary cannabis authorisation.

12.10 Medical marijuana in schools

  • Enrolment protection — 63 O.S. § 425(A) (verbatim in §12.7): no school may refuse to enroll or otherwise penalise a person solely for status as a licensed medical marijuana patient, unless doing so would cause the school the potential to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law/regulations.
  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-63/section-63-425v1/ — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Administration on school property — no Oklahoma law authorising student self-administration or staff administration on school property was located, and the official guidance says the opposite:
  • OSDE FAQ (10 Sept 2018, non-binding, general guidance, not legal advice): "Can a student self-administer medical marijuana on school property? No. There is not a current Oklahoma law authorizing a student to use, possess and/or self-administer medical marijuana on school property. Oklahoma laws authorizing students to self-administer medication are limited to sunscreen, inhaled asthma medication and anaphylaxis medication. See 70 O.S. §§ 1-116.2 – 1-116.3." "Can school personnel, including but not limited to a school nurse, possess (on behalf of) and/or administer medical marijuana to a student?" — the FAQ's answer (truncated in the copy opened) is in the same "No" direction; the full answer must be opened before quoting it verbatim — Verify the full Q10 answer.
  • Source: https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/OKSDE/bulletins/20b973d — accessed 2026-10-30.
  • Caveat: the OSDE FAQ is from September 2018, under the former OAC 310:681 rules, and states it is non-binding and does not replace a district's retained counsel. Whether any later statute, OMMA rule or OSDE guidance has changed the school-administration position since 2018 is Verify — do not present the 2018 FAQ as current law without that check. No later school-administration statute was located in this run.
  • School discipline / possession on school property: a student patient licence does not, on the FAQ's reasoning, authorise possession/use on school property; general school discipline and drug-free-school-zone law would apply, but no specific penalty for student possession on school property was located in this run — Verify against 70 O.S. and the district's policy before advising.
  • School location buffer (for businesses, not students): dispensary location prohibited within 1,000 feet of a school entrance (§ 425(G) / § 421, Run 1 — measurement conflict flagged in Run 1: door-to-door vs property-line-to-perimeter-wall). That buffer is a business-location rule, not a student-use rule, and must not be cited as the school-administration rule.
  • Custody / medical care protections that touch schools indirectly: § 425(C) — authorised patient use is equivalent to use of any other medication under a physician's direction for medical-care purposes including organ transplants, and does not disqualify a patient from medical care; § 425(D) — no denial of custody/visitation/parenting time and no presumption of neglect/child endangerment for conduct allowed under the law, unless the person's behaviour creates an unreasonable danger to the minor child. These are quoted from the Justia 2024 § 425 reproduction — Verify current numbering on OSCN (see §12.7 citation trap).

Research Notes — Combined, Both Runs

Every gap, unverified item, conflicting figure and recommended follow-up from Run 1 (Parts 0–6) and Run 2 (Parts 7–12). The full per-part Verify registers are in the underlying track files; this section consolidates them and resolves what Run 2 resolved. Nothing here is presented as settled law unless the underlying section says so.

A. Resolved in Run 2 (corrections to Run 1)

  • Official Oklahoma hemp response — RESOLVED, with limits. ODAFF Hemp Clarification Letter, 16 Jan 2026: Total THC = THC + 87.7% THCA; PL 119-37 final products ≤0.4 mg/container — CORRECTED PER FEDERAL BASELINE (audit): the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg/container cap apply AFTER 11 Dec 2026 (PL 119-103 §2019 staging), not from 12 Nov 2026 as stated in the letter; 12 Nov 2026 is only the staged start for non-naturally-produced/synthesised cannabinoid exclusions; delta-8 and similar isomers expressly excluded. Still Verify: PL 119-103 §2019 staging to 11 Dec 2026, and the letter's weight vs statute/rule. Source: https://ag.ok.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/2026-Hemp-Clarification-Letter.pdf
  • THCA 0.877 factor — CONFIRMED for ODAFF's stated method (letter + grower form postdecarboxylation definition). Whether OAC 35:30-24-2 itself prints 0.877 was not directly opened — Verify.
  • HB 3770 / §420A hemp-THC-to-dispensaries claim — REJECTED. Legislature Subject Index: HB 3770 is a 2026 Rules (H) bill, not a 2022 enacted confinement law. Run 1's “no confining statute found” stands, now strengthened by 63 O.S. §1-1431(C) licence-free retail sale of legally grown hemp.
  • SB 1257 vs §1-1431(C) interaction — UNRESOLVED / Verify. SB 1257 (eff. 1 Nov 2026) moves THC to state Schedule I, expressly including synthesised hemp THC; AG reported as saying OMMA licensees are unaffected. Interaction with federal Schedule III and with hemp retail law is Verify, not resolved.

B. Conflicting figures — not harmonised

  • Sales 2025: OMMA excise-implied retail (excise ÷ 7%) $647.2m vs Oklahoma Voice dashboard-based “over $670m retail / over $1.1bn wholesale in 2025”. The dashboard combines retail + wholesale; do not merge the two series. Follow-up: live-browser read of the NCS Analytics dashboard for monthly sales and county counts.
  • Edmond cannabis park price: 3275 E Waterloo Rd, Edmond — $2,395,000 (Apr 2026 brochure) vs $2,895,000 (Aug 2026 brochure), different cap rates/NOI. Status Verify.
  • Enforcement totals are separate series, never added: Run 1 secondary AG/OBN figures (2.4m+ plants / 295k+ lbs since 2021) vs OCTF Oct 2025 (>7,000 operations closed, 329,075 plants / 152,612 lbs / 26,520 lbs concentrate) vs OBN MET Aug 2026 (>2.5m plants / 300,000 lbs / 450+ arrests). OBN “1,200–1,350 grows” is a registrations denominator, not OMMA licences.
  • Licence-count snapshots differ by report date: Sep–Oct 2026 ranges (growers ~1,703–1,735, dispensaries ~1,259–1,295, processors ~557–574) reflect different OMMA table dates, not errors. Headline adopted: 1 Oct 2026 table only.
  • Excise apportionment: Justia 2025 text prints the FY2022 split (59.23% schools / 34.62% OMMA-as-division / 6.15% rehab) — historical text, not asserted as current. SB 18X (2023) two-fund structure (Medical Marijuana Tax Fund / OMMA Fund) flagged against it — current apportionment Verify against OTC/OMMA.
  • Expungement waiting periods conflict: misdemeanour deferred 1 year vs 2 years; nonviolent felony deferred 5 years vs 10 years — Verify current 22 O.S. §18(A)(8)–(12).
  • Price figures conflict: dashboard-derived $2.42/g (Sep 2026, Verify), OKC menu medians Oct 2026 (eighth ~$17, ounce ~$146, secondary sample), wholesale ~$1,100/lb June 2026 (secondary). A $345/$266 per-ounce secondary figure is inconsistent and not used. No official price series exists in extractable form.
  • Tribe count: 38 federally recognised tribes (brief) vs one secondary source saying 39 — Verify against BIA 91 FR 4102, 30 Jan 2026.
  • OMMA leadership after 30 Oct 2026: OMMA About page as opened lists Adria Berry; secondary Oct 2026 reporting says she steps down effective 30 Oct 2026 with Jason Yingling interim — holder after 30 Oct is Verify.

C. Do NOT present as law (proposed, failed, or unconfirmed enrolled status)

  • HB 3144 (2,550 grower cap) — House 82–15 / Senate 34–12 with amendments 29 Apr 2026, no governor's signature/chapter located.
  • HB 4454 enrolled mg cap — committee versions say 10 mg/serving (100 mg package dropped); Sept 2026 analysis of enrolled bill says no mg cap, labelling + shape bans only. Enrolled text must be opened.
  • SB 1242 grower bond — CORRECTED (audit): $100,000 appears only in the Senate-engrossed version; the House version deletes the bond and substitutes a $2,000 reclamation fee. Neither version is shown as enacted. OMMA page still says $50,000, which remains the confirmed figure.
  • HB 3143 transfer bar — REMOVED FROM THIS LIST (audit): HB 3143 was approved by the Governor 5 May 2026 and is enacted law, including its transfer restrictions (see §11.2.2).
  • HB 4248 hemp beverages only, 21+ — Senate floor/committee form, eff. 1 Nov 2026 if enacted; enrolled status Verify, not law.
  • [Audit correction] CORRECTED: HB 4248 is NOT law — fourth reading and signing rescinded 6 May 2026 after recall from enrollment (see §12.2).
  • SB 2053 local excise up to 10% — proposed only. HB 3347 (2022) / HB 2101 (2023) §280E decoupling — proposal versions only, no enacted act located.
  • SQ 805 — FAILED 3 Nov 2020 (Yes 38.92%, No 61.08%), not law. SQ 837 — never reached the ballot (172,993 signatures needed by 3 Nov 2025, withdrawn after falling short).
  • HB 3019 / SB 1581 (brief's hemp-THC candidates) — neither confirmed as enacted law. HB 4055 / HB 1711 / SB 801 utility water/electricity reporting — final codified status Verify.
  • Cherokee Nation employment-protection file 20-015 — marked “FOR DISCUSSION ONLY”, not enacted. DIAL-style proposals from other states are not Oklahoma law.

E. Sources and method

Official sources wherever possible: Oklahoma Statutes via oklegislature.gov/OSCN (Title 63, Title 2), Oklahoma Administrative Code (Titles 442, 35, 475), OMMA (omma.ok.gov / oklahoma.gov/omma), OBN/OBNDD, ODAFF (ag.ok.gov), Oklahoma Tax Commission, Attorney General, State Election Board, Oklahoma and federal court records, official tribal government sources and codes, official county/municipal websites and codes, USDA AMS. Secondary sources were used only for non-law facts (market figures, polling, events, listings) and are dated and marked as such in the sections. Where official sources gave different figures for the same thing, the most authoritative and most recent official figure was adopted and the others are listed above. Underlying tracks: part02.md, part34.md, part56.md, part78.md, part910.md, part1112.md in ~/workspace/research_notes/oklahoma-cannabis-hemp-run1/.
